# Preface

---

The more ancient a branch of knowledge or a race is, the more shrouded in darkness its earliest history remains. The ancient civilization of the Indo-Aryans—their knowledge, intellect, discernment, and the antiquity of their religious institutions—has been proved beyond dispute by numerous evidences. Even today, the <term>evolution</term><note>original: "vikash"; here referring to the unfolding or discovery of historical layers</note> of various archaeological elements before the public continues to be unanimously honored as a source of traditional pride. Nevertheless, a continuous and factual understanding of the ancient state of sciences, arts, and skills, and their gradual progress or decline, remains nearly impossible. In many instances, one must be satisfied with mere conjecture. As with other sciences, the history of <term>Astronomy</term><note>original: "Jyotish-shastra"; the traditional Indian science of celestial observation and time-keeping</note> suffers the same fate. This is because countless "jewels" among manuscripts can no longer be traced. Many that do exist in domestic or foreign royal libraries remain inaccessible to the general public. One gains only a nominal knowledge of them by scanning through vast catalogs.

The most ancient text of the Indo-Aryans is the <term>Rigveda</term><note>The oldest of the four Vedas, the foundational scriptures of Hinduism</note>. In the Vedas, the <term>Samhitas</term><note>The core ritual hymns of the Vedas</note>, and the <term>Aranyakas</term><note>"Forest Books" containing philosophical interpretations of rituals</note>, discussions of astronomy are found in the form of aphorisms as the context requires. Ancient and modern commentators have detailed these in various ways, and there has been no lack of arbitrary attempts to harmonize ancient and modern scientific thoughts. The primary objective of this was, and remains, to show that our ancestral sages and seers were <term>seers of the three periods of time</term><note>original: "Trikaldarshi"; those who can perceive the past, present, and future</note>;

<summary>This preface discusses the difficulty of reconstructing the history of ancient Indian sciences due to lost manuscripts and highlights the astronomical references found within the oldest Vedic texts.</summary>
<keywords>Indo-Aryans, Astronomy, Jyotish-shastra, Rigveda, Samhitas, Aranyakas, Vedic science, historiography</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between the Vedas and the specialized sciences, specifically transitioning into the history of Vedic astronomy.</meta>

<page-num>2</page-num>

Nothing was beyond their knowledge. And this is only right. The connection of the six <term>Vedangas</term><note>The "limbs" or auxiliary disciplines of the Vedas: phonetics, ritual, grammar, etymology, meter, and astronomy.</note> is the primary means of the Veda's very existence. However, it was not the intention of the ancient teachers to prove that all comprehensive knowledge and science originated solely from the Vedas; otherwise, they would not have initiated the creation of countless texts on individual subjects. In the present time, no further proof of this is required.

Aside from the Vedas themselves, an independent ancient text on <term>Jyotisha</term><note>Astronomy and astrology.</note> is famous by the name 'Vedanga Jyotisha.' For the performance of sacrifices and other rituals, it describes the determination of lunar days (<term>tithis</term>), festival times, and so on. Currently, three types of Vedanga Jyotisha are available: † one contains 36 verses and is related to the <term>Rigveda</term>; the second includes a commentary by Somakara, at the end of which is written, <insert>The Vedanga Jyotisha of the Yajurveda, composed by Shesha</insert>. This contains 43 verses. Among these, 30 verses from the Rigvedic Jyotisha are included, while the remaining 13 verses are new. Taking the 36 from the Rig-Jyotisha and the 13 from the Yaju, there are 49 verses in total. According to Somakara’s writings, his commented Jyotisha is considered to belong to the <term>Yajurveda</term>, and it was composed by Shesha. At its beginning, it is written:
-> "I shall proclaim the knowledge of time, as taught by the high-souled Lagadha." <-
<note>original: "कालज्ञानं प्रवक्ष्यामि लगधस्य महात्मनः"</note>

From this, it is known that Lagadha had written some work on astronomy, and the present Jyotisha was written based on that original. It appears that—just as the Panini grammar was created based on ancient Vedic grammar, and the Pingala manual of prosody was based on the foundations of Vedic meter—this Vedanga Jyotisha of the Mahatma Lagadha was composed upon the foundation of ancient Vedic astronomy. This is, in a sense, related to <term>Muhurta</term><note>The selection of auspicious moments for performing rituals or actions.</note>. It mentions seven planets and seven days of the week. The names of the twelve zodiac signs, such as Aries (<term>Mesha</term>), are not present. This should be known as the primary text on the subject of Muhurta.</margin>

Nothing was beyond their knowledge. This is indeed correct. The connection of the <term>Six Vedangas</term><note>The six auxiliary disciplines of Vedic study: phonetics, ritual, grammar, etymology, meter, and astronomy.</note> to the Veda is the primary means of its existence. However, it was not the intention of the ancient teachers to prove that all knowledge and science originated solely from the Veda; otherwise, the creation of countless texts on individual subjects would never have begun. In the present time, no further proof of this is required.

Apart from the Vedas, the independent ancient text of astronomy is famous by the name **"Vedanga Jyotisha."** For the performance of sacrifices and other rituals, it describes the <term>Tithi</term><note>A lunar day in the Hindu calendar.</note>, the timing of festivals, and so on. At this time, three types of Vedanga Jyotisha are available. † One contains 36 verses; this is related to the **Rigveda**. The second includes a commentary by Somakara; at its end is written, <note>original: "Shesha-krita Yajurvedanga-Jyotisham"</note> "The Yajurveda-Jyotisha composed by Shesha." This contains 43 verses. Within these, 30 verses from the Rigvedic Jyotisha are included, while the remaining 13 verses are new. Taking the 36 from the Rig-Jyotisha and the 13 from the Yaju, there are 49 verses in total. According to Somakara's writings, his commented astronomy text is considered to belong to the **Yajurveda**, and it is the work of Shesha. At its beginning is written, <note>original: "Kalajnanam pravakshyami lagadhasya mahatmanah"</note> "I shall proclaim the knowledge of time as taught by the high-souled Lagadha." From this, it is known that Lagadha had written some work on astronomy, and the present Jyotisha was written based on that original source. It appears that—just as the Panini grammar was created based on ancient Vedic grammar, and the Pingala manual of prosody was based on the foundations of Vedic meter—similarly, this Vedanga Jyotisha of the great soul Lagadha was composed upon the foundation of ancient Vedic astronomy. Lagadha or...

---

† The **Atharva-Jyotisha** is the third—in this, the Grandfather <note>Pitamaha, often referring to Brahma</note> gave instruction to Kashyapa. This is, in a way, related to <term>Muhurta</term><note>The selection of auspicious moments for performing rituals or actions.</note>. It mentions seven planets and seven days of the week. The names of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, such as Aries <note>Mesha</note>, are not present. This should be known as the primary text on the subject of Muhurta.

It highlights that while these sciences are rooted in the Vedas, they developed into independent specialized disciplines.</summary>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the authorship and textual corruption of the Vedanga Jyotisha, specifically focusing on the identity of the commentator Shesha and the history of modern scholarship on the text.</meta>

<page-num>3</page-num>

Who was Shesha? There is no actual evidence of this. The commentary of Somakara is also of two types—in the larger version, Somakara's name appears at the beginning and Shesha's at the end. In the smaller version, neither name is present. All the ancient manuscripts that have been found are in a severely degraded state, filled with omissions, errors, and variant readings. Due to numerous contradictions in the original commentary, both local and foreign mathematical scholars have long been distressed in their attempts to interpret its meaning. †

From the *Vedanga Jyotisha* <note>The "Vedanga Jyotisha" is one of the earliest known Indian texts on astronomy, dated to the first millennium BCE, used to determine the timing for Vedic rituals.</note> we learn—the Sun's northward journey <term>Uttarayana: the winter solstice</term> begins from the start of the Shravishtha (Dhanishtha) <note>The 23rd lunar mansion or nakshatra.</note> constellation, and the southward journey <term>Dakshinayana: the summer solstice</term> begins from the middle of the Ashlesha constellation.

---

† The late Honorable Shankar Balkrishna Dikshit of Poona wrote a very important historical book in Marathi titled *Bharatiya Jyotishshastra* <note>History of Indian Astronomy</note>. To date, such a book has not been written in any other language. In it, he demonstrated the interpretation and mathematical rationale of some verses of the *Vedanga Jyotisha* as the occasion arose, and Dr. Thibaut <note>George Thibaut (1848–1914), a German-British Indologist</note> of Benares also derived the rationale for several verses. However, the consistency of the entire text was not established—scholars untangled the meaning only as far as their individual insights allowed. This miserable state of "grinding the already ground" <note>A Sanskrit idiom (pishta-peshana) referring to repetitive, fruitless effort</note> persisted for years, and eventually, people fell silent. In 1907, Barhaspatya (Lala Chotelal, Executive Engineer, P.W.D., United Provinces), having collected the writings of old scholars and ancient books of the *Vedanga*, determined the correct readings and published his own English commentary with full mathematical proofs. He was completely successful in this task and received full credit. That commentary appeared in the *Hindustan Review* of Prayag and was also issued as a reprint; it caused a great sensation. Great scholars praised it. Immediately upon its publication, Shri Sudhakar Dwivedi also released the *Vedanga Jyotisha* along with his own "Sudhakar Commentary." While critiquing the explanations of the ancient commentators, Dikshit, Thibaut, and Barhaspatya, he became an independent commentator himself. At that time, a debate also took place between Dwivedi and Barhaspatya—articles were published, and a great spectacle unfolded. Articles were also published in the journal *Saraswati*.

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the evolution of the Indian calendar system, specifically focusing on the transition from the Vedic Samhita period to the Vedanga Jyotisha and eventually to the era of Varahamihira.</meta>

->( 4 )<-

began. This time of the northward and southward movement occurred in the months of Magha and Shravana. During the <term>Uttarayana</term><note>The six-month period of the sun's northward journey</note> and <term>Dakshinayana</term><note>The six-month period of the sun's southward journey</note>, the increase and decrease of the day was equal to one *prastha* <note>A traditional unit of volume</note> of water. In these two solstices, there was a difference of 6 *muhurtas* <note>A unit of time; 1 muhurta is approximately 48 minutes</note> in the measure of day and night. The beginning of the year was considered to be at the start of the *Dhanishtha* constellation, and so on. In earlier times, the year's beginning was sometimes counted from the vernal equinox and sometimes from the end of the sun's northward journey. Previously, the lunar month was counted from the full moon, but from the time of the <term>Vedanga Jyotisha</term><note>The "Science of Light," an auxiliary Vedic text focused on astronomy for ritual timing</note>, it began to be reckoned from the new moon. In the time of the <term>Taittiriya Samhita</term><note>A primary collection of Vedic hymns and rituals</note>, the year began with the full moon of Magha, but in the Vedanga Jyotisha, it began with the new moon of Magha. From these points, it is clear that the system of calculation prevalent in the Samhita period had changed by the time of the Vedanga Jyotisha. Subsequently, in the time of <term>Varahamihira</term><note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath</note> (the 5th century of the Shaka era), another change occurred, and it is that refined form which currently defines the nature of the *Panchang* <note>The traditional Hindu almanac</note>. Be that as it may. In reality, the Vedanga Jyotisha was not composed with the intention of providing a complete education in astronomy. Rather, it is merely for the performance of Vedic rituals; ❊ it provides only a rough description of necessary matters. To believe that this was the ultimate limit of our ancient Aryans' astronomical knowledge is a mere delusion. Acharya Varahamihira—

---

> * Several foreign scholars, upon seeing the ‘Vedanga Jyotisha,’ assumed that the ancient Aryans had no knowledge of astronomy beyond this. However, listen to what the purpose of the Vedanga Jyotisha is—in the words of <term>Max Müller</term><note>A famous 19th-century German-born philologist and Orientalist</note>:
> 
> ‘Nor is it the object of the small tract to teach astronomy. It has a practical object, which is to convey such knowledge of the heavenly bodies as is necessary for fixing the days and hours of the Vedic sacrifices.’ —History of Ancient Sanskrit Literature, 1859.

<summary>This page details the historical shifts in the Indian calendar, specifically the changing definitions of the New Year and lunar months between the Samhita and Vedanga periods. It argues that the Vedanga Jyotisha was a practical ritual manual rather than a comprehensive scientific treatise, supported by a quote from Max Müller.</summary>
<keywords>Vedanga Jyotisha, Varahamihira, Uttarayana, Dakshinayana, Max Müller, Taittiriya Samhita, Hindu Calendar, Vedic Astronomy</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the antiquity of Indian astronomical texts, specifically focusing on the Vedanga Jyotisha and the works of the sage Parashara.</meta>

<page-num>5</page-num>

He considered the <term>Vedanga Jyotisha</term> <note>The "limb of the Vedas" pertaining to astronomy/astrology, used to determine the timing for rituals.</note> to be very ancient. For this reason, while writing about the movement of the solstices in his *Brihat Samhita*, he stated—

> "The southward movement of the sun once began from the middle of the constellation Ashlesha, and the northward movement from the beginning of Dhanishtha.
> This was certainly the case at some time, as stated in the ancient scriptures." <note>original: 'आश्लेषार्द्धाद्दक्षिणमुत्तरमयनं रवेर्धनिष्ठाद्यम् । नूनं कदाचिदासीद्येनोक्तं पूर्वशास्त्रेषु ॥'</note>

In this verse, by using the phrase "ancient scriptures," he has recalled the *Vedanga Jyotisha* or perhaps the *Parashara Tantra*. In the work *Indian Astronomy*, the scholar Dikshit has written about the era of the Rig-Vedic and Yajur-Vedic astronomy using various arguments and evidence. It has been established as 1400 BCE. There are many controversies regarding its chronological determination. † The aforementioned *Parashara Tantra* is not currently available; a version has been found in some places, but it is a modern compilation because it contains a description of the precession of the equinoxes <note>original: अयनगति (ayanagati)</note>, which was unknown in this country even in the fifth century. How then can it be considered the original *Parashara Tantra*? Parashara was the father of <term>Krishna Dvaipayana Vyasa</term> <note>The traditional compiler of the Vedas and author of the Mahabharata.</note>. According to the <term>Nirukta</term> <note>An ancient treatise on etymology and lexicography.</note>, he was the son of Vashistha; however, according to the <term>Mahabharata</term> and the <term>Vishnu Purana</term>, he was the grandson of Vashistha and the son of Shakti. Some consider this Parashara to be the original author of the *Siddhantas* <note>Scientific astronomical treatises.</note>, but the *Siddhanta* created by the first sage, Brahma, is the origin of all astronomy. The <term>Brahma Siddhanta</term> is another name for the <term>Vedic Siddhanta</term>, because the Vedas are the creation of Brahma. Be that as it may, the *Parashara Siddhanta* is the name of the *Parashara Tantra* itself. In many places in the <term>Brihat Samhita</term>, the commentator <term>Bhattotpala</term> has cited the opinions of Parashara and Garga in his commentary. Both are very ancient. According to astronomical calculations, between the fifth and fourteenth centuries BCE—

Upon examining all these evidences, the *Brahma-Siddhanta* <note>The "Treatise of Brahma," considered one of the foundational texts of Indian astronomy</note> is understood to be the most ancient of all. The Vedas are the root of the entire science of astronomy <term>Jyotish-shastra: the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</term>, and they manifested from Brahma. This knowledge was gradually propagated under various names through a succession of disciples and grand-disciples. By relying on a single fundamental system and introducing refinements and changes alongside the growth of knowledge, many different systems originated over the course of time. This proposal will conclude after providing some specific details regarding these five systems.

**(1) Paitamaha-Siddhanta** — The *Paitamaha-Siddhanta* that Varahamihira <note>A 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath</note> compiled in the *Pancha-siddhantika* <note>The "Five Astronomical Treatises"</note> is very old. Dr. Thibaut <note>George Thibaut (1848–1914), a noted Indologist who translated many Sanskrit astronomical texts</note> considers it as ancient as the *Vedanga-Jyotisha*, *Garga-Samhita*, and *Surya-Prajnapti*. Instead of the 360-day year of the Vedic period, this system assumes a solar year of 366 days. It records the constellation Dhanishtha as the beginning of the zodiacal cycle and the maximum length of daylight as 18 *muhurtas* or 36 *dandas* <note>Traditional units of time; a danda is approximately 24 minutes</note>. However, it appears that Varahamihira did not find the original ancient treatise, but rather a later version of the *Paitamaha-Siddhanta* from the second Shaka era. He wrote five verses <term>Arya: a specific meter in Sanskrit poetry</term> regarding it, and there is no mention of planets other than the Sun and the Moon. According to previous writings, the mathematics of this system had become inaccurate by the teacher's time; it seems for this reason—

---

<margin>* This is the ancient astronomy of the Jains, similar to the *Vedanga-Jyotisha*. In this, there is the concept of two Suns, two Moons, and two zodiac cycles, which Bhaskaracharya refuted in the *Goladhyaya* <note>The "Chapter on the Celestial Sphere" from his major work, Siddhanta Shiromani</note>. Dr. Thibaut published the *Surya-Prajnapti* in the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal many years ago.</margin>

...has merely performed a salutation. However, the complete <term>planetary mathematics<note>original: "Grahaganita"; the mathematical calculations used to determine the positions and motions of celestial bodies.</note></term> certainly existed; otherwise, why would Aryabhata and Brahmagupta consider it the root of their own systems? The inaccuracies in the mathematics were well-known, which is why Brahmagupta explicitly wrote:

> "The planetary mathematics spoken by Brahma had, over a great length of time, become decayed. Therefore, it is now being clearly stated by Brahmagupta, the son of Jishnu. Having calculated the most accurate <term>corrections<note>original: "Beeja"; algebraic corrections applied to astronomical formulas to match observed reality.</note></term> using instruments such as the sighting-tube, the final determinations and predictions should be made from the planets thus corrected." <note>original: "Brahmoktam grahaganitam mahata kalena yatkhilibhutam..."</note>

From ancient times until today, four types of *Brahma-Siddhanta* have been known:
(1) That included within the *Pancha-Siddhantika*.
(2) That included within the *Vishnudharmottara Purana*.
(3) That included within the *Shakalya Samhita*. <margin>The catalog of Sanskrit manuscripts of the Bengal Asiatic Society mentions the name 'Shakalya Samhita'. Ranganatha Daivajna has quoted two or four verses from this Samhita in his commentary on the *Surya Siddhanta* (Chapter on Planetary Conjunctions, Verse 14). It contains 6 chapters and 764 verses. Brahma gave these instructions to Narada. Besides astronomical theory, it also covers <term>auspicious timing<note>original: "Muhurta"; the selection of the best time to perform a specific ritual or action.</note></term>, hence it was named a 'Samhita'. It is based on the *Pancha-Siddhantika*. Mr. Dixit determines its composition date to be around 743 Saka era (821 CE).</margin>
(4) Brahmagupta’s *Brahma-Sphuta-Siddhanta*.

Prithudaka Swami, the ancient commentator on the *Brahma-Siddhanta*, wrote that "the *Brahma-Siddhanta* within the *Vishnudharmottara Purana* is the original source for Brahmagupta." The system in this Purana is likely a reflection of the extremely ancient *Paitamaha Siddhanta*. It should be observed that the *Paitamaha Siddhanta*—which Brahma extracted from the Vedas—became the root for the systems of Aryabhata, Brahmagupta, and finally Bhaskara. In this way, the Veda itself is the root of <term>astronomy<note>original: "Jyotish"; the traditional Indian science of astronomy and astrology.</note></term>. Dada Bhai, the commentator on the *Surya Siddhanta*, wrote in his work *Kiranavali* that Brahmagupta’s system is merely an expanded version of the *Paitamaha Siddhanta*.

Whether it is true that "the commentary by Prithudaka Swami is merely a commentary on the *Paitamaha Bhashya* <note>Paitamaha Bhashya: An ancient commentary on the Paitamaha Siddhanta, one of the five early astronomical systems</note>" or not, it is universally accepted and evident that Brahmagupta <note>Brahmagupta (c. 598–668 CE): A legendary mathematician and astronomer who defined the rules for calculating with zero</note> gave a new form to the ancient *Paitamaha Siddhanta* by organizing and revising many subjects. Otherwise, Bhaskaracharya <note>Bhaskara II (1114–1185 CE): A prominent mathematician-astronomer who built upon Brahmagupta's work</note> would never have accepted Brahmagupta's system as his foundation.

(2) **Vasistha Siddhanta.**—Like the *Paitamaha* collected in the *Panch-Siddhantika* <note>Panch-Siddhantika: "The Five Astronomical Canons," a seminal compendium by Varahamihira</note>, this is also ancient but in a somewhat more advanced state. It contains 12 *Arya* verses and does not include calculations for planets other than the Sun and the Moon. Varahamihira has described both the *Paitamaha* and *Vasistha* as "far removed from the truth" <note>original: "दूरविभ्रष्टौ" (duravibhrashtau) - meaning inaccurate or outdated in their calculations</note>. This also dates to the beginning of the Shaka era. From the statements of Brahmagupta and one or two other commentators, it is known that the author of the *Vasistha* mentioned in the *Panch-Siddhantika* was Vishnuchandra. Previous writings suggest that Lord Vishnu gave astronomical instruction to the sage Vasistha. However, that Vishnu and this Vishnuchandra cannot be the same person. In the opinion of Dr. Thibaut <note>George Thibaut (1848–1914): An Indologist known for translating Sanskrit scientific texts</note>, there was a person named Vishnuchandra who revised the ancient *Vasistha Siddhanta*, and thus became known as its creator (See his introduction to *Panch-Siddhantika*). Shri Shankar Balkrishna Dikshit has proved in his *History of Indian Astronomy* <note>original: "भारतीय ज्योति:शास्त्र" (Bharatiya Jyotish-shastra)</note> that during Brahmagupta's time, there were two types of *Vasistha*: one original, and the other by Vishnuchandra. After Varahamihira, Vishnuchandra created a new edition of the ancient *Vasistha* by incorporating certain subjects from the *Romaka Siddhanta* <note>Romaka Siddhanta: The "Roman" or "Greek" system of astronomy influenced by Western methods</note> composed by Shrishena. Currently, the *Laghu Vasistha Siddhanta* <note>The "Short" or "Abridged" Vasistha system</note> is available as published from Kashi (Varanasi)*.

---

* Several years ago, Mahamahopadhyaya Shri Vindhyeshwari Prasad Dwivedi of Kashi began publishing the *Jyotish-Siddhanta-Sangraha* (A Collection of Astronomical Treatises). In it, the *Siddhantas* of Vyasa, Vasistha, Soma, etc., were published. It is not known how many have been published by now.

This contains about 94 verses. It is a modern adaptation of the ancient *Vasistha-Siddhanta* <note>One of the five early systems of Indian astronomy</note>. The quotations from the *Vasistha-Siddhanta* cited by Bhattotpala in his commentary on the *Brihat Samhita* are not found in this version.

(3) **Romaka-Siddhanta**.—Latadeva is the commentator on the *Romaka-Siddhanta* mentioned in the *Panchasiddhantika*. Brahmagupta <note>A famous 7th-century mathematician and astronomer</note> has also mentioned Latadeva’s name:

> ‘The daily ignorance of Srishena, Vishnuchandra, Pradyumna, Aryabhata, Lata, and Simha is proven because of the discrepancies in their calculations of eclipses and other phenomena.’ <note>original: "श्रीषेण-विष्णुचन्द्र-प्रद्युम्नार्यभट-लाल-सिंहानाम् । ग्रहणादि-विसंवादात् प्रतिदिवसं सिद्धमज्ञत्वम् ॥"</note>

That is to say—because the calculations for eclipses, risings, and settings by all these authors are seen to be contrary to direct observation, their lack of expertise is becoming daily renowned among the learned community. It is evident from the calculation style of this *Siddhanta* <term>Siddhanta: A comprehensive astronomical treatise</term> that it is composed based on some Roman or Greek system. The *Ahargana* <note>The number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch</note> is calculated for the meridian of Yavanapura <note>Literally "City of the Greeks," often identified with Alexandria or a Greek-influenced center</note>. Some speculate that the *Romaka-Siddhanta* was written in Sanskrit based on the books of the famous astronomer Ptolemy of Alexandria. Brahmagupta says that Srishena constructed the *Romaka-Siddhanta* based on the works of these four: Lata, Vasistha, Vijayanandi, and Aryabhata. Alberuni <margin>Alberuni was born in 895 Shaka era (973 CE) into the Islamic faith. Coming to India, he received education in the Puranas, Philosophy, and Astronomy from scholars. He had a great passion for astronomy. The book he wrote about India contains a detailed description of the astronomical knowledge of that time. The date of his Arabic work is 953 Shaka era (1031 CE). Its English translation is famous as *Alberuni's India*. A Hindi translation of the first volume has also been published by the Indian Press of Prayag.</margin> is also of this same opinion. Dr. Thibaut says that Srishena did not create the original *Romaka*, but rather used many texts of that time...

The subjects have been included in the <term>Romaka Siddhanta</term> <note>A mathematical astronomical treatise influenced by Greek/Roman systems</note>. First Latadeva, and after him Shrishena, revised the Romaka system.

Brahmagupta wrote in his own treatise:

> "The Yugas, Manvantaras, and Kalpas <note>Cycles of cosmic time</note> are considered the measures of time. Because these are not present in the Romaka, it stands outside of sacred tradition."

Because the original Romaka did not mention the <term>Yuga</term> <note>An age or epoch</note> or <term>Manvantara</term> <note>The lifespan of a Manu, a cosmic period</note>, it did not gain wide acceptance. In his commentary on the <term>Brihat Samhita</term>, Bhattotpala provided evidence from the <term>Paulisa</term> and others, but nowhere did he cite the Romaka. However, in Shrishena’s revised Sanskrit Romaka, there is discussion of the Yugas—this proves that two types of Romaka existed during Brahmagupta’s time. Mr. Dikshit has written in "Indian Astronomy" that according to the calculations of the Romaka, the Sun and Moon were not together at the <term>Beginning of Kaliyuga</term> <note>The current dark age in Hindu cosmology</note>; what’s more, even the lunar month was not complete. The original Romaka was very inaccurate. Be that as it may, the original Romaka was composed after Hipparchus † and before Ptolemy—that is, at the beginning of the Christian Era.

**Paulisa Siddhanta.**—The mathematics of the Paulisa is also not precise. In this, the calculation of Solar and Lunar eclipses is very crude. Al-Biruni is of the opinion that it was composed based on the Greek treatise of Paulus of Alexandria (Paulus Alexandrinus). Dr. Kern, while not considering this opinion entirely correct, still believes some Ionian <note>Greek</note> text to be the source. ✱

---

† The Greek astronomer Hipparchus lived 150 years before Christ; his work is lost—Ptolemy wrote his book near that same period. However, there is no uniformity between that book and the Romaka.

\* <note>original: "We have no right whatever to infer that (Paulus Alexandrinus) and Paulica are one and the same..."</note> "We have no right whatever to infer that (Paulus Alexandrinus) and Paulisa are one and the same, for identity of name is too slender a ground, especially when the name happens to be a common one." —Dr. Kern's Preface to his Brihat-Samhita.

In this, the longitude of Ujjain and Kashi from Yavanapur <note>literally "City of the Greeks," referring here to Alexandria</note> or Alexandria is recorded. Based on the similarity of names or the mention of Yavanapur, any assumption <note>that the text is purely foreign</note> is groundless. After all, in Varaha's *Paulisha Siddhanta*, the longitude from Avanti to Kashi is also provided. Yes, it can be said that at that time, the Aryas were aware of Yavanapur. Varaha’s *Paulisha* is structured according to the theoretical compositions of this country. The name *Paulisha* is famous in ancient scriptures. There was not just one version of the *Paulisha*. Bhattotpala and Prithudaka Swami, the commentator on Brahmagupta, have quoted several verses from the said Siddhanta. They bear some resemblance to the views of the *Surya Siddhanta* and Aryabhata. Mr. Thibaut <note>George Thibaut, a 19th-century Indologist</note> estimates—a second Siddhanta of this name was created by revising and updating Varaha’s *Paulisha*, and it is from that version that later commentators have quoted verses (Introduction to *Panch-Siddhantika*). In reality, neither the ancient nor the modern *Paulisha* is currently available. Mr. Dikshit has shown that Varaha’s and Bhattotpala’s *Paulisha* are not the same, and that two types of the said Siddhanta existed during Utpala’s time, etc. (See, *History of Indian Astronomy*).

**Surya-Siddhanta.**—Lord Surya <note>the Sun God</note> created this himself and, being satisfied with the rigorous penance of Mayasura, instructed him in it. This legend is famous at the beginning of the *Surya-Siddhanta* and at the end of the final chapter on time-reckoning—

-> x &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; x &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; x <-

> "A part of the Sun ascended to heaven and entered its own orb; Maya, having realized that divine knowledge directly from the Sun..." <note>original Sanskrit: 'divamācakrame'rkaṃśaḥ praviveśa svamaṇḍalam | mayo'tha divyaṃ tajjñānaṃ jñātvā sākṣādvivasvataḥ'</note>

The famous German historian Mr. Weber has written—the text of the Greek Paulus that has been found contains predictive astrology, not mathematics. It bears no equality to Varaha’s *Paulisha*.

->“He considered himself to have fulfilled his life’s purpose, his sins washed away. When the Sages learned that Maya had received these boons from the Sun, they approached and surrounded him, asking for knowledge with great respect. Pleased, he imparted to them the great movement of the planets—the most wonderful secret in the world, equal to the Divine Vedas.”<- <note>original Sanskrit: "Kritakrityamivatmanam... Rahasyam Brahmasammitam." These verses describe the mythical transmission of astronomical knowledge from the Sun God to the architect Maya, and then to the Sages.</note>

The personified fragment of the Sun disappeared—the Sages then surrounded Mayasura <note>The divine architect of the Asuras, credited with receiving the revelation of astronomy.</note> and, having learned the planetary movements relevant to them, went their ways. This is the origin of the ancient <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> <note>The "Sun Precept," the most influential astronomical text of ancient India.</note>. These events belong to the beginning of the *Treta Yuga* <note>The second age of the world in Hindu cosmology.</note>. The original text upon which <term>Varahamihira</term> <note>A 6th-century polymath who compiled five major astronomical systems.</note> based his compilation of the Solar system was the root text, and it was more systematically organized than the five previously mentioned systems; for this reason, it was written that "The Solar system is the most accurate." However, there is a great difference between the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> as it exists today and the ancient version. There are discrepancies in the revolutions of the planets, variations in the number of verses, and the inclusion of contradictory subjects such as the chapter on corrections (*Bijopanayana*) and the calculation of the precession of the equinoxes (*Ayanamsha*). Several ancient masters have acknowledged this. <term>Bhattotpala</term> <note>A 10th-century commentator on astronomical works.</note> wrote at the end of his commentary on the <term>Brihat Jataka</term> <note>A foundational text on Vedic astrology.</note>:

> “On the fifth day of the bright half of the month of Chaitra, on a Thursday, in the Shaka year 888 <note>966 CE</note>, this explanation was completed by me.”

<term>Bhattotpala</term> lived in the Shaka year 888, and in his commentary on the <term>Brihat Samhita</term>, he quoted several verses from the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> which are no longer found in the current version. In the eleventh century of the Shaka era, the motion of the precession of the equinoxes mentioned by <term>Bhaskaracharya</term> <note>Also known as Bhaskara II, a leading 12th-century mathematician and astronomer.</note> does not match the currently prevalent <term>Surya Siddhanta</term>.

In the Shaka year 1221 <note>1299 CE</note>, Tailanga Kuchanacharya wrote a set of tables titled ‘Graha Chakra’ (The Planetary Wheel). Two parts of it have been found written in Oriya script. The book is inaccurate and incomplete. It is the opinion of many scholars that—

The first discoverer of the astronomical tables <term>Sarini; a set of mathematical tables used for planetary calculations</term> is Kuchanacharya. Be that as it may, he has included several verses from the *Surya Siddhanta* in his work, which are found in the current versions. In the Shaka year 1422 <note>1500 CE</note>, Lakshmidasa wrote a commentary titled *Ganita-Tattva-Chintamani* on Bhaskara’s *Shiromani*; in it, he provided verses under the name *Brihat Surya Siddhanta* <note>The "Great" or expanded Surya Siddhanta</note> which can no longer be traced (Colebrooke's Essays). In the Shaka year 1561 <note>1639 CE</note>, Nityananda, the author of *Siddhanta-Raja*, writes:

> "Thus, although some parts were <unclear>interrupted</unclear> by me, 
> for the joy of my own heart and for those whose understanding is not far-reaching, 
> they have cast their own works, though flawed in meaning, 
> while claiming to follow the best of teachers. 
> When 3600 years of the Kali Yuga had passed, 
> or perhaps slightly more or less due to the cycles of the planets, 
> the position of the equinox was formerly established 
> by the stars and other markers through the ignorance of those who calculated it."
> <note>original: "तथा मया विच्छुलतोऽपि केचित्... बभूव पूर्वं विषुवत्स्थलं हि ॥"</note>

Nityananda’s opinion is that the currently prevalent *Surya Siddhanta* is not the original one. He believes the authentic version was composed after 3600 years of the Kali Age <note>approx. 499 CE</note> had passed. Sudhakar-ji has also clearly published his opinion in his commentary on the *Pancha-Siddhantika* ❈. From a review of historical investigations, it is known that from the 13th century BCE until approximately a thousand years later, no astronomical texts are available. However, progress in astronomy must certainly have occurred in some form. It is possible that during that time, the *Brahma*, *Vasishtha*, and *Surya* Siddhantas were composed.

Al-Biruni <note>Abū al-Rayḥān al-Bīrūnī (973–1048), a Persian scholar who wrote extensively on Indian science.</note> is of the opinion that Varaha's *Surya-Siddhanta* <term>Surya-Siddhanta: a foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy</term> was authored by Latadeva. Mr. Weber <note>Albrecht Weber (1825–1901), a prominent German Indologist.</note> holds a similarly mistaken view; he considers the *Vedanga-Jyotisha* and the *Surya-Siddhanta* to be the work of a single author, Latadeva, and even suggests that Lagadha <note>The traditional author of the Vedanga-Jyotisha.</note> and Latadeva were the same person. However, Latacharya existed before Varahamihira and must have authored a specific text, which is why his independent opinions are recorded separately from the *Surya-Siddhanta*. In the *Panchasiddhantika* <note>Varahamihira's "Treatise on the Five Astronomical Canons."</note>, it is written:

->‘The calculation of the elapsed days and the determination of the weekday<-
->The count of days is indeed linked to specific places and times.<-
->As stated by Latacharya,<-
->In Yavanapura <note>Literally "City of the Greeks," often identified with Alexandria.</note>, it is so when the sun is half-set.’<-

It is only because of this connection to Yavanapura that Lata is considered a foreigner. He had no connection to the ancient *Surya-Siddhanta*. The currently prevalent *Surya-Siddhanta* is a refined <insert>Sanskrit</insert> version of the ancient one; it has undergone several revisions at different times. There is no firm evidence that this was composed by Lata. According to previous writings, it is estimated that it took its current form in the twelfth century of the Shaka era <note>Approximately 1278 CE.</note> *. Mr. Dikshit <note>S. B. Dikshit, author of the "History of Indian Astronomy."</note> has also written that the ancient *Surya-Siddhanta*—that is, the one from Varaha's time—is not the work of Lata. Its time is generally estimated to be around 88 Shaka (166 CE).

Whatever the case may be, the *Surya-Siddhanta* has enjoyed great authority from ancient times to the present day; no other ancient astronomical system has received such prestige. The ancient masters preserved it with great care and, by compiling increasingly organized subjects, made it popular. It spread throughout almost the entirety of India, and based upon it—

This is very distinguished and is adorned with both ancient and modern principles.

A few years ago, a Bengali translation of the *Surya-Siddhanta* <note>The "Sun Treatise," a foundational text of Indian astronomy</note> by Vijnanananda was published by the Panini Office in Prayag. It includes mathematical proofs. I have not seen it myself, but I suspect it follows the style of Burgess’s translation.

Up to this point, I have briefly described the state of the *Vedanga Jyotisha* <note>The astronomical appendix to the Vedas, used for timing rituals</note> and the five systems accepted by Varahamihira. Among the eighteen originators of the astronomical systems mentioned earlier, the names of Parashara, Kashyap, Narada, Garga, Vyasa, Manu, and Bhrigu \* are currently famous as authors of *Samhitas* <note>Compendiums covering omens and natural phenomena</note> and as Yavana <note>A term originally referring to Greeks, later used for foreign or specific astronomical schools</note> authors. In his commentary on the *Brihat-Samhita*, the scholar Bhattotpala has quoted their words as authoritative evidence on subjects suitable for *Samhitas*, but there are no authoritative quotes from them regarding the actual mathematical systems (*Siddhantas*). In such instances, the words of Pulisa, Vasishtha, the *Surya-Siddhanta*, Aryabhata, and Brahmagupta are found in greater numbers. See the "Chapter on the Rules for the Astrologer" in the *Brihat-Samhita* to see how the master Varahamihira has organized this. When the ancient texts themselves are missing, what decision can be made regarding their subject matter or period of composition? In some places, only weak evidence is found; in others, one must rely solely on legend. In such a situation, there is no benefit in spreading a web of baseless imagination. Here ends the account of the systems of the Rishis and Sages. Now, it is necessary to write something about the principal scholarly authors of the systems. Thoughtful gentlemen of astronomy should remember that from ancient times to the present, <term>Jyotish-shastra</term> <note>The science of light, encompassing astronomy and astrology</note> has undergone more changes than perhaps any other branch of Sanskrit literature. Jyotish-shastra—

Because it is based on science, both ancient and modern teachers were compelled to rectify its deficiencies. Science is inherently a progressive subject; its form can never remain the same for all time. * To hold anyone at fault for this does not, in any sense, seem consistent with justice.

**Aryabhata**—In reality, this great soul was the founder of the science of astronomy <term>Jyotish-shastra: the traditional Indian system of astronomy and mathematics</term> and the protector of ancient virtues and glory. No human-authored treatise <term>Manusha-siddhanta: a scientific text attributed to a human author rather than divine revelation</term> prior to him is available. The name of his treatise is the *Aryabhatiya*. Its authority has been recognized from ancient times until today. He considered the *Brahma-siddhanta* to be his primary source. The introductory invocation <note>Mangalacharan: a prayer for success at the beginning of a work</note>—

> "Having bowed to the One and the Many, to the True Deity, the Supreme Brahman, Aryabhata speaks of the three: Mathematics, the Reckoning of Time, and the Celestial Sphere." <note>original Sanskrit: 'Pranipatyekamanekam kam satyam devatam parabrahma | Aryabhatastrini gadati ganitam kalakriyam golam ||'</note>

There are two sections in this treatise: first—the *Dashagitika*, and second—the *Aryashtottara-shata*. In the *Dashagitika* there are 10 verses, and in the section on Mathematics, Time-Reckoning, and the Celestial Sphere, there are 108 verses. Aryabhata devised the letters k, kh, g, etc., as indicators of the numbers 1, 2, 3, etc. That is to say, by assigning a specific numerical value to each vowel like a, ā and each consonant like k, kh, he expressed very large numbers. No ancient teacher before him had devised such a method of using letters as numerical indicators.

* **Dr. Kern also writes**—

> And in no branch of Sanskrit literature have changes been made so freely as in astronomical works. Not from unworthy motives; on the contrary, the Hindu astronomers were the only class of learned men in their country who had an idea of science being progressive, not stationary or retrogressive—Dr. Kern's preface to his *Brihat Samhita*.

Such a custom existed among the Greeks <note>original: "Yavanas"</note>, which is why Dwivedi, in his work *The River of Mathematicians* <note>original: "Ganaka-Tarangini"</note>, expressed doubt that Aryabhata might have learned this method and his astronomical knowledge from some Greek source. * In the aforementioned numerical notation, the writing order is assumed to follow the leftward movement <note>the "Vama-gati" rule where digits are read from right to left</note>. At that time, the calculation system based on the Shaka Era <note>an epoch starting in 78 CE</note> was not in vogue; therefore, the Kali Era <note>an epoch starting in 3102 BCE</note> was used. Later, Varahamihira popularized the Shaka Era. Instead of writing the planetary cycles for a *Kalpa* <note>a vast cosmic period of 4.32 billion years</note>, he wrote them for a *Mahayuga* <note>a smaller cycle of 4.32 million years</note>. He recorded his own time in the section on the Measurement of Time <note>original: "Kalakriyapada"</note>—

> "When sixty times sixty years and three quarter-ages <note>Yugapadas</note> had elapsed, twenty-three years had then passed since my birth."

This means that when 3600 years of the Kali Era had passed, his age was 23 years. Therefore, by subtracting 3176 from 3577 Kali years—in the Shaka year 378, or 476 CE <note>The text calculates the birth year as 476 CE and the composition of the work around 499 CE</note>—he composed his *Siddhanta* <note>astronomical treatise</note>. In the said treatise, by writing "having honored that knowledge at Kusumpura," he revealed that it was composed while residing in the present-day "Patna" district. Kusumpura, Pushpapur, and Pataliputra are all names for Patna. In ancient times, it was the capital of India and, like Ujjain and Dhara, it was a gathering place for scholars.

The ancient commentators on the *Aryabhatiya* are Parameshvara and Suryadeva Yajva. Their respective works are titled *Light on Aryabhata* <note>original: "Bhata-Dipika"</note> and *Illumination of Aryabhata* <note>original: "Bhata-Prakashika"</note>. Parameshvara mentions Suryadeva in his commentary; thus, Suryadeva is ancient and Parameshvara is more recent than him. Furthermore, based on the *Illumination of Aryabhata*, Bhaskaracharya also pointed out some errors made by Aryabhata.

And Paramesvara <note>A 15th-century mathematician and astronomer from Kerala</note> has written the statements of Bhaskaracharya in his commentary. Therefore, it is proven that Suryadeva lived before Bhaskara, and Paramesvara lived after him. Dr. Kern was the first to publish the *Aryabhatiya* along with the aforementioned *Bhata-Dipika* commentary. The Doctor has written many things regarding Aryabhata in his introduction to the *Brihat Samhita* (See his Preface to Brihat Samhita P. 55-61).

It is well known that Aryabhata wrote about the rotation of the Earth <term>Bhu-bhramana: the axial rotation of the Earth</term>. However, his commentators and others like Lalla, Sripati, and Brahmagupta have shown their scholarship only in attempting to refute it. In Europe, Copernicus determined this matter in the 15th century of the Shaka era <note>The Shaka era begins in 78 CE; the author is aligning European history with Indian chronology</note>. Today, it has been solidified by numerous proofs and arguments, and even school children know the truth of the Earth's rotation; this is the manifestation of the unimaginable glory of science. †

Varahamihira wrote in the *Pancha-siddhantika*:
> "Aryabhata stated that the day begins at midnight in Lanka; 
> and again, he said it begins from sunrise in Lanka." 
> <note>original: "लङ्कार्द्धरात्रसमये दिनप्रवृत्तिं जगाद चार्यभटः । भूयः स एव चार्कोदद्यात्प्रवृत्त्याह लङ्कायाम् ॥"</note>

This means that Aryabhata considered the start of the day from midnight at Lanka (the equator) and also considered it from sunrise. He stated both things. In the *Aryabhatiya* published by Kern, the rule for the start of the day is from sunrise, not midnight. For this reason, people speculate that there has been some confusion or alteration in the ancient *Aryabhatiya* as well.

### The Second Aryabhata—The First Aryabhata and his Treatise, the Elder Aryabhata

And it later became famous under the name **Laghv-Aryabhatiya** <note>The "Small" or "Brief" Aryabhatiya</note>. The reason for this is that a second version of the **Aryabhatiya** was produced by an unknown scholar; its name appears differently in various written manuscripts as **Maha-Aryasiddhanta**, **Aryabhata-Mahasiddhanta**, and **Mahasiddhanta** <note>The "Great Treatise"</note>. This work contains 18 chapters and 625 verses in the Arya-Upagiti meter—it also includes <term>Patiganita</term> <note>arithmetic</note>, <term>Kshetravyavahara</term> <note>geometry/mensuration</note>, and <term>Bijaganita</term> <note>algebra</note>. The author has expressed numbers using letters, but has written them from left to right <note>literally "southern-motion"</note>; "I have refined it following the <term>Vriddharyabhata</term> <note>The Elder Aryabhata</note>. The planetary calculations etc. are taken from the <term>Parashara-Siddhanta</term>, as the opinion of Parashara is considered most excellent in the Kali age." And so forth.

In this work, there is an attempt to clear the faults that <term>Brahmagupta</term> <note>a 7th-century mathematician who famously criticized Aryabhata</note> first pointed out in <term>Aryabhata</term>. Furthermore, while <term>Aryabhata</term>, <term>Varahamihira</term>, <term>Brahmagupta</term>, and <term>Lalla</term> did not write about <term>Ayana-gati</term> <note>the precession of the equinoxes</note>, it is present in this Siddhanta; therefore, its author must have lived after <term>Brahmagupta</term>. <term>Bhaskaracharya</term>, in the section on planetary visibility in his work **Shiromani**, provides the <term>Dreshkanodaya</term> <note>rising of the decans</note> from the **Aryabhatiya**; since no one else mentioned this except for this specific work, he must be older than <term>Bhaskara</term>. <term>Bhattotpala</term> has given evidence from many texts in his commentary, but this **Mahasiddhanta** is not named anywhere, and full knowledge of the <term>Ayana-gati</term> had already been established in this country by the 8th century of the Shaka era. For these reasons, it has been determined that the **Mahasiddhanta** was composed in the 9th century of the Shaka era. Shri Sudhakar Dwivedi has published this along with his own commentary in the "Benares Sanskrit Series." The popularity of the <term>Arya-paksha</term> <note>the school of Aryabhata</note> school of mathematics is currently very high in the Malabar and Tamil regions of the South. Here, among the Vaishnava sects as well, the <term>Arya-paksha</term> calculations have been predominant for a long time regarding fasts and festivals. The religious authorities have given their opinion—

<page-num>25</page-num>

> "The birthdays of Vishnu and the days of Hari <note>referring to religious festivals and lunar calendars</note>, and all ritual duties should be performed only according to the *Aryabhata-shastra* <note>The Treatise of Aryabhata</note>." and so forth.

Aryabhata is considered a resident of Patna, but while his mathematics is promoted in distant lands, it is not prevalent in Bihar or Bengal. For this reason, Mr. Dikshit says—Aryabhata's 'Kusumapura' is not Patna. <note>Kusumapura is the ancient name for Pataliputra/Patna; the author is noting a scholarly dispute over Aryabhata's true birthplace.</note> *

**Lalla.**—Based on the <term>Aryabhatiya</term> <note>Aryabhata's primary astronomical compendium</note>, Lallacharya composed a theoretical treatise named '**Shishyadhivriddhida**' <note>literally: 'That which increases the intelligence of students'</note>, as he writes at the beginning:

> "The movements of the celestial bodies <note>original: 'vyomaukasam'</note> as declared by the teacher Aryabhata are very difficult to grasp; therefore, Lalla now speaks this 'Intelligence-Increaser' for the benefit of students." <note>original: 'Acharyaryabhatoditam suvishamam...'</note>

Further on, he says again:

> "Although his disciples composed various treatises <note>Tantras</note> after mastering the science produced by Aryabhata, they did not truly explain the sequence of calculations. Therefore, I shall state the procedures clearly and in their proper order." <note>original: 'Vijnaya shastramalamaryabhatapranitam...'</note>

Taking the *Aryabhatiya* as the foundation, his disciples wrote several treatises but did not provide instructions for the sequence of calculation; therefore, I am describing the entire mathematics in order. He did not name any specific disciples. Some speculate it might be Pradyumna, Shrisena, or Latadeva, among others. At the end of the *Dhivriddhida*, Lalla has described his lineage.

In that work, he describes himself as the grandson of Shamba and the son of Trivikramabhatta. He provides the <term>Karanabda</term> <note>The epoch year used for astronomical calculations</note> as 420 Shaka <note>Approximately 498 CE, though scholars often debate if this refers to the era of his work or his birth</note>; his period is estimated to be around this time. Lallacharya was a famous astronomer of his era, and his work *Dhivriddhika* was very popular in educational circles.

He also authored a <term>Samhita</term> <note>A compendium or encyclopedia of omens and natural phenomena</note> text named *Ratnakosha*, which is no longer available. Sripati based his *Ratnamala* on this very work. Mahadeva, the commentator on the *Ratnamala*, has cited Lalla’s views regarding the number of <term>Nakshatras</term> <note>Lunar mansions or star clusters used in Indian astrology</note>. Bhaskaracharya refuted Lalla’s methods for calculating the surface area of the Earth, which indicates that Lalla also wrote a work on *Patiganita* <note>Arithmetic and measurement</note>. Some people claim that Lalla was a disciple of Aryabhata. However, Lalla actually refuted Aryabhata’s theory of the Earth's rotation. At that time, the "wind of refutation" <note>A culture of intellectual debate and critique</note> blew very strongly. That Lalla was a devotee of Aryabhata is evident from his writings; whether he was a direct disciple or not is of little consequence. He was a promoter of the <term>Arya-paksha</term> <note>The school of thought following Aryabhata's system</note>. Based on his astronomical handbook, Brahmadeva composed the *Karanaprakash* in 1014 Shaka, and Damodara composed the *Bhattatulya* in 1666 Shaka. Shri Sudhakarji Dwivedi has published the *Karanaprakash* with proofs from Benares.

**Varahamihira.**—A master of the secrets of the <term>Triskandha</term> <note>The three branches of Jyotisha: Astronomy (Gola/Ganita), Omens (Samhita), and Horoscopy (Hora)</note> Astrology, a treasury of diverse sciences, the beloved shelter for the natural vine of poetry, the supreme teacher Shri Varahamihira has been illuminating the world with the moonlight of his fame from ancient times to the present day. The wealth of knowledge you <note>The author shifts to a respectful second-person address</note> developed is entirely praiseworthy and wonderful. In truth, you were high-minded and universally respected. For this reason, scholars have praised him with an open throat <note>An idiom meaning "unreservedly" or "loudly"</note>—

<meta>This page introduces the works and biography of the 6th-century astronomer Varahamihira, establishing his lineage and his legendary connection to King Vikramaditya's court. It follows a general history of Indian astronomy.</meta>

->“I bow to Varahamihira, who is like the Sun <note>original: 'Mihira'; a play on the astronomer's name and the sun</note>, the destroyer of doubts for the world.”<-

And so forth. Varahamihira composed several works: the *Panchasiddhantika* <note>The Five Astronomical Canons</note>, *Brihat Samhita* <note>The Great Compilation</note>, *Yogayatra*, *Brihat Jataka*, *Laghu Jataka*, *Vivahapatala*, and *Samasa-Samhita*. Among these, *Vivahapatala* and *Samasa-Samhita* are currently unavailable. Of the remaining works, all except the *Panchasiddhantika* have commentaries written by Bhattotpala. The *Yogayatra* is also an excellent text, but until now, no scholar has made the effort to publish it.

At the end of the *Brihat Jataka*, Varahamihira wrote:

->“The son of Adityadasa, from whom he obtained knowledge; having received a boon of grace from the Sun-god at Kapitthaka; Varahamihira of Avanti, having thoroughly examined the teachings of the sages, composed this beautiful work on Horoscopy <note>original: 'Hora'</note>.”<-

He received a boon from the Sun-god in the city of Kapitthaka and obtained his education in the science of astronomy <term>Jyotishshastra: the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</term> from his father, Adityadasa. Afterward, he went to live in Ujjayini. At that time, learning was highly honored in Ujjayini (also known as Avanti). Tradition holds that King Vikramaditya of Avanti was always surrounded by a circle of scholars, and Varahamihira was one of the "Nine Gems" <note>Navaratna: the legendary group of nine extraordinary scholars at the royal court</note> of his assembly. ※ The Teacher <note>referring to Varahamihira</note> in the *Panchasiddhantika* mentions the epoch year <term>Karanabda: the reference year used for astronomical calculations</term>—

---

<margin>※ In the 12th century of the Shaka era, an astrologer named Kalidasa composed a work on auspicious timing <term>Muhurta: the selection of favorable moments for rituals</term> called *Jyotirvidabharana*. In its 22nd chapter, it is written: ‘Kalidasa wrote this book during the time of Shri Vikramarka, the Lord of Malwa.’ Not only this, but he unhesitatingly discusses many stories regarding Vikramaditya’s fame, the Assembly of Nine Gems, and the establishment of the Shaka era. He lists several scholars such as Vararuchi, Shanku, Amara, Jishnu, Badarayana, Trilochan, and Hari as members of the assembly. <meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the historical dating and biography of the astronomer Varahamihira, specifically addressing the discrepancies between various historical eras and texts.</meta>

->( 28 )<-

The year 427 of the Shaka era <note>The Shaka era began in 78 CE; thus 427 Shaka is approximately 505 CE</note> is written; from this, his existence in the fifth century of the Shaka era is indisputable. Doctor Bhau Daji has written that Amaraja Daivajna, the commentator on the astronomical treatise titled *Khandakhadyaka* composed by Brahmagupta, has revealed that—'In the Shaka year numbered five hundred and nine, the teacher Varahamihira went to heaven!' <note>original: "नवाधिकपञ्चशतसंख्यशके वराहमिहिराचार्यो दिवं गतः !"</note>. The teacher died in 509 Shaka <note>approx. 587 CE</note>. This is also the opinion of Al-Biruni <note>An 11th-century Persian scholar who studied Indian science</note> and others, that 427 Shaka is the epoch year <term>Karunabda: the reference year used for astronomical calculations</term> of the *Panchasiddhantika*, not the value of the teacher's birth year. The teacher must have compiled his astronomical treatise between the ages of 18 and 25. The major works he created are vast—it is not impossible that they took a long time to produce, which proves the teacher lived a long life. Due to a lack of evidence, the death date written by Amaraja has been considered unauthentic.

The *Brihat Jataka* and *Laghu Jataka* of Teacher Varahamihira are prevalent everywhere in teaching and study, and are considered the most authoritative and profound texts on the subject of predictive astrology. Regarding the time of the composition of his works—'When 3068 years of the Kali Yuga had passed' <note>original: "वर्षैः सिन्धुरदर्शनाम्बरगुणै ३०६८ याते कलेः संमिते"</note>, meaning 111 years before the Shaka era, the *Jyotirvidabharana* and other works were composed in the court of Vikramaditya. It appears that someone added this chapter later; otherwise, it must be considered a deception by Kalidasa <note>The famous Sanskrit poet</note>—for what is this besides self-praise? It is a dream-creation. Even if he himself existed 111 years before the start of the Shaka era, in the first chapter of the aforementioned book, the calculation of the years beginning with Prabhava is done from the Shaka era—after giving the formula for calculating the precession of the equinoxes <term>Ayanamsha: the angular distance between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</term>, he subtracted 442 from the Shaka year, meaning you were present even in the fifth century of the Shaka era. The very precession that Brahmagupta (6th century Shaka) could not determine, you had already fixed before the start of the Shaka era. Because of all these mutually contradictory points, the *Jyotirvidabharana* and its author were never held in high regard. Be that as it may! There have been several kings named Vikramaditya; it is possible that Varahamihira lived during the time of Harsha-Vikramaditya. There have been several poets named Kalidasa—but no one became like the original Kalidasa.

It is full of various differing opinions. In the *Brihat Jataka* <note>The Great Birth Chart, a foundational text by Varahamihira</note>, the Greek names for the signs of the zodiac starting with Aries are mentioned, along with many technical terms and references to the Greek masters <note>original: "Yavanacharya"</note>. Names such as Maya, Shakti, Jivasharma, Manittha, Vishnugupta (Chanakya), Devasvami, Siddhasena, Satyacharya, and Bhagadatta are included. In the commentary by Bhattotpala, the opinions of many other astrologers are also compiled. From this, it is clear that in ancient times, the influence of the Greeks <note>original: "Yavanas"</note> on predictive astrology <term>Phalit Jyotish: the branch of astrology concerned with predicting future events</term> was very strong, and predictive astrology spread in many forms throughout this country because the devotion of the ancients toward it was very intense. For this reason, through contact with the Greeks, the branch of natal astrology <term>Jataka-skandha: the division of astrology dealing with individual birth charts</term> became very well-developed. From the time of Garga, knowledge from other lands was introduced to this country; first, the science of hour-based astrology <term>Hora-shastra: from the Greek 'hora', focusing on natal and elective astrology</term> became popular, and later, through contact with the Arab world, the *Tajik* system <note>A Persian-influenced system of annual solar returns</note> caused a great stir. In reality, the abundance of Greek-derived words is found specifically in *Hora* and *Tajik* astrology, not in the mathematical section.

There is a description of the *Brihat Jataka* ※ written by Mahidhara. There is also a "Ten-Chapter Commentary" by a Southerner. However, the commentary by Bhattotpala is excellent. Master Utpala was a resident of Kashmir and a versatile scholar. There are also commentaries by Utpala on the *Shatpanchashika* (a book on queries) by Prithuyashas, the son of Varahamihira, and on the *Khandakhadyaka* by Brahmagupta. The truth is that just as a master commentator like Mallinatha emerged for the poet Kalidasa, so too did Bhattotpala emerge as a uniquely talented commentator for Varahamihira. From ancient times until today, there has not been another such profound commentator on astrological texts. Everyone maintains an unwavering faith in him. †

※ There is a large ancient text on natal astrology called *Saravali* composed by Kalyanavarman. It was created around 500 Saka era <note>approximately 578 CE</note>. The name *Saravali* <note>meaning 'Collection of Essences'</note> was given because it compiles the essence of the Greek science of *Hora*. Bhattotpala has quoted many passages from this book in his own commentary. Recently, this book has been published by the Nirnaya Sagar Press in Bombay.

# 30

**Brahmagupta**. — His name is world-renowned. In his time, he was a highly distinguished and extraordinary scholar, particularly skilled in <term>observational astronomy</term> <note>original: "vedha-vidya" — the science of astronomical observation and calculation</note>. His primary work is the **Brahmasphutasiddhanta**. Based on the ancient commentary by Prithudaka Swami Chaturvedacharya, Shri Sudhakar Dwivedi has recently published it along with his own new commentary titled "Tilaka." In that work, it is written:

->During the reign of King Shri Vyaghramukha, the ornament of the Chapa dynasty,<-
->when five hundred and fifty years of the Shaka era had passed,<-
->the **Brahmasphutasiddhanta**<-
->was composed by Brahmagupta, the son of Jishnu, at the age of thirty.<-

That is to say, Brahmagupta composed this Siddhanta in the year 550 of the Shaka era <note>approximately 628 CE</note> during the reign of King Shri Vyaghramukha, when he was thirty years old. Later, in his old age—specifically in Shaka 587 <note>665 CE</note>—he composed the **Khandakhadyaka**, a <term>karana</term> <note>a practical astronomical handbook used for quick calculations</note> based on the Aryasiddhanta. Varuna of Kashmir wrote a commentary on this in Shaka 662. In that commentary, Brahmagupta is referred to as "Bhillamalakacharya" <note>The Teacher from Bhillamala</note>. In his work *History of Indian Astronomy*, Mr. Dikshit has written that Bhinmal, Bhilmal, and Shrimal are all names for the same village. When the Chinese traveler Xuanzang was in this country (650 CE), Bhillamala was the capital of the northern Gurjara kingdom. The poet Magha also lived there. This place is located on the northern border of Gujarat, within southern Marwar. Al-Biruni considered the aforementioned place to be near Multan. In the *Ganakatarangini*, Dwivedi writes that Brahmagupta was a dependent of the King of Rewa, Shri Vyaghramukha. However, Dikshit’s view seems more accurate.

> "We owe the knowledge of nearly all the particulars about the predecessors of Varahamihira to Bhatta Utpala. This astronomer who, as we have had occasion to notice, flourished in the middle of the 10th century of our era"................P. 61.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the historical development of Indian astronomy, focusing on the lineage of the Brahmapaksha school and the influence of Brahmagupta.</meta>

<page-num>31</page-num>

->( 31 )<-

Brahmagupta is the very root of the *Brahmapaksha* <note>One of the major schools of Indian astronomical thought</note>. It was on the basis of his Sanskrit work, the *Brahmasphuta-siddhanta*, that Bhojaraja created the astronomical handbook titled *Rajamriganka* in 994 Shaka <note>approx. 1072 CE</note>, even before the time of Bhaskaracharya. A Jain scholar named Gunabhadra recorded planetary positions according to Brahmagupta’s system in the *Uttara Purana*, which was composed in 820 Shaka <note>approx. 898 CE</note>. In 980 Shaka, King Dashabala of the Vallabha dynasty wrote the *Karana-Kamala-Martanda*; later, Bhaskara’s *Karana Kutuhala*, the *Mahadevi Sarani*, and in 1500 Shaka, the *Kheta Siddhi* and *Chandrarki*—all these astronomical handbooks follow the *Brahmapaksha* tradition. While algebra certainly existed before Brahmagupta, he can be considered its primary pioneer. The root of European algebra is Arabia, and for the Arabs, our Brahmagupta was the source! The Arabs named their translation of the *Brahma-siddhanta* as *Sindhind* and the *Khandakhadyaka* as *Al-Arkand*. Before the works of Ptolemy became widespread, the astronomical principles of this country were prevalent in various other nations.

Aryabhata and Brahmagupta wrote nothing regarding the precession of the equinoxes <term>Ayanagati: the slow movement of the rotation axis of an astronomical body</term>. At that time, observations might not have yielded precise results, and knowledge of this motion may not have been attained. How could knowledge of such a subtle subject—where the movement is only one degree every 50 or 60 years—be easily gained with the crude instruments of ancient times? Whatever the case, Acharya Brahmagupta was a person of entirely supernatural genius and a model for true critics from a scientific perspective.

**Sripati.** —Sripati’s *Jataka-paddhati* <note>A manual on horoscopy</note> and *Jyotish-ratnamala* are both like "wish-fulfilling trees" for astrologers. Mahadeva, a commentator on the *Ratnamala*, wrote that Sripati was the grandson of Keshava of the Kashyapa lineage and the son of Nagadeva. Mr. Dvivedi found a handbook by Sripati titled *Dhikoti* concerning the calculation of the Sun and Moon, which cited the year 961 Shaka <note>approx. 1039 CE</note>. Sripati was likely born near this date. In his time...

->( 32 )<-

There is no doubt that he was an extraordinary scholar and a respected figure in the three branches of <term>Jyotish-shastra</term> <note>The three branches are Siddhanta (mathematical astronomy), Samhita (omens/astrology), and Hora (horoscopes)</note>. Your poetry was also simple, sweet, and of a high caliber. You composed a theoretical treatise named ‘Siddhanta-Shekhara,’ but its whereabouts are now unknown—
> ‘Time is the devourer of the world.’ <note>original: "कालो जगद्भक्षक: ।" (Kalo jagadbhakshakah)</note>

**Bhaskaracharya.**—Your name is well-renowned in the world today. After Varahamihira and Brahmagupta, there has not been another <term>astronomer</term> <note>original: Jyotirvid</note> as talented and endowed with all virtues as you. You were born into a highly fortunate Brahmin family, rich in both knowledge and humility. The following texts of yours are prevalent everywhere and are studied and taught with great respect— Lilavati, Bijaganita, Siddhanta-Shiromani, Karana-Kutuhala, and Sarvatobhadra. On all these texts, scholars have written various ancient and modern <term>commentaries and annotations</term> <note>original: Tika-Tippani</note> from time to time, and these are well-known to all lovers of astronomical theory.

At the end of the Shiromani, you yourself provided a description of your lineage, country, and village. Having been born in the Shaka year 1036 <note>approx. 1114 CE</note>, you composed the Shiromani at the age of 36. The excellent edition by Shri Bapudeva Shastriji is famous. Shastriji also wrote his own annotations in verse. However, its <term>mathematical proof</term> <note>original: Upapatti; the logical derivation of a formula</note> cannot be understood by anyone without a detailed explanation; very few scholars or students can benefit from it. Those among his chief students who understood it during Shastriji’s lifetime would certainly know it, and those to whom they subsequently explained it would surely be familiar with its <term>key</term> <note>original: Kunji; a guide or solution manual</note>.

Taking Brahmagupta’s Brahmasphuta-Siddhanta and Prithudakasvami’s (<term>Chaturvedacharya</term>) <term>commentary</term> <note>original: Bhashya</note> as the primary basis, Bhaskaracharya composed his Shiromani, and in specific places, he [analyzed/criticized] <note>The text cuts off at "alo-", likely for "alochana" (criticism or analysis)</note> the opinions of Aryabhata, Lalla, Brahmagupta, and others—

He has also performed [critiques]. He has pointed out the errors of everyone with great joy. Besides this, he has written many special points that he conceived himself. He also composed a commentary named *Vasana-Bhashya* <note>A "Vasana" commentary typically explains the underlying logic or "proof" behind mathematical rules</note>. Your prose and poetry were both very simple and flavorful. He described himself as a poet and provided glimpses of his poetry throughout the book on one pretext or another. The same thing is found in *Lilavati* <note>his work on arithmetic</note> and *Bijaganita* <note>his work on algebra</note>. He mostly imitated the poetic style of the teacher Varahamihira, which he also found very pleasing. For this reason, at the beginning of the *Shiromani*, he wrote—"Victory to those of elegant speech, who possess the logic of the renowned systems, such as Varahamihira and others—" <note>original Sanskrit: 'जयन्ति ललितोक्तयः प्रथिततन्त्रस्रग्युक्तयः, वराहमिहिरादयः—'</note>. In the *Shiromani*, there are many sentences such as "The poet Bhaskara composed this system of principles to crush the ignorant" <note>original Sanskrit: 'सिद्धान्तग्रथनं कुबुद्धिमथनं चक्रे कविर्भास्करः'</note>. There is no lack of proud proclamations either. He had a great passion for poetry, and his descriptions of the seasons are proof of this. One can see the splendor of wordplay and double meanings <term>Yamak and Shlesh: rhetorical devices involving repetition and puns</term> throughout. Be that as it may.

Bhaskaracharya's *Patiganita* <note>arithmetic</note> and *Bijaganita* <note>algebra</note> are both unprecedented. In these, several mathematical methods and question-and-answer formats were unknown in Europe until two or three hundred years ago; even today, they remain a source of wonder for leading mathematicians. Bhaskaracharya wrote in his *Bijaganita*—

-> "Because the algebras of those named Brahma, Sridhara, and Padmanabha <-
-> are exceedingly extensive..." etc. <note>original Sanskrit: 'ब्रह्माह्वय-श्रीधर-पद्मनाभ—बीजानि यस्मादतिविस्तृतानि ।'</note> <-

After examining the works of Brahmagupta, Sridhara, Padmanabha, and others, he created his own Algebra as their essence. Sridhara's *Trishatika* has been published. Padmanabha's Algebra is unavailable. In this way, Bhaskaracharya took refuge in the authoritative works of his predecessors ❈ and refined them with many new specialties.

At this time, students of the advanced teacher-grade study his <term>Siddhanta</term> <note>A comprehensive treatise on Indian astronomy</note>. Considering the superiority of the *Saurapaksha* <note>The school of thought based on the Surya Siddhanta</note> as traditional, he did not accept other schools such as the *Brahmapaksha*. For this reason, he opposed Bhaskaracharya and attempted to point out flaws throughout his entire work wherever possible. Because of this, devotees of Bhaskaracharya continue to criticize him to this day. In the *Siddhanta-Tattva-Viveka*, it is written:

> "Those lowest of men who act contrary to this science, which is endowed with direct perception, tradition, and logic—their work is false and utterly devoid of Vedic authority." <note>original: "प्रत्यक्षागमयुक्तिशालि तदिदं शास्त्रं विहायान्यथा । यत्कुर्वन्ति नराधमास्तु तदसत् वेदोक्तिशून्यं भृशम् ॥"</note>

Every individual has their own unique tastes and variations in thought. Kamalakara was highly intelligent, and the arguments he wrote against the *Shiromani* <note>Referring to Bhaskaracharya's famous work, Siddhanta Shiromani</note> are not all to be dismissed as useless chatter or baseless. Furthermore, Kamalakara’s mastery of <term>Gola</term> <note>Spherical astronomy and geometry</note> is praiseworthy in many respects. Did Bhaskaracharya himself not leave behind critiques of topics like the <term>Lagna</term> <note>The ascendant or rising sign</note>? Why then should Kamalakara’s work not be examined! Astronomy is based on science; the things considered proven by various evidences today may, in the course of time, be found to contain errors or oversights. In this regard, Kamalakara also made several mistakes—which modern mathematicians have identified and understood.

> "What concern is that of ours?" <note>original: "किं नस्तया चिन्तया ।"</note>

**Nilambara Jha**—Born in the year 1745 of the Shaka era <note>approx. 1823 CE</note> into a prestigious and learned family of Maithil Brahmins. He was a resident of Patna and a protégé of King Shri Shivdas Singh of the Alwar State. He obtained the Hindi translations of Todd Hunter’s <note>Referring to the British mathematician Isaac Todhunter</note> works on Mensuration and Trigonometry—both plane and spherical—along with notes on other English mathematical texts. Based on these, he composed a work titled *Gola-prakash*, which was later refined by Shri Bapudeva Shastri in Kashi <note>Modern-day Varanasi</note> in the Shaka year 1763 <note>approx. 1841 CE</note>

**Samanta Chandrasekhar Singh**—There is a small princely state named 'Khandapara', located 30 <term>kos; a traditional unit of distance, roughly 2 miles</term> west of Cuttack in the province of Odisha. At the age of 16 or 17, his passion for astronomy grew, and through constant labor, he determined the corrections for astronomical observations <note>original: "vedhadi" - through instruments and observation</note> to make the calculations of ancient principles consistent with visual reality <term>drik-siddha; verified by observation</term>. In this, he has bound all the subjects of astronomy in beautiful poetry. The famous and excellent edition of 'Siddhanta Darpana' was prepared by the honorable Babu Yogesh Chandra Roy, M.A., Professor of Science at Cuttack College. In his English preface, Professor Roy has included many noteworthy subjects—upon seeing it, no amount of praise for your <note>The author uses a respectful 'your' here to address the subject's legacy</note> astronomical knowledge and insightful scholarship would be enough.

The Jagannath <note>original: "Jagdish" - referring to the Lord of the Universe/Puri</note> almanac <term>Panchang; a Hindu calendar and register of celestial events</term> currently prevalent in Odisha was initiated by the honorable Chandrasekhar according to his observation-verified mathematics. He was a great reformer. 'Siddhanta Darpana' is also studied and taught in the province of Bihar.
