**Mr. Sudhakara Dvivedi**—You were born in 1860 AD in Kashi <note>Modern-day Varanasi</note>. Your grand residence still stands beautifully in the village of Khajuri there. You were a Sarayupari Brahmin. Beyond the science of astronomy <note>original: "Jyotish-shastra"</note>, you had mastery over other subjects as well. You were a scholar of French, English, and Marathi, and a lover of Hindi. You possessed supernatural power and unprecedented talent for writing poetry, prose, and verse in both Sanskrit and the vernacular. Indeed, you were the savior of the science of astronomy. At this time, the commentaries and proofs of the ancient and complex theoretical mathematical texts—

---

—there is a mess of calculation manuals <note>term: "Karana-granthas" - concise astronomical treatises used for practical calculations</note> from the Arya, Brahma, and Surya schools, and now the Nautical school as well. This has spread like an incurable disease. Since the time of the Shastri, a new dispute regarding the almanac <note>term: "Panchang" - the Hindu calendar and almanac</note> arose, and to this day, great mathematicians across all of India have campaigned for it. In the South, Kero Laxman Chhatre (Saka 1746–1806) <note>The Saka era is a historical Hindu calendar system; 1746 Saka is approx. 1824 AD</note> wrote the 'Table of Planets' from English into Marathi and published the 'Patwardhani Almanac.' Raghunath Lele of Nasik (Saka 1746–1813) started the Tropical <note>original: "Sayan"</note> Almanac based on Nautical data. Mr. Chintamani Raghunath Acharya (Saka 1750–1801), an official at the Madras Observatory, published the 'Drigganita Almanac' in the Telugu language. The accounts of these reformers were written by Mr. Shankar Balkrishna Dikshit (Saka 1772) in 'Indian Astronomy.' Currently, Mr. Venkatesh Bapuji Ketkar has also composed two excellent calculation manuals named 'Ketaki' and 'Jyotirganita.' Meanwhile, in Bengal, the world-renowned Mr. Mahesh Chandra Nyayaratna issued reports on the subject of the almanac and conducted an examination of the strengths and weaknesses of the ancient and modern methods. Mr. Satkauri Siddhantabhushan wrote 'Refinement of the Bengali Almanac' and published several other booklets. Madhav Chandra Chattopadhyay promoted the 'Pure Theory Almanac' <note>original: "Vishuddha-Siddhanta-Panjika"</note> according to Nautical calculations. However, no universally accepted opinion was established. In 1904 AD, an 'Almanac Assembly' of all Indian astronomers was held in Bombay; questions were printed, a proposal to create a new calculation manual was made, and a reward was announced for the gentleman who could create it—in the end, no result was achieved. At present, two sides—the first being 'the seen and unseen' <note>referring to traditional methods that include metaphysical factors</note> and the second being 'the purely seen' <note>referring to observation-based calculation</note>—have been clashing with each other for years.

# Conclusion—

Up to this point, I have provided a brief introduction to the ancient and modern primary subjects of the <term>Science of Light<note>original: "Jyotish-shastra"; refers to the combined study of astronomy and astrology</note></term>, as well as the great gentlemen who have authored, corrected, and advanced it. This has been done so that contemporary lovers of astronomy and students may learn the essential facts. I have not sat down here to write a complete, exhaustive history of the Science of Light.

At present, the study and teaching of the <term>Sun Treatise<note>original: "Surya-siddhanta"; a foundational Sanskrit text on Indian astronomy</note></term>, the <term>Crest-Jewel of Siddhantas<note>original: "Siddhanta-shiromani"; the 12th-century masterpiece by Bhaskara II</note></term>, and the <term>Discrimination of Siddhanta Truths<note>original: "Siddhanta-tattva-viveka"; a 17th-century astronomical work</note></term> are prevalent in schools, and by studying these, one attains the title of <term>Master<note>original: "Acharya"</note></term>. In 1911, my translation of the "Chapter on the Celestial Sphere" <note>original: "Goladhyaya"</note> with its logical proofs was published by this very press. The community of scholars looked upon it with a favorable eye and adopted it—therefore, this translation of the "Chapter on Mathematics" <note>original: "Ganitadhyaya"</note> has been prepared following that same style and method.

As far as possible, I have attempted to make the subject matter of the original text simple and easy to comprehend. I have omitted the opinions and proofs of modern European theories. The reason for this is that the subject would have become excessively difficult, and writing a few scattered points here and there would have been of no benefit. This is because there is a vast difference—as wide as the distance between the earth and the sky—between Indian and Western mathematics and astronomy. Those who are thoughtful know for themselves that the secrets of Western theories cannot be understood in any way without first knowing the foundational mathematical subjects that support them from the beginning. It is a common practice among today's translators and commentators to provide a "taste" of miscellaneous information just to demonstrate their own vast knowledge. However, in my view, that is worthless. For such a task, an independent and detailed volume is required. Enough then;

<summary>The author concludes his introductory remarks, explaining that this translation of the 'Ganitadhyaya' follows his successful previous work and intentionally focuses on Indian systems rather than mixing them with Western theories.</summary>

# The Crest-Jewel of Siddhāntas
## With the Author’s Own Commentary
### The Chapter on Mathematics

---

> Victorious in the world is the Sun, who, out of deep compassion for mankind, reveals hidden objects through his own radiance; he who is the unique light revealing the Supreme Truth to those yogis whose minds are purified through the disciplined practice of meditating on the Eternal.

He is victorious—meaning he exists in a state of supreme excellence. Who? This Sun <note>original: "Bhānu"</note>. What is his nature? He is one, without a second. What does he do? He reveals or makes manifest. What? All objects. By what means? By his own light. Where? In the world. What kind of objects? Those that are hidden or invisible. Under what condition? When there is darkness. By what motive? Out of deep compassion for people—meaning a dense or profound mercy toward all living beings. And he does not only reveal physical objects like pots or cloths; he also reveals the Supreme Truth <note>original: "Paramatattva"</note>, which is the Supreme Brahman. To whom? To the yogis. In what state is this Truth? It is deeply hidden by the darkness of ignorance and a clouded mind. To what kind of yogis? To those of purified minds—those whose consciousness has been made stainless. By what means? Through the disciplined practice of meditating on the Eternal. Thus, the Sun alone shines, revealing the Supreme Truth to those yogis whose hearts are cleansed by the yoga of constant reflection on the True Being <note>original: "Sadvāsanā"</note>.

<summary>This opening page of Bhāskara II's mathematical treatise features a traditional invocation to the Sun, metaphorically equating the physical light of the sun with the spiritual illumination of the Supreme Truth.</summary>
<keywords>Siddhanta Shiromani, Bhaskara II, Sun God, Brahman, Yoga, Mathematics, Astronomy, Sanskrit Commentary</keywords>

# On the Calculation of the Planets

> Now, by the grace of the Divine, I shall reveal the hidden meanings within my own scientific work in a manner suited for students. I do this so that those with purified minds, through the practice of true reasoning <note>original: "vasana" — the underlying physical or geometric rationale of a mathematical rule</note>, may attain a realization of the fundamental truths within their hearts.
> 
> A clear understanding of these rationales cannot be achieved by one who is ignorant of the Sphere <note>the celestial sphere or armillary sphere used in ancient astronomy</note>. Therefore, those difficult statements regarding the Sphere have been explained first.

->First, having offered salutations to the desired deity with mind, speech, and body,<-
->the author expresses the hope for the desired goal from that deity:<-

> When the Friend of the Lotus <note>The Sun, whose light causes the lotus to bloom</note> rises to protect this world, acting as the means to destroy darkness and washing away the entire mass of faults, the sacrifices begin and the gods, led by Indra <note>original: "Shatakratu" — he of a hundred sacrifices</note>, shine in heaven. May that Sun, worshiped by the immortals, swiftly manifest in us a voice that pours forth eloquent speech. || 1 ||

"May he manifest" means may he illuminate. Who is he? The Sun. What? Our speech or voice. Of whom? Ours. What kind of speech? "That which pours forth eloquent speech" <note>original: "sukti-muc" — releasing well-spoken or wise words</note>. How? Swiftly. What is the nature of the Sun? "Worshiped by the immortals." This means he is to be praised by the gods.

Furthermore, what is the nature of the Sun? "When he has risen" — when this Sun has risen all around this earth to protect the world, to raise it up as if it had fallen dead during the night, then "they proceed." What proceed? The "sacrifices" <note>original: "kratu" — Vedic ritual offerings</note>. These include the five great daily sacrifices, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and the *Jyotistoma* <note>a major Soma sacrifice</note> rituals. The meaning is that wherever and whenever the Lord Sun rises, it is then and there that the sacrifices are performed. By using the phrase "when he has risen," the Teacher <note>the author, Bhaskara II</note> should not be suspected of supporting only the view of the *Uditahomin* <note>those who offer oblations after sunrise</note>. Because even for the *Anuditahomin* <note>those who offer oblations before sunrise</note>, it is because of the impending sunrise...

<summary>This page contains the opening invocation to the Sun God (Surya) and emphasizes the importance of understanding the "Vasana" or underlying rationale of astronomical calculations through the study of the celestial sphere.</summary>
<keywords>Sun God, Surya, planetary calculation, celestial sphere, Vedic sacrifice, Uditahomin, rationale, Bhaskara II</keywords>

--- Page 57 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Sun's influence, transitioning from the timing of sacrifices to the broader cosmic and spiritual effects of solar light.</meta>

# Chapter on the Measurement of Time in the Section on Mean Motions

The underlying sense is that the time for sacrifice is indeed near at hand. It is not only that the sacrifices <term>Yajnas; ritual offerings that maintain cosmic order</term> are set in motion. For this very reason, they also shine and sport. Where? In the heavens, in the celestial realm. Who? The Gods. Of what nature are they? Indra and the other deities, who are headed by the "Performer of a Hundred Sacrifices" <note>original: "Shatakratu," an epithet for Indra</note>. This is because they are the consumers of the sacrificial portions. 

Furthermore, what is the nature of the Sun <note>original: "Ravau"</note>? He is the performer of the destruction of darkness; he who ordains the annihilation of gloom is the "Dispeller of Darkness." What else is his nature? He is the washer away of the entire heap of faults of those who bow down. He by whom the entire collection of sins of those offering salutations is cleansed and removed is the "Purifier of the Humble." 

What else is his nature? He is the "Kinsman of the Water-born" <note>original: "Jalajini-bandhu," usually meaning the Sun as the friend of the lotus</note>. He is the friend of the lotus pond. Here, by the word "Water-born," the night-blooming lily is also included. This is because he causes even the lily to bloom by his own rays reflected through the orb of the Moon. 

In this way, may he—whose very nature is to benefit all things existing within the belly of the three worlds, whether born in water or on land—bestow upon me the gift of speech. 

One might ask: "Oh! From the Lord Sun, who possesses such great attributes, is only the gift of speech being requested?" It is true, and the reason is stated: For here, for poets intent on the composition of poetry, the primary desire is indeed the flow of excellent speech. This is the intended meaning.

<summary>This page describes the Sun as the catalyst for Vedic sacrifices and the purifier of sins, concluding with a prayer for eloquent speech. It explains the Sun's relationship to both day-blooming lotuses and night-blooming lilies through reflected light.</summary>

### The Radiance (Prabha Commentary) ###

> We worship that Supreme Goddess, who, though she possesses the appearance of a fresh dark cloud, destroys the inner darkness of the heart; she is the very sprout of supreme bliss. (1)
>
> May this "Radiance" commentary on the *Shiromani* shine forever in the hearts of the learned, its body blossoming with the arrangement of essential truths. (2)

Now the Teacher, in order to pacify the multitude of obstacles, performs an auspicious invocation at the beginning of the work he desires to compose. The phrase "Wherein to protect..." is explained clearly in the *Vasana* commentary <note>The author's own auto-commentary</note>. In various regions, the performance of rituals such as the *Agnihotra* <note>The sacred fire ritual</note> is ordained by traditionalists as being strictly tied to sunrise. Accordingly, the *Taittiriya* scripture <note>A branch of the Yajur Veda</note> provides understanding on this matter: "One offers the oblation at sunrise; one offers it before sunrise; one offers it at the time the stars have faded."

Regarding the Five Great Sacrifices <note>Pancha Mahayagna: the daily duties of a householder</note>, they are: "There are exactly five great sacrifices. These are the great sessions: the sacrifice to beings, the sacrifice to men, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the gods, and the sacrifice to the Creator." These are described in the *Shatapatha Brahmana* (11.5.6). Furthermore, in the third chapter of the *Laws of Manu*, the Five Great Sacrifices are enumerated beginning with "Teaching is the sacrifice to the Creator..."

The terms *Jalajini*, *Kamalini*, and *Kumudini* all refer to the lotus. Its blooming is caused solely by the rays of the sun in conjunction with the lunar orb. As it has been said:
> "The sun is a globe of fire; the planets and stars are globes of water.
> They appear luminous because they are lit by the rays of the sun."

Thus, the adjectives used here are scientifically sound. The meter used is <term>Shardulavikridita</term> <note>A classical Sanskrit poetic meter of 19 syllables per line, literally meaning 'the tiger's sport'</note>.

Sacrifices are commenced, and the gods such as Indra, who are the rightful recipients of the sacrificial portions, sport with joy in heaven. May that Sun, worshiped by the gods, who dispels the darkness of the universe and thoroughly washes away all the sins of his devotees, swiftly illuminate my speech so that it may bring forth beautiful expressions. || 1 ||

Now, he humbly offers praise to the ancient teachers—

> Victorious is the accomplished son of Jishnu <note>original: "Jishnujo"; referring to the great 7th-century mathematician and astronomer Brahmagupta</note>, the crest-jewel of the circles of astronomers. Victorious are Varahamihira and others, whose sayings are elegant and whose sound reasonings are famous in the scientific treatises <term>Tantra: a class of astronomical works providing rules for calculations from a specific epoch</term>. By observing their works, even one of small intellect like myself becomes capable of composing a vast scientific treatise. || 2 ||

The meaning of this is clear.

-> Light <note>original: "Prabha"; likely the name of a specific commentary or sub-commentary</note> <-

Brahmagupta, the son of Jishnu, is the accomplished scholar who is victorious, existing with supreme excellence. Of what kind is he? He is the crest-jewel—the head-gem—among the circles or groups of astronomers <term>Jyotirvid: one who knows the lights; an astronomer or astrologer</term>. Those whose sayings are beautiful and elegant; those whose reasonings are true and correct within the famous scientific treatises; Varahamihira and others are victorious. By observing their works—their books—even one like me, though of small intellect, becomes "accomplished" or capable in the "composition of a vast treatise" <note>original: "atanu-tantra-bandhe"</note>, meaning the construction of a great scientific work. Here, by praising Brahmagupta first, it is implied that this composition is rooted in the tradition accepted by him.

-> Vernacular Commentary <-

Brahmagupta, the son of Jishnu and the crest-jewel among astronomers, and the great poet Varahamihira and other teachers who promoted the reasonings of the scriptures, are famous in the world. By looking at their compositions, even one of meager intelligence like me becomes capable of creating a great scientific work. || 2 ||

Now, the author speaks to establish the connection between himself as the creator and the work he is about to begin—

> Having placed the lotus feet of my own teacher in my heart with devotion, and having obtained from him a fragment of enlightenment, the accomplished Bhaskara composes this *Siddhanta-shiromani* <note>The "Crest-jewel of Mathematical Astronomy"</note> for the pleasure of good mathematicians. It is a work that illuminates the intellect of the wise, contains excellent meters, is adorned with elegant expressions, is pure, offers clear understanding, and is lucid. (3)

This is also easy to understand.

### The Radiance <note>This refers to the *Prabha*, a Sanskrit commentary on the text.</note>

*Of my own teacher:* of his own father, Maheshvaracharya. *Illuminates the intellect:* a light for the wisdom or intelligence of those with good minds. *Excellent meters:* it contains proper poetic rhythms <note>original: "vrittani chhandamsi"</note>.

### Vernacular Exposition

I, Bhaskaracharya, after meditating with devotion in my heart upon the lotus feet of my teacher (my father) and receiving a small portion of knowledge from him, am composing this beautiful *Siddhanta-shiromani*. I do this for the delight of learned astronomers <term>Jyotishis (practitioners of the traditional Indian sciences of astronomy and astrology)</term>. This work is a light for the intellect of the wise, composed with excellent verses and beautiful expressions; it is flawless, easy to comprehend, and clear. (3)

Now, having specifically stated the reason for not beginning the book without cause, and stating another reason for the commencement in the first half of the verse, he addresses a prayer to the virtuous mathematicians in the second half—

> Although the ancients have composed works with clever expressions, this work is nevertheless undertaken to describe the specific details mentioned by them. These details have been arranged by me in their proper places throughout; therefore, let this work of mine also be examined in its entirety by virtuous mathematicians. (4)

Even though the ancient teachers <note>referring to predecessors like Aryabhata or Brahmagupta</note> created compositions with clever and polished words, this work was still begun by me. By the use of the word "this," he refers to the present work, whether it be cleverly expressed or not. If it is not cleverly expressed—

Then why should this work be commenced? To answer this, he says: *To speak of the distinctions [not mentioned] by them.* That which was spoken by them is "that which was said"; the distinctions from that are the "distinctions of what was said." This means those things which were not mentioned by them. Now, he addresses the virtuous people: *Virtuous people who are also mathematicians* <note>Sanskrit: sujanagaṇakāḥ</note>—by them, this work of mine should also be looked upon. The word "also" is used in the sense of inclusion. Therefore, O virtuous mathematicians! You have indeed looked upon the works of Brahma and others. Now, my work should also be looked upon, out of consideration for me. If it is to be looked upon, then it should be looked upon *entirely*, in its completeness. Why? Because those distinctions have been placed or deposited by me here and there in this book in their proper places. The meaning is that without looking at the entire book, all [these distinctions] cannot be known.

### Light <note>This is the 'Prabhā' commentary, likely by a later scholar explaining the primary text.</note>

*By the first ones*: by the previous teachers such as Brahmagupta, Pṛthūdakasvāmin, and others. The rest is clear in the commentary. **Shikharini meter** <note>A classical Sanskrit poetic meter consisting of 17 syllables per line</note>.

### Vernacular Commentary

Even though the previous teachers have composed works full of logic, this work has been started to bring to light the specific subjects they intended to prove. I have written all those distinctions in various places in between; therefore, virtuous mathematicians should see this book in its entirety. Because without seeing it in its entirety, the distinctions are not known. || 4 ||

Now, while requesting the virtuous mathematicians, he states the purpose:

> Let the virtuous be satisfied by understanding the distinctions uttered by me;
> The wicked, laughing at me out of ignorance, will [also] attain satisfaction. || 5 ||

Why the adjective "virtuous"? Because the wicked will attain satisfaction on their own. When the wicked see the distinctions spoken by me...

Then, not knowing these principles and having minds agitated by wickedness, they do not understand the specific meanings. ### Vernacular Commentary

May virtuous men be satisfied by understanding the specific details I have set forth. As for the wicked, they—failing to understand these specifics due to ignorance—will find their satisfaction only by mocking me. || 5 ||

Now, in the following verse, he states the definition of a <term>Siddhanta</term><note>A comprehensive astronomical treatise</note> and, in the two subsequent verses, speaks in praise of the Siddhanta:

> That is declared by the wise to be a **Siddhanta** in this collection of the branch of mathematical astronomy, wherein are discussed: the calculation of time beginning from a <term>Truti</term><note>An atom of time, approx. 1/33,750th of a second</note> up to the final dissolution of the universe; the various systems of time measurement; the motions of the celestial bodies; the two types of mathematics <note>Arithmetic/Algebra and Spherical Geometry</note>; questions with their answers; and the description of the positions of the Earth, the stars, and the planets, as well as instruments and the like. || 6 ||

> One who knows the <term>Jataka</term><note>Horoscopy/Natal astrology</note> and the <term>Samhita</term><note>Omens and mundane astrology</note>, and even a portion of the mathematical branch, but does not know the **Siddhanta**—which is expanded through infinite reasoning—is rendered useless when faced with clever questions regarding the essence of the science of astronomy. He is like a king painted on a wall, or a skillfully carved lion made of wood. || 7 ||

> Just as a royal army, though powerful with horses and infantry, appears diminished without trumpeting elephants; or a garden without mango trees; or a lake without water; or a young woman whose lover is away—so too, the wise have declared, does this science of astronomy appear without the **Siddhanta**. || 8 ||

The meaning is clear.

# Section on Mean Motions: Chapter on the Measurement of Time
<page-num>6</page-num>

### The Illumination <note>Sanskrit: Prabha; the name of the commentary</note>

In this composition regarding the branch of mathematics <note>Sanskrit: Ganitaskandha</note>: that which is counted or calculated is "mathematics." Because it is a specific part of the great tree of the science of the stars <note>Jyotishastra</note>, it is like a "branch" <note>skandha</note>; thus, it is the "mathematics-branch." In this composition, there is the calculation and consideration of Time, which has the *truti* <note>the smallest unit of time, approx. 1/33,750 of a second</note> as its beginning and the dissolution of the universe <note>Pralaya</note> as its end. 

There is a thorough investigation into the distinctions of the various measurements of time, such as Solar, Lunar, and others. It sets forth the motion of the planets as they move through the sky. Mathematics is twofold: manifest <note>arithmetic/algebra</note> and unmanifest <note>geometry/higher calculus</note>. Furthermore, there are problems along with their solutions. There is the description of the stable arrangement of the Earth, the asterisms <note>Nakshatras</note>, and the planets. There are instruments and so forth—the well-known tools for knowing the time. The word "and so forth" implies other related matters. Where these are discussed—this is called a **Siddhanta** <note>a comprehensive astronomical treatise</note> by the wise. This means that a treatise where these subjects are fully explained deserves the title of *Siddhanta*.

Thus:
> "Where the motions of the planets are investigated through extensive mathematical construction, that is a **Siddhanta**. Within this, the various high and low variations that assist those motions are included. Thus, the definition results in: a treatise that explains the motion of planets while being achievable through superior mathematics."

So said my venerable father, the teacher Sri Durgaprasada Dvivedi, in his review of the *Surya Siddhanta*.

Furthermore:
> "Where the matter declared in the Siddhanta is composed using one's own reasoning and relies on one's own instruments, that is a **Tantra**."

Based on the verse above, a work where the planets are calculated using the "heap of days" <note>Ahargana; the number of days elapsed since a fixed epoch</note> starting from the beginning of a *Yuga* <note>an immense cosmic cycle</note> is known as a **Tantra**. Similarly:
> "Where only certain parts of what is stated in the Siddhanta are described, and which is constructed with simplified methods, that is called a **Karana**."

Based on this verse, a work where the planets are calculated using the "heap of days" starting from the *Saka* era <note>an era beginning in 78 CE, used for practical daily calculations</note> is to be understood as a **Karana**.

The branches of **Horoscopy** <note>Jataka</note> and **Natural Astrology** <note>Samhita</note> exist alongside this mathematical branch. *Jataka* is the science that describes the good and bad results produced by the planets based on the time of birth of living beings. Likewise, *Samhita* is the science that explains universal effects such as abundance or famine based on the planetary movements at any given time. Knowing this, even a learned man who understands the essence of the deliberations of the science of the stars...

Regarding the significance of the subjects under discussion: one who is incapable of answering the questions posed by experts in these matters is considered insignificant and unqualified. One who does not know or understand the <term>Siddhanta</term><note>The foundational mathematical treatise of Indian astronomy</note> which is expanded and spread out through infinite and various types of logical proofs, is like a king painted on a wall or a lion made of wood—he is effectively useless and serves no practical purpose. This is the intended meaning.

Just as a royal army, though strengthened and driven forward by horses and other mounts, does not shine or appear magnificent if it is devoid of thundering elephants; or as a garden is lacking when the mango trees have withered away; or as a lake is empty without water; or as a young woman does not shine when her beloved—a fresh youth who is exceedingly dear to her—has gone abroad to another country; so too do the wise say that this science of light <note>original: "Jyotish-shastra"</note> does not shine at all when it is bereft of the Mathematical Pillar.

### Vernacular Commentary

The science of light is divided into three pillars: <term>Siddhanta</term><note>Mathematical astronomy</note>, <term>Samhita</term><note>Omens and collective destiny</note>, and <term>Hora</term><note>Natal horoscopy</note>. Among these, the pillar in which there is a detailed description of time calculations ranging from a tiny fraction <note>original: "truti"</note> to the end of a cosmic cycle <note>original: "pralayanta-kala"</note>, the explanation of time-measures such as Solar and Lunar, the determination of planetary motions, the application of algebra and arithmetic <note>original: "vyakta-avyakta ganita"</note>, various methods of questions and answers, the positions of the Earth, planets, and stars, and various types of instruments—that is what scholars call the **Siddhanta Pillar** (the Mathematical Pillar).

By knowing only the branches of Horoscopy and Omens, which are merely parts of the Mathematical Pillar, an astrologer cannot understand the questions of learned mathematicians, nor can he know the subject of Siddhanta which is expanded by infinite logical proofs. Such a mathematician is considered as useless as a king depicted in a painting on a wall or a lion crafted out of wood.

Just as a royal army, even if full of horses, camels, and chariots, does not look splendid without trumpeting elephants; or a garden without mango trees, a lake without water, and a young woman whose new husband is away in a foreign land—

# Vernacular Commentary

The Vedas are the initiators of the sacrificial rituals. And all sacrificial acts are said to be dependent on time. Since the knowledge of time comes from this science, *Jyotisha* is called a limb of the Veda.

The ancient teachers have said: Grammar is the mouth of the Veda-Purusha, *Jyotisha* is the two eyes, Etymology <note>Nirukta</note> is the ears, the Ritual Manuals <note>Kalpasutras</note> are the two hands, Phonetics <note>Shiksha</note> is the nose, and Prosody <note>Chandas</note> is the two feet. This science of light is the form of the eyes for the Veda-Purusha; therefore, it is the most excellent among all the limbs. For even a man possessed of ears, nose, and other limbs is of no use without eyes.

Therefore, this meritorious, secret, and essential science should be studied by the twice-born. The man who knows the science of *Jyotisha* partakes in Virtue, Wealth, Desire, and Fame. || 6-12 ||

# Chapter on Time Measurement in the Section on Planetary Motion

Now, in two verses, the author describes the movement of the zodiac <note>original: "bhacakra," literally the wheel of stars</note> along with the planets, which forms the very foundation of the science of astronomy <note>original: "jyotiḥ-śāstra"</note>:

> Having created the wheel of stars along with the planets situated at the beginning of the zodiacal signs, the Lotus-born Creator appointed them to perpetual revolution; he likewise fixed the stars at the poles to remain stationary. || 13 ||
>
> Thus, while the cage of the stars—including the planets—rotates very rapidly toward the western direction, the celestial wanderers <note>the planets</note> move toward the direction of Indra <note>the East</note> at a slower pace, traveling along their own paths which vary in height and depth. || 14 ||

This wheel of stars which is seen rotating along with the planets was created at the beginning of time by the Lotus-born Brahma, the creator of the universe, and was then appointed to perpetual, ceaseless revolution. This is what is being said: the stars <note>original: "bhāni"</note> are the specific lights such as Ashvini and others; their collection is the "wheel" <note>chakra</note>. This was created together with the planets, starting with the Sun. Those stars were arranged all around in an eastward sequence. The planets, however, were placed at the very beginning of the zodiac—at the start of the constellation Ashvini—arranged one above the other. Among them, the Moon is at the bottom. Above that is Mercury. Then Venus. Then the Sun. Above that is Mars. Then Jupiter. Then Saturn. Far above all of them is the wheel of the stars. The measurements of their orbits <note>term: "kakṣā" (orbital circles)</note> will be explained in the Chapter on Orbits.

One might ask: "Since the planets are placed one above the other, and the zodiac is far above them, how can it be said that the planets are 'situated at the beginning of the zodiac'?" 

It is true. Imagine a string where one end is tied to the center of the Earth and the second end is tied to the beginning of Ashvini on the wheel of the stars. The planets, such as the Moon and others, were placed by Brahma at the beginning of creation like beads threaded onto that string. The stellar sphere is divided into twelve parts...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial mechanics, specifically the construction of the zodiac and the forces driving planetary motion. It follows the description of dividing the celestial sphere into signs.</meta>

<page-num>14</page-num>
->On Planetary Calculations<-

Having divided the sphere in this manner, lines are drawn from the center of the Earth to every part. The points where these lines intersect the planetary orbits <note>The paths along which planets are believed to travel</note> mark the boundaries of the zodiac signs within those orbits. This is a brief explanation of how the signs are formed. I shall explain this in greater detail in the chapters on Orbits and the Celestial Sphere.

After creating a zodiac of this kind, the Creator <note>Brahma</note> placed it in the sky. In the place where it was stationed, there exists a wind named *Pravaha* <term>Pravaha: The "pro-propelling" cosmic wind believed to drive the daily rotation of the heavens</term>. This wind moves eternally toward the west. Driven by it, the entire circle of stars, along with the planets, is engaged in a westward rotation. This westward revolution is very rapid, completing one full turn of the celestial sphere in a single day.

Even as this "cage of stars" <note>The celestial sphere</note> containing the planets rotates so rapidly, the planets themselves move toward the direction of Indra <note>The East</note>; they travel eastward. They move along their own individual paths, which consist of epicycles <insert>high and low points</insert> as previously described. Their eastward motion is due to their own specific velocities. Because the westward motion <note>of the daily rotation</note> is so much greater, the planets—which are moving eastward at a much slower pace—do not appear to be moving eastward to the observer. Furthermore, at the northern and southern extremities of this celestial cage, there are two stars fixed as the Poles <note>The North and South celestial poles</note>.

### The Radiance <note>Commentary</note>

By the Creator of the Universe, the lotus-born Brahma, this "circle of stars"—the collection of constellations beginning with Ashvini—was created along with the planets like the Sun, stationed at the beginning of the zodiac. According to the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>original: "Sauravacana"</note>, the zodiac begins at the end of the constellation Revati <note>original: "Paushnanta"</note>; thus, the planets were stationed there at the start of the age. The meaning is that they were placed in that circular region of space defined by the ecliptic <term>Ecliptic: The sun's apparent path, divided into the signs of the zodiac</term>, proceeding eastward from the junction star of Revati.

Having created them, He fixed them in the *Pravaha* wind, which possesses a constant westward rotation. The two stars located at the southern and northern edges of the sphere governed by this zodiac are appointed as the two Poles. Therefore, because it is assigned to this constant westward rotation, the planet's own motion—its eastward progress—is slower than the motion of the zodiac, which completes its turn in sixty *ghatikas* <term>Ghatika: A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 ghatikas make a full day</term>.

## Vernacular Commentary

The Creator of the Universe, the lotus-born Brahma, having fashioned this Celestial Sphere <term>Bhachakra: the circle of asterisms or the zodiac</term> along with the planets and their satellites, appointed it to the ever-moving Prohibitive Wind <term>Pravaha-vayu: the cosmic wind believed to drive the stars westward</term>. He designated the stars at its southern and northern extremities as the "Poles" <note>Dhruva</note>. Because this Celestial Sphere is established in the Prohibitive Wind, it always revolves with great velocity toward the West along with the planets. However, the planets also move toward the East in their respective high and low orbital paths by their own slower eastward motion, which is less than the speed of the Prohibitive Wind. In other words, although the planets are seen going toward the West because of the Prohibitive Wind, they continue to move East by their own inherent motion. || 13-14 ||

<margin>The implication here is that the Celestial Sphere, or the Zodiac, which is fixed at the North and South poles, is turned like a wheel from West to East <note>The text likely means "East to West" in the context of the wind, or is describing the relative motion</note> by the Prohibitive Wind. > "Driven by the Prohibitive Wind for the sake of rising and setting, the cage of the stars <note>the firmament</note> together with the planets moves westward, level with Lanka."

## The simultaneous commencement of days, months, years,
## and Ages, beginning with the bright half of the month of Madhu. || 15 ||

<note>Madhu is a poetic name for the lunar month of Chaitra, which marks the beginning of spring.</note>

Now, in the previous commentary, time was described as beginningless and endless. And yet, it is said to have a "commencement" at the start of creation. Commencement implies a beginning. At the time of universal dissolution <term>pralaya; the periodic destruction of the cosmos</term>, there is an end. As it is stated in other scriptures:

> Time matures all beings, together with the Self.
> At the end of the cycle, when all is ripened, Time itself dissolves into the Unmanifest.

If this is so, how can time be called beginningless and endless? It is true that for the Lord Time—who is both embodied and all-pervading—there is a "dissolution" in the sense that after the previous Great Dissolution, there is an absence of the Sun and other celestial bodies which act as the "manifestors" of time. This state, where the manifest resides within the Unmanifest, is what is called its dissolution. However, there is no final, absolute destruction of Time itself. As for the quote, "At the end... it dissolves into the Unmanifest," that refers specifically to this state of remaining in an unmanifest condition. Therefore, it is correct to call Time beginningless and endless. 

When the planets, which are the causes of manifestation, appeared at the start of creation, then the specific divisions of time—such as days, months, years, and Ages <term>Yugas</term>—all commenced simultaneously and in a single stroke. This is what is meant: when the Moon and Sun were both situated at the beginning of Aries, it was the first lunar day <term>pratipat</term> of the bright half of the month of Chaitra. Thus, the sequence of days, solar months, years, Ages, Manvantaras <note>vast periods of time ruled by a Manu</note>, and the Kalpa <note>a "Day of Brahma" lasting 4.32 billion years</note> all began at that very moment. Furthermore, this began from the sunrise. In which place did that sunrise occur? In the city of Lanka <note>In Indian astronomy, Lanka refers to a hypothetical location on the equator used as the prime meridian, not necessarily modern Sri Lanka</note>. Likewise, it began on the day of that same planet: meaning, on Sunday.

In the city of Lanka—meaning at the horizon of the Earth's center as marked by Lanka—from the time of the Sun's rise, which is its contact with the horizon. After the establishment of the zodiac, the movement of the planets began—

## Vernacular Commentary

In the city of Lanka <note>the theoretical equatorial point used as the prime meridian in Indian astronomy</note>, on Sunday, at the moment of sunrise during the first day of the bright fortnight of Chaitra, the day, month, year, and *Yuga* <note>an immense cycle of time</note> all began simultaneously. That is to say, the commencement of all these calculations occurred on that very day, and that day is considered the fundamental epoch. No calculation began from any middle point. || 15 ||

Now, he describes the divisions of the measurements of time in three verses:

That which is the thirtieth part <note>original: "kharaama-bhaga," where 'kha' is 0 and 'raama' is 3, signifying 30</note> of the blinking of an eye (*nimesha*)
->is called a *tatpara*; a hundredth part of that is a *truti*.<-
With eighteen <note>original: "dhriti," a numerical code for 18</note> *nimeshas* a *kastha* is formed;
->by thirty of those, the calculators define a *kala*. || 16 ||<-
Thirty *kalas* make a *ghatika*; a *kshana*
->is two *nadis* <note>another term for ghatika</note>; thirty of those make a day.<-
With ten <note>original: "khendu," where 'kha' is 0 and 'indu' is 1, signifying 10</note> long syllables <note>the time taken to pronounce a long vowel</note> an *asu* <note>a breath</note> is formed;
->with six of those a *pala* is made, and with sixty of those a *ghatika*. || 17 ||<-
Sixty *ghatikas* make a day; with thirty <note>original: "svaraama," where 'sva' is 0 and 'raama' is 3</note>
->of those days a month is made, and with twelve of those a year.<-
In the circle of the sky, the divisions are equal to those of time, beginning with the year:
->they are the Circle, Sign, Degree, Minute, and Second. || 18 ||<-

The falling of the eyelids of the eyes is a *nimesha*. The amount of time in which that action is completed is also called by the word *nimesha* by figurative extension. A thirtieth part of that is designated a *tatpara*. A hundredth part of a *tatpara* is a *truti*. Furthermore, eighteen *nimeshas* make a *kastha*. In some other scientific texts, the reading is "fifteen" <note>original: "tithibhi," referring to the 15 lunar days</note> instead of eighteen. Thirty *kasthas*...

# On the Calculation of Planets
<page-num>18</page-num>

The <term>Kala</term><note>A unit of time; 1/30th of a Ghatika</note> has been described. Thirty *Kalas* make one <term>Ghatika</term><note>A standard Indian unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. This is also called an *Akshi* <note>literally "eye," referring to the blink of an eye</note>. It is the sixtieth part of the sky <note>referring to the division of a circle</note>. Two *Ghatikas* make a *Kshana* or a <term>Muhurta</term><note>A period of 48 minutes</note>. Thirty *Kshanas* make a day.

Now, the day is described by another method: by "long syllables" <note>original: *Gurvakshara*</note> measured by the number ten <note>original: *khendu* (moon-zero), a numerical code for 10</note>, which constitutes one <term>Asu</term><note>A unit of time based on a single breath</note>. A short syllable has one beat. A long syllable has two beats. As it is stated:

> That which has an *Anusvara* <note>nasal sound</note>, ends in a *Visarga* <note>aspirated sound</note>, is long by nature, or is followed by a conjunct consonant.

This is explained in the rules of prosody <note>meter/rhythm</note>. A syllable with a nasal, an aspirate, a long vowel, or one followed by a cluster of consonants is known as "long" even if the vowel itself is short. The time it takes to pronounce ten such long syllables is one *Asu* or <term>Prana</term><note>literally "breath"</note>. This is the time taken for the inhalation and exhalation of a healthy man. Six *Pranas* make one *Paniya-pala*. Sixty *Palas* make one *Ghati*. Sixty *Ghatis* make one day. Thirty days make one month. Twelve months make one year. Thus, the divisions of time are shown.

In this context, the division of space <note>original: *kshetravibhaga*</note> is also mentioned. In space, the divisions are equal to the divisions of time. In the "field" or the orbit, the divisions of the year are to be understood as equal parts. What are they? The Circle <note>the whole zodiac</note>, Signs, Degrees, Minutes, and Seconds <note>original: *Chakra, Rashi, Amsha, Kala, Villipta*</note>. Just as a year has divisions of months and days, the Great Circle has divisions of Signs and Degrees.

---

->Vernacular Commentary<-

The time it takes for an eyelid to fall (<term>Nimesha</term>) is divided: one-thirtieth of that is a *Tatpara*, and one-hundredth of a *Tatpara* is called a <term>Truti</term><note>The smallest unit of time, often compared to the blink of an eye or the piercing of a leaf</note>. The time it takes for the eyelid to fall eighteen times is designated as a <term>Kashtha</term>. Thirty *Kashthas* make one *Kala*. Thirty *Kalas* make one sidereal <term>Ghati</term>, two *Ghatis* make one *Muhurta*, and thirty *Muhurtas* make one day. The time taken to pronounce ten long syllables...

# Chapter on the Measurement of Time in the Section on Mean Motions

The time it takes <note>referring to the respiration of a healthy man</note> is called a *Prana* <term>Prana: literally 'breath', a unit of time approximately equal to 4 seconds</term>. Six *Pranas* make one *Pala*, and sixty *Palas* make one *Ghari* <note>also known as a Nadika, approximately 24 minutes</note>. Sixty *Gharis* constitute one day, thirty days make one month, and twelve months make one year. In the same manner, within the orbit of the planets, the divisions of a Revolution, Sign, Degree, Minute, and Second are arranged in sequence.

In this way —

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Nimesha time / 30 = Tatpara | Tatpara / 100 = Truti |

18 $\times$ *Nimesha* = *Kashtha* ; 30 $\times$ *Kashtha* = *Kala* <note>unit of time</note>.
30 $\times$ *Kala* = Sidereal *Ghari*. 2 *Gharis* = *Muhurta*. 30 *Muhurtas* = one day.
Time to pronounce 10 long syllables = *Asu* = *Prana*. 6 *Pranas* = *Pala*. 60 *Palas* = *Ghari*.
60 *Gharis* = one day. 30 days = one month and 12 months = year.
In the planetary orbit, the nomenclature according to the year etc. is divided as follows —

->Year = Revolution (*Bhagana*)<-
->Month = Zodiac Sign (*Rashi*)<-
->Day = Degree (*Ansha*)<-
->Ghari = Minute of Arc (*Kala*)<-
->Pala = Second of Arc (*Vikala*)<-

In the *Asus* <note>breaths</note> of a full day and night, there are nine hundred seventy-two thousand *Nimeshas*. And the value of the minutes in a full circle is twenty-one thousand six hundred. From this, the proportion is calculated —

21,600 : 972,000 :: 1 *Asu* = 972,000 / 21,600 = 45.

Thus, it is proven that there are 45 *Nimeshas* in one *Asu*. || 16-18 ||

# On the Calculation of the Planets

### Now, using these same definitions of time divisions, he describes the standards of the Solar and other systems—

-> A single revolution of the Sun through the circle of the zodiac is declared to be a Solar Year; that same period is a single day and night for the Gods and the Demons. The time from one conjunction of the Sun and Moon until the next is a Lunar Month; this is also a day and night for the Ancestors. (19) <-

-> The interval between two successive sunrises is a Solar Civil Day. That same period is known as a Terrestrial Day, while a Sidereal Day is defined by one complete rotation of the stars. (20) <-

The amount of time in which the Sun, moving eastward, completes a full circuit of the zodiac beginning with Aries <note>original: "meshadibhachakram"</note> is declared to be a Solar Year. A twelfth part of that is a Solar Month. A thirtieth part of that month is a Solar Day. A sixtieth part of that day is a Solar *Ghatika* <note>a unit of 24 minutes</note>, and a sixtieth part of that is a Solar *Vighatika*. This should be understood everywhere according to the previous definitions. This concludes the Solar standard.

Now, the Divine standard. "That same period is a day and night for the Gods and Demons." That which is a Solar Year is a single "day-night" <note>original: "dyuratram," a full 24-hour cycle</note> for the Gods and the Daityas <note>Demons or Titans</note>. They share the same day-night cycle, but what is day for the Gods is night for the Daityas. This will be explained further in the section on the Sphere <note>the *Goladhyaya*</note>. From this day-night, the months and years are calculated using the same previous definitions. Thus, a Year of the Gods consists of three hundred and sixty Solar Years. This concludes the Divine standard.

Now, the Lunar standard. "The time from one conjunction of the Sun and Moon until the next is a Lunar Month." The conjunction of the Sun and Moon occurs at the end of the New Moon <note>original: "amavasya"</note>. The duration of time from that conjunction until the next is one Lunar Month <note>term: *Vidhumasa* (Lunar Month)</note>. Thus, it is stated here that the month ending with the New Moon is a Lunar Month. From that month, the years and other divisions are calculated according to the previous definitions. This concludes the Lunar standard.

# Page 21
## Chapter on Time Measurement in the Section on Mean Motions

Now, **the Ancestral measurement**. This ancestral measurement constitutes a day and a night. That which is a <term>Lunar Month</term> <note>original: vidhumasa; the period from one new moon to the next</note> is exactly one <term>Day-and-Night</term> <note>original: ahoratram</note> for the Ancestors <note>The Pitris or spirits of the departed</note>. From this, the calculation of their months, years, and so on follows as previously described.
Thus ends the Ancestral measurement.

Now, **the Civil measurement**. It is the interval between two rises of the Sun. The interval between two <term>Solar Risings</term> <note>original: arkodaya</note> is a Solar Civil Day. This same measurement should be known by the name <term>Earth-Day</term> <note>original: kudina; literally "day of the earth"</note>. From this also, the calculation of months, years, and so on follows as before. Here, the mention of the "Sun" is an illustration; therefore, for other planets as well, the interval between two of their respective risings is their specific Civil Day.
Thus ends the Civil measurement.

Now, **the Sidereal measurement**. A stellar day is one revolution of the starry sphere. The meaning is that one rotation of the stars is a <term>Sidereal Civil Day</term> <note>original: nakshatra-savana</note>.
Thus ends the Sidereal measurement.

---
->**The Illumination (Commentary)**<-

The completion of the circle by the Sun's own motion—traveling through the twelve signs of the zodiac—is declared to be a Solar Year or <term>Sauravarsha</term>. Although the Teacher <note>the author of the primary verses</note> has not specified whether this <term>Completion of the Circle</term> <note>original: chakrabhoga</note> is <term>Tropical</term> <note>original: sayana; with precession</note> or <term>Sidereal</term> <note>original: nirayana; without precession</note>, both should be considered. A "Day-and-Night" refers to a full twenty-four-hour cycle. According to the statement in the <term>Surya Siddhanta</term> <note>A foundational Sanskrit text on astronomy</note>, the day and night of the Gods and Demons are mutually opposite. The "conjunction of the Sun and Moon" refers to the time starting from when their positions on the ecliptic are identical.
"Union" or "Yoga" here means the absence of east-west distance between them on the orbital circle. The interval between two such unions is a Lunar Month. The definition of the word "Month" (Masa) is as follows:
> "They are called 'Masa' because they are measured <note>masyante</note> by the increase and decrease of their own digits <note>phases of the moon</note>. These months are known to consist of thirty lunar days (tithis)."
This measurement of a lunar month becomes one Day-and-Night for the Ancestors.

"Rising" is the contact of the Sun's disk with the horizon. The time produced by the interval between two sunrises is a Solar Civil Day; it is called a "Land-Day" or "Earth-Day" <note>kudina</note>. By the term "Earth-Day," the civil day relating to the Earth is grasped. It is inferred that this technical name entered common usage due to the Earth's rotation. Similarly, for the planets and stars, the period from one rising to the next rising is to be understood as their respective Civil Day. In some places, the time it takes for the Moon to pass through a lunar mansion (nakshatra) is called a sidereal day.
> "By the passage of the Moon through a lunar mansion, a sidereal day is defined."
This is according to a statement in the <term>Vishnudharmottara</term> <note>An ancient encyclopedic scripture</note>. The verses are composed in the <term>Bhujangaprayata</term> and <term>Pramanika</term> meters.

## Vernacular Commentary

The time it takes for the Sun to traverse the twelve signs of the zodiac is called a **Solar Year**, and this same duration is considered a full day and night <note>Aho-ratra: literally 'day-night'</note> for the Gods and the Demons. The period from one conjunction of the Sun and Moon (at the end of the new moon) to the next is called a **Lunar Month**. This is considered a full day and night for the Ancestors <note>Pitris: the spirits of departed ancestors who, in Vedic cosmology, reside on the dark side of the moon</note>. The interval between two sunrises is called the Sun's <term>Civil Day</term> <note>original: "Savana-dina"; a day measured from sunrise to sunrise</note>. A Civil Day is also called a "Ku-dina" <note>literally 'earth-day'</note>. The time it takes for the circle of stars to complete one revolution is called a <term>Sidereal Day</term> <note>original: "Nakshatra-dina"</note>.

## Mathematical Proof

The number of days in which the Sun, through its own eastward motion, traverses the twelve signs is called a <term>Solar Year</term>. In practice, this is used in two ways: Tropical <note>Sayana: with precession</note> and Sidereal <note>Nirayana: without precession</note>. In this manner, the time taken to traverse one sign is a Solar Month, and the time taken to traverse one degree is a Solar Day. 

Here, we consider the relationship between Civil, Lunar, and Sidereal <term>Ghatikas</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 ghatikas make one full day</note>. In one Civil Day, the motion of the Sun in minutes of arc is produced; from this, a proportion is made: if sixty Civil Ghatikas are obtained in the daily motion, what is obtained in one degree of arc? Thus, even though the value varies every moment in a Solar Day, the mean Civil Ghatikas are established. 

Similarly, if sixty Lunar Ghatikas are found within the Civil Ghatikas of a Lunar Day, what is found within the Civil Ghatikas of a Solar Day? Thus, the mean Lunar Ghatikas in a Solar Day are found. And if sixty Sidereal Ghatikas are found within Sidereal Civil Ghatikas, what is found within Solar Civil Ghatikas? Thus, the mean Sidereal Ghatikas in a Solar Day are established. 

In the same way, if sixty Solar Ghatikas are found in Solar Civil Ghatikas, what is found in Lunar Civil Ghatikas? The result will be the mean Solar Ghatikas in a Lunar Day. Likewise, Civil and Sidereal Ghatikas will also be established for a Lunar Day. Then the proportion is made again: if sixty Solar or Lunar Ghatikas are found in Solar or Lunar Civil Ghatikas, then sequentially for the Sidereal...

Now, he describes **the measurement of Brahma**:

> The quarters of a Yuga <note>an epoch or age</note>, such as the Kruta, are composed of solar years multiplied by 4,320,000 in sequence. (21)
> These are joined with their respective dawn and twilight periods, which are one-tenth of their own measure; the sum of these four ages is a Yuga, totaling 4,320,000 years. (22)
> A Manu <note>a period ruled by a progenitor of humanity</note> consists of 71 such Yugas; a day of the Lotus-Born (Brahma) is formed by fourteen such Manus, and his night is of the same duration. (23)
> There are transitional periods (Sandhyas) between the Manus equal to the length of a Kruta age, placed at the beginning, middle, and end; thus, a day of Brahma consists of a thousand Yugas. This day is also called a Kalpa, and a full day and night consists of two Kalpas. (24)
> The lifespan of Brahma (Shatananda) is said to be one hundred such years; this total lifespan is called a Mahakalpa by the ancients. Since time is beginningless in these measurements, I do not know how many such Brahmas have already passed away. (25)

**Regarding the phrase "Khakha-abhra-danta-sagarai" <note>A mnemonic numerical notation representing 4,320,000</note>:** By four times four hundred and thirty-two thousand solar years, the first quarter of the Yuga named Kruta is formed, totaling 1,728,000 years. By three times that amount, the second Yuga named Treta—

The [Krita] quarter consists of 1,296,000 years. The third quarter, Dvapara, is twice the base unit at 864,000 years. The fourth, Kali, is one unit at 432,000 years. <note>The text describes the 4:3:2:1 ratio of the four ages: Krita, Treta, Dvapara, and Kali.</note> What are the specific characteristics of these age-quarters <term>Yuga-charanas; the four stages of a Great Age</term>? They are joined with their own "twilight periods" and "twilight-portions" equal to one-tenth of their respective lengths. <note>The "twilight" (Sandhya) occurs at the start, and the "twilight-portion" (Sandhyansha) at the end of an age.</note> One-twelfth of the total measurement of an age-quarter is the measurement of that quarter's dawn. That occurs at the beginning of the quarter. An equal portion is the dusk, which occurs at the end of the quarter. Thus, it is meant that these age-quarters are described along with their respective dawns and dusks.

At the beginning of the Krita age, the dawn years are 144,000. At the end of Krita, the dusk is 144,000. At the beginning of Treta, the dawn is 108,000. At the end of Treta, the dusk is 108,000. At the beginning of Dvapara, the dawn is 72,000. At the end of Dvapara, the dusk is 72,000. At the beginning of Kali, the dawn is 36,000. At the end of Kali, the dusk is 36,000.

"The sum of these is a Great Age." The sum of these four quarter-measurements is the measurement of a <term>Mahayuga; a full cycle of four ages</term>. That total is 4,320,000 <note>original: "radabdhyo'yutahatah" - a mnemonic for 4,320,000</note>.

"A Manu is composed of seventy-one Great Ages." One <term>Manvantara; the lifespan of a Manu or progenitor of humanity</term> is measured by seventy-one of those Great Ages. Fourteen such Manus, along with their transitional periods, constitute a day of the "Lotus-Born" <note>Brahma, the Creator</note>, and his night is of the same duration. A night equal to Brahma's day also occurs. By the word "measured" <note>Pramanika</note>, the poetic meter is also indicated.

Behold: a Manu is said to be seventy-one Great Ages. There are fourteen Manus in a day of Brahma. When seventy-one is multiplied by fourteen, it equals 994. However, in the sacred Smritis and Puranas, it is said:

> A day of Brahma is said to be one thousand Great Ages.

To resolve the doubt of how this is stated, the author says: "There are transitional twilights for the Manus, equal to the years of a Krita age, occurring at the beginning, the middle, and the end." "Beginning, middle, and end" refers to the junctions between the fourteen Manus. Thus, there are fifteen such junctions. In these beginnings, middles, and ends of the Manus—

# Chapter on Time Measurement in the Section on Mean Motions

There are fifteen transitional periods <term>Sandhyas; periods of junction between ages</term>. These are equal in duration to the years of the Golden Age <note>original: "Krita-abda"</note>. When the years of the Golden Age are multiplied by fifteen, they become equal to the years of six Great Ages <note>original: "Yuga-shatka"</note>. Therefore, when these are combined, a thousand Great Ages are called a Day of Brahma. How this is calculated might seem inconsistent, but it is logically established. That which is a Day of Brahma is also known by the term *Kalpa* <term>a cosmic eon lasting 4.32 billion years</term>. Likewise, his night is of the same duration. A full day and night consists of two *Kalpas*. One hundred years, measured by the previously defined units of time, constitutes the lifespan of Brahma. That lifespan is called a *Mahakalpa* <term>Great Eon</term>. According to the *Puranas* <note>ancient Indian encyclopedic texts of mythology and cosmology</note>, it is said and heard that after that period, another Brahma arises. In the *Vishnu Purana*:

> By his own measurement of time, his lifespan is recorded as one hundred years.
> That total is called a *Para*, and half of that is designated as a *Parardha*.

In response to the doubt regarding how many such cycles have passed, it is said: "Because time is beginningless," and so on. Since time has no beginning, I do not know how many have passed.

---

->The *Prabha* Commentary<-

The phrase "Zero, zero, sky, teeth..." <note>a mnemonic for large numbers</note> and so on, corresponds to the statement in the *Surya Siddhanta*: "This arrangement of the Golden Age and others is determined by the quarters of Virtue." From the time of creation, when a period equal to the Golden Age has passed in the Iron Age <note>Kali Yuga</note>, the reign of a *Manu* <term>progenitor of humanity</term> begins; after its completion and the passage of a similar period, the second *Manu* appears. In this sequence, there are fifteen transitional periods for the fourteen *Manus*—this is the clear meaning. "The hundred-joyed one" refers to Brahma. Thus, by the previously mentioned definition of time, he has a lifespan of one hundred years. According to the words of the *Surya Siddhanta*, his maximum life is one hundred. That lifespan—the life of Brahma—is called the *Mahakalpa*, the Great Dissolution, or the Elemental Dissolution <note>original: "Prakritika-pralaya"</note>. This was established by the ancient Sages. Because this famous Time is "beginningless"—meaning it lacks an ultimate point of origin—therefore, I, Bhaskaracharya, do not know how many such "Lotus-born" Brahmas have passed up to the present time. The meaning is that infinite numbers have passed.

The twelfth part of each Age <note>Yuga</note> at its beginning and end constitutes its Dawn <note>Sandhya</note> and Twilight <note>Sandhyansha</note> years. That is to say, at the start of an Age, a period equal to one-twelfth of the Age is the Age-Dawn, and at the end, an equal amount is the Age-Twilight. Therefore, by adding the Dawns and Twilights, the full measure of the Age is completed. In this manner, the value of a Great Age <note>Mahayuga</note> is 4,320,000 years.

The measure of one Manu <note>a progenitor of humanity; a period of time</note> consists of seventy-one Great Ages. A Day of Brahma is composed of fourteen such Manus, and his Night is equal in length to his Day. At the beginning, middle, and end of these fourteen Manus, there are Manu-Intersections <note>Manusandhi</note> equal to a Golden Age <note>Satyayuga</note>; thus, there are fifteen intersections across the fourteen Manus. Including these, the total measure of fourteen Manus becomes one thousand Great Ages. This is the length of Brahma's day, which is also called a Kalpa <note>an eon</note>. In this way, a full day and night <note>Ahoratra</note> of Brahma consists of two Kalpas.

The maximum lifespan <note>Paramayu</note> of Brahma, according to his own definition of time, is one hundred years. The ancient teachers <note>Purvacharyas</note> have called this total lifespan a Great Kalpa <note>Mahakalpa</note>. Because time is without beginning and without end, I do not know how many years of Brahma's life have passed up to the present moment.

### Mathematical Proof

The arrangement of the Ages such as the Golden <note>Krita</note>, Silver <note>Treta</note>, and others is described in the Puranas <note>ancient Hindu texts</note> according to the "Feet of Virtue" <note>Dharmapada</note>. That is, the Golden Age stands on four feet, the Silver on three, the Copper <note>Dvapara</note> on two, and the Iron <note>Kali</note> on one foot. Therefore, the measure of these Ages in solar years is as follows:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 432,000 <note>The base unit or 'tenth' of a Mahayuga</note> | × 4 = | 1,728,000 | = Golden Age <note>Krita</note>. |
| ” | × 3 = | 1,296,000 | = Silver Age <note>Treta</note>. |
| ” | × 2 = | 864,000 | = Copper Age <note>Dvapara</note>. |
| ” | × 1 = | 432,000 | = Iron Age <note>Kali</note>. |

A Great Age <note>Mahayuga</note> is formed by the sum of all the feet of virtue. The sum of these feet of virtue is ten. From this, the proportion is calculated—in the sum of ten equal feet of virtue...

# Chapter on the Measurement of Time in the Section on Mean Motions.

When the Great Age <note>Sanskrit: *Mahayuga*; a cycle of 4,320,000 solar years</note> is assembled, what is the value in each of the quarters of Virtue <note>Sanskrit: *Dharmapada*; referring to the belief that righteousness decreases by one quarter in each successive age</note>? In this manner, the distinct value of all the ages is established. Therefore, it is written in the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit text on Indian astronomy</note>: **"The tenth part of a Great Age multiplied by four, three, two, and one [respectively]..."** and so forth.

The twelfth part of these ages—*Krita*, *Treta*, and the others—constitutes the "Dawn" <note>Sanskrit: *Sandhya*; the transitional period before an age</note> and the "Twilight" <note>Sanskrit: *Sandhyansha*; the transitional period after an age</note>. Their values are written above in the *Vasana Bhashya* <note>The author's own explanatory commentary on the mathematical verses</note>. These four ages are counted along with their Dawns and Twilights.

This same Brahma-measurement is written in the *Manusmriti* <note>The Laws of Manu, an ancient legal and social text</note>:
> They say the *Krita* Age consists of four thousand years.
> Its Dawn is as many hundreds, and its Twilight is of the same amount.
> In the other three ages with their Dawns and Twilights,
> The thousands and hundreds decrease by one in each.
> This four-age cycle which has been enumerated,
> This total of twelve thousand [divine years] is called an Age of the Gods.
> One thousand such Ages of the Gods
> Should be known as a single Day of Brahma, and his Night is of the same length.
> Those who know the measurement of Day and Night know that
> The holy Day of Brahma ends after a thousand Ages, and the Night is of the same duration.
> — *Chapter 1, Verses 69-73* <note>original: "१ अ. ६९-७३ श्लो."</note>

The values of the quarters of the ages, such as *Krita*, along with their respective Dawns:

| | Dawn | + | Age Proper | + | Twilight | | Total |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---|
| **Krita** | 400 | + | 4000 | + | 400 | = | 4800 |
| **Treta** | 300 | + | 3000 | + | 300 | = | 3600 |
| **Dvapara** | 200 | + | 2000 | + | 200 | = | 2400 |
| **Kali** | 100 | + | 1000 | + | 100 | = | 1200 |

<note>The ages including their Dawns and Twilights.</note>

->12000 = A Great Age.<-

Here, from the quarters of the ages alone, the quarters of the ages including their Dawns and Twilights are [calculated] according to their own...

# In Planetary Mathematics —

Since there are more than two tenths, according to the rule "Now, when exceeding one's own portion—" the teacher has written that the <term>Sandhyā-Sandhyāṃśa</term><note>The dawn and twilight periods of a cosmic age</note> values, when combined with their twelfth parts, are "measured by their own twelve parts." Furthermore, regarding the combination of both twilights, it is written in the *Sūrya Siddhānta*: "One-sixth is the measure of the two twilights."

| Calculation Type | Formula and Result |
| :--- | :--- |
| One Manvantara | 71 x 120,000 = 8,520,000 |
| Kalpa measure (less junctions) | 14 x 8,520,000 = 119,280,000 |
| Junction (Sandhi) measure | 15 x 4,800 = 72,000 |
| Total Day of Brahma | 119,280,000 + 72,000 = 120,000,000 |

These figures are in <term>Divya-māna</term><note>Divine years, where 1 divine year equals 360 human years</note>; therefore, multiplying by 360 will give the <term>Mānuṣa-māna</term><note>Human years</note>. Now, the state of Time is described:

4,320,000 = Measure of a <term>Yuga</term><note>An epoch or Great Age</note>.
4,320,000 x 71 = 306,720,000 = Measure of a <term>Manu-varṣa</term><note>The years in the reign of one Manu</note>.
And, 306,720,000 x 14 = 4,294,080,000 = The Day of Brahma. However, within the fourteen Manus, there are fifteen <term>Sandhis</term><note>Junction periods between reigns</note>, and the duration of a Sandhi is equal to the <term>Kṛta-varṣa</term><note>The Golden Age, or Satya Yuga</note> of 1,728,000 years. This is $2 + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{5}{2}$ <gloss>two and a half parts</gloss> of the Yuga (4,320,000). Therefore, multiplying the two-and-a-half parts of a Yuga by fifteen: $\frac{2 \times 4,320,000 \times 15}{5}$ <note>The text likely intends the ratio of the Kṛta Yuga to the total Mahāyuga</note> = 25,920,000. This becomes the six-fold Yuga measure. Adding this to the previously established Day of Brahma, the exact Day of Brahma becomes 4,320,000,000 years.

By doubling the day's measure, we get the measure of a full day and night (<term>Ahorātra</term>). Multiplying that by thirty gives the measure of a month, and multiplying that by twelve gives the measure of a year: 31,104,000,000,000. Multiplying this by 100 results in the total lifespan of Brahma. || 21–25 ||

->Now he says something else—<-

> Similarly, of the current lifespan, half
> has passed; some say eight and a half years remain.

<note>original: "tathā vartamānasya kasyāyuṣo'rdhaṃ gataṃ sārdhavarṣāṣṭakaṃ kecidūcuḥ"</note>

->**Whatever the tradition may be, it is of no practical use here;**<-
->**The planets are to be calculated from the time elapsed in the current day.**<- <note>Verse 26</note>

Likewise, I do not know exactly how much of the current Brahma's <term>Brahma: the creator deity whose lifespan defines the cosmic cycle</term> life has passed. Regarding this, some teachers say half of his life has passed, while others say eight and a half years have passed. In this matter, sacred tradition is the authority. As to which authority is correct among these differing traditions, we are not insistent. This is because there is no practical need for the years, months, or days that have already passed in his life. The planets, however, are to be calculated from the time elapsed within the *current* day.

### The Radiance <note>original: "Prabha" — a Sanskrit commentary</note>

Of which Brahma? Half of his life, measuring fifty years. This is based on the Surya Siddhanta <note>original: "Saura-vacanat"</note> statement that half of his life has passed. There is no use or purpose in investigating the years and other units of his life that have already passed. The meaning is that because the past days, months, and years of Brahma are irrelevant to our calculations, they lack utility. "From the time elapsed in the current day" means they should be calculated from the total number of solar years <term>Solar year: the time taken for the Sun to return to the same position relative to the stars</term> that have passed within Brahma's current day.

### Vernacular Commentary <note>original: "Bhasha-bhashya" — a Hindi explanation</note>

In this way, many hold the opinion that half of Brahma's life—that is, fifty years—has passed at the present time. According to some others, eight and a half years have passed. However, there is no practical purpose for these opinions. This is because there is no benefit gained from knowing the past years of Brahma's life. The calculation of the planets should be performed using the solar years that have elapsed within the current day.

The significance is this: since time is beginningless and endless, no fixed period can be imagined for it. Because it would be impossible to describe the motion of the planets without a starting point, some kind of epoch became necessary. The ancient teachers, following the Vedas and the Smritis <note>Traditional legal and social texts</note>, accepted a period of 4,320,000,000 solar years <note>This period is known as a Kalpa, or one day of Brahma</note> and performed planetary calculations based on that. Within these years, the planets, their apogees <term>Mandocca: the point where a planet is furthest from Earth and moves slowest</term>, and their conjunction points <term>Shighrocca: a point used in calculating the variable motion of planets</term>...

The revolutions of the nodes and other points are considered complete. Therefore, this duration has been established as being without fractional remainders. || 26 ||

**Now, he explains the reason for this—**

->Since their creation occurs at the start of the day, and their dissolution at the end of the day, the study of their motion should only be conducted while they exist. Therefore, this practice is appropriate; as for those who perform these calculations even when the planets do not exist, I offer my salutations to those "great" men. || 27 ||<-

Because the creation of these planets occurs at the beginning of the day <note>The "Day of Brahma," a vast cosmic cycle known as a Kalpa, lasting 4.32 billion years.</note> and their dissolution occurs at the end of the day. If the planets are calculated based on the time elapsed since the Great Aeon <note>original: "Mahakalpa"</note>, then during the many nights that have passed, the planets simply did not exist. Therefore, it is only fitting to study their motions while the planets are actually present. Regarding those who have calculated the current positions based on the time elapsed in the Great Aeon—even during periods when the planets were non-existent—the author speaks with irony and mockery, saying: "I offer my salutations to those great men."

### Light <note>original: "Prabha," the name of the commentary.</note>

"At the start of the day" means at the commencement of the Kalpa, which is the form of Brahma's day. "At the end of the day" means at the time the Kalpa concludes. Here is the Divine statement: <quote>"From the Unmanifested <note>original: "Avyakta"</note>, all manifested beings come forth at the arrival of the Day; at the arrival of the Night, they dissolve into that very same thing called the Unmanifested."</quote> <note>A citation from the Bhagavad Gita, 8.18.</note> "The study of their motion" refers to the investigation of planetary movement. The point being made is this: since planets exist only during the time-period defined by a Kalpa, it is proper to calculate them only from the elapsed days of the current cycle.

### Vernacular Commentary

The creation of the planets occurs at the beginning of Brahma's day and their dissolution occurs at the end of the day; for this reason, their calculation should be performed during the period of the planets' existence. That is to say, it is proper to calculate the planets based on the years elapsed in the current Day of Brahma. To those "great souls" who have calculated the planets by taking the Great Aeon <term>Mahakalpa: a cycle of 311 trillion years</term> as the elapsed time—even when the planets had vanished—I offer my respectful bows. The implication is that at the end of Brahma's day...

### Mathematical Proof

One <term>Manvantara</term><note>The lifespan of a Manu.</note> consists of seventy-one <term>Mahayugas</term><note>A Great Age consisting of 4,320,000 years.</note>. Therefore—

Manvantara value = 71 x 4,320,000 = 306,720,000.

Six times the Manvantara value = 1,840,320,000.

By adding the <term>Krita-age</term><note>The Golden Age or Satya Yuga, the first of the four cycles.</note> years multiplied by seven to this, the actual elapsed Manvantara time in the current period is found. Thus—

Krita-age value = 1,728,000 x 7 = 12,096,000.

-> Six Manus = 1,840,320,000 <-
-> + 12,096,000 <-
---
-> Actual Manu total = 1,852,416,000 <-

27 Mahayugas = 4,320,000 x 27 = 116,640,000.

By adding this number of Mahayugas to the actual Manu total and then adding the three elapsed age-quarters <insert>Krita, Treta, and Dvapara</insert>, the following number is obtained—

-> 1,969,056,000 <-
-> + 3,888,000 <-
---
-> 1,972,944,000 <-

-> 1,972,944,000 <-
-> + 3,179 <-
---
-> 1,972,947,179 <-
