The revolutions of the planets <term>khēṭaparyayāḥ; the number of full orbits a planet completes in a Kalpa</term> are derived by mutually adding or subtracting these quantities. || 10 ||
These same values are produced by proportion from the total pool of solar civil days <term>sāvana-dyupiṇḍa; the total number of days elapsed since the start of the epoch</term>.
In that same manner, the mean positions of the planets are likewise determined by addition or subtraction. || 11 ||
In this context, the phrase "intercalary months, omitted days, lunar months, and so forth" uses the word "forth" to imply that other desired quantities may also be used. One should first determine how these quantities, when mutually added or subtracted, equal the revolutions of the desired planet. Then, treating those quantities as the "revolutions," one should calculate the results using the proportion of the elapsed days <term>ahargaṇa; the count of days since the epoch</term>. By adding or subtracting those results in the same way, the position of the planet is found. For example:

->The intercalary months are the difference between<-
->thirteen times the solar revolutions and the lunar revolutions.<-

This means that if the intercalary months are the difference between thirteen times the solar revolutions and the lunar revolutions, then the lunar revolutions are equal to the sum of thirteen times the solar revolutions and the intercalary months. Therefore, by calculating the "intercalary planet" <note>the mean position of the intercalary month cycle</note> from the elapsed days and adding it to thirteen times the solar position, the Moon's position is found. In this way, hundreds of other methods can be derived.

### Vernacular Commentary

By adding or subtracting intercalary months <term>adhimāsa</term>, omitted days <term>avama</term>, lunar months, and so on, one should establish the planetary revolutions. Then, using the proportion of the Sun's civil days (the elapsed day-count), the results should be added or subtracted in that same manner to establish the mean planets <term>madhyagraha</term>.

### Mathematical Proof

"The intercalary months are the difference between thirteen times the solar revolutions and the lunar revolutions."
According to this:
(13 × Solar Revolutions) — Lunar Revolutions = Intercalary Months. <note>original: 13 रविभगण—चन्द्रभगण = अधिमास</note>

Therefore: 13 Solar Revolutions + Intercalary Months = Lunar Revolutions.

The proportion is calculated as follows: If the total revolutions in a *Kalpa* <note>A vast cosmic age consisting of 4.32 billion years</note> correspond to the total terrestrial days in a *Kalpa*, then what would the value be for the Intercalary Months? By establishing the Intercalary Month planet in this way and adding "13 Solar Revolutions" to it, the Moon's position in signs and degrees is established.

Similarly, using the rule "The difference arises from the cycles of the Sun and Moon," one can use the inverse method to establish the Lunar Months in revolutions for a desired time. By subtracting the Moon from that value, the Sun is found; by adding the Sun, the Moon is found. In the same way, using the method "The sum of lunar cycles and days—" etc., one can establish the *Avama* <note>omitted lunar days</note>, Lunar Months, Lunar Days, and the Sidereal Revolutions <term>Bhabhrama: the total rotations of the starry sphere</term> for a desired time via the *Ahargana* <note>the number of elapsed days since the start of an epoch</note>.

### Furthermore —

Sidereal Revolutions + Omitted Days + Lunar Months — Lunar Days = Lunar Revolutions. By whatever method the *Kalpa* revolutions of a specific planet are generated, that planet will be established for the desired time using that same logic. || 10-11 ||

Now, showing other methods as examples of this, he says:

> The planet produced from the sum of two cycles, when added to or subtracted by the planet produced from their difference,
> and then halved, results respectively in the fast-moving and slow-moving planets. || 12 ||
> The fast-moving planet, when diminished by the planet arising from the difference of two revolutions,
> becomes the slow-moving one; and the slow-moving one, when added to it, becomes the fast-moving one. || 13 ||

Here too, the rationale for the calculation is based on transitional mathematics <note>algebraic substitution or simultaneous equations</note>.
The second method is extremely easy to understand.

### Vernacular Commentary

To calculate the mean planet from the sum and difference of the revolutions of two desired planets: add the result of the difference to the result of the sum in one place, and subtract it in another. Then halve both results. In this manner, one becomes the fast-moving planet and the other the slow-moving planet.

In Planetary Mathematics—

By subtracting the planet resulting from the difference between two planetary revolutions from the fast-moving planet, it becomes the slow-moving planet. And by adding it to the slow-moving planet, it becomes the fast-moving planet.

## Proof

It is well known that adding the difference between a large and a small quantity to the smaller quantity results in the larger quantity, and subtracting it from the larger results in the smaller. Therefore, by knowing the sum and the difference of the large and small quantities, both can be easily understood through <term>Sankramana-ganita</term> <note>Sankramana-ganita refers to the mathematics of concurrent equations, specifically finding two quantities when their sum and difference are known.</note>.

->Mean Planet = (Planetary Revolutions $\times$ Civil Days) / Days in a Kalpa. Here, Planetary Revolutions = Sum-based = Difference-based.<-

(1) Sum-based Planet = Fast-moving planet + Slow-moving planet.
(2) Difference-based Planet = Fast-moving planet — Slow-moving planet.
By taking the sum and difference of (1) and (2), we get:
2 $\times$ Fast-moving planet = Sum-based Planet + Difference-based Planet.
2 $\times$ Slow-moving planet = Sum-based Planet — Difference-based Planet.

By halving the first equation, the fast-moving planet is known, and by halving the second, the slow-moving planet is known.

Similarly,

Difference-based planet = Fast planet — Slow planet. In this, if the difference-based planet is subtracted from the fast planet, the slow planet is established:
Fast planet — Difference-based planet = Slow planet. And if that difference-based planet is added to the slow planet, it becomes the fast planet:
Slow planet + Difference-based planet = Fast planet. Thus, everything is proven. || 12-13 ||

Again, it is stated in another way—
->In the subtraction of the two moving apsides...<- <note>original: "केन्द्रोच्चयोश्चञ्चलयोर्वियोगे" (kendroccayoścañcalayorviyoge)</note>

# Chapter on Calculating Planets in the Section on Mean Motion

> Or, the planet to be determined may be found through the sum of the slow apex and its anomaly. 
> Alternatively, the known planet multiplied by the revolutions of the planet to be determined, 
> and divided by its own revolutions, yields the desired planet. || 14 ||

Here is the rationale: When the planet is subtracted from the fast apex <note>original: "shighrochcha"; the point of highest velocity, often associated with the sun in ancient Indian astronomy</note>, the fast anomaly <note>original: "shighrakendra"</note> is produced. If the fast anomaly is then subtracted from the fast apex, the planet is recovered—what is the wonder in that? Similarly, a planet diminished by its slow apex <note>original: "mandochcha"; the apogee or point of slowest motion</note> results in the slow anomaly. That this anomaly, when added back to the slow apex, results in the planet—what is so strange about that? If a known planet is obtained through the age-revolutions <note>original: "yuga-bhagana"; the total number of orbits a planet completes in a vast cosmic cycle</note> of that known planet, then what would be obtained by the revolutions of the planet to be determined? The result is the desired planet; thus, it is proven.

-> The Radiance <-

The "to be determined" <note>sadhya</note> should be understood as the desired planet. The "known" <note>prasiddha</note> is the already calculated desired planet.

-> Vernacular Commentary <-

By subtracting the fast anomaly from the fast apex, the mean planet is found. Alternatively, by adding the slow anomaly to the slow apex, the mean planet is found. By multiplying the known mean planet by the revolutions of the planet to be determined, and dividing by the known revolutions, the result is the mean planet to be determined.

-> Mathematical Proof <-

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Mean Planet = | (Revolutions in a Kalpa × Civil Days) / Total Days in a Kalpa |
| Therefore, Known Mean = | (Known Revolutions × Civil Days) / Total Days in a Kalpa; (1) |
| Desired Mean = | (Desired Revolutions × Civil Days) / Total Days in a Kalpa; (2) |

From both of these, it follows:

-> Desired Mean / Known Mean = Desired Revolutions / Known Revolutions <-

# On the Calculation of Planets

$\therefore$ Desired Mean Position = ———————————————— |\

Thus, the rule beginning with "Multiplied by the revolutions of the desired..." is proven. || 14 ||

Having brought forth the mean planets from the <term>Ahargana</term><note>The total count of civil days elapsed from the beginning of a specific epoch, such as the start of the Kalpa or Kali Yuga.</note>, he now describes finding the <term>Ahargana</term> from the mean planet:

### From the planet, including its remainder and its completed revolutions, multiplied by the civil days,
### and divided by its revolutions in a Kalpa, the elapsed days (Ahargana) are found.
### I shall also explain later how to find it from revolutions without remainders, from the remainder alone,
### or from the sum of remainders, using the Pulverizer method. || 15 ||

One should multiply the revolutions, signs, degrees, minutes, and seconds of a planet—including the final remainder of the seconds—by the <term>Kudina</term><note>Civil days in a cosmic cycle or Kalpa.</note>. Divide this by its own divisor and add the results upwards step by step. For example: starting from the remainder of the seconds in a planet's position, multiply by the Kalpa civil days, divide by the remainder's place, and add the quotient to the seconds place. Divide that by 60 and add to the minutes place, continuing this until the revolutions are reached. There, divided by the Kalpa revolutions, the result is the <term>Ahargana</term>. The proof here is by inverse calculation. Furthermore, I shall explain in the "Chapter on Questions" how to calculate the <term>Ahargana</term> from a planet without its remainder, from the remainder alone, or from the sum of two or more remainders using the <term>Kuttaka</term><note>The "Pulverizer" or "Grinder": an algebraic algorithm (similar to extended Euclidean algorithm) used to solve indeterminate equations of the first degree.</note> method.

->The "Prabha" Commentary<-

"With the remainder" (<term>Sāgrāt</term>) means including that which remains as the dividend when obtaining the seconds. "From the revolutions without remainder" means from that which is devoid of such. From such a planet consisting of parts from signs down to seconds. "From the front" refers to the method starting with "The seconds of the signs, etc." "From the remainder" refers to using only the remainder of the seconds, as in "Having imagined the remainder of the seconds as the clear gain..." "From the sum of remainders" refers to the sum of the remainders of revolutions and others, as in "The specified planet multiplied by the civil days and divided by four..." I shall state the <term>Ahargana</term>, meaning I will demonstrate it in the Chapter on Questions.

->Vernacular Exposition<-

The fractional parts of the seconds are called the "remainder" (<term>Agra</term>). Of any planet's revolutions and so on...

By multiplying the fractional parts of a planet—down to the last second—by the total terrestrial days in a Kalpa <note>A Kalpa is a vast cosmic cycle of 4.32 billion years</note> and dividing by the total revolutions in a Kalpa, the *Ahargana* <note>term: Ahargana; the number of elapsed civil days from the start of an epoch</note> is established. The method for finding the *Ahargana* from a planet stripped of its full revolutions and remainders—using only a single remainder or the sum of two or more remainders—will be explained later in the Chapter on Problems using the *Kuttaka* <note>term: Kuttaka; an algebraic method for solving indeterminate equations</note> method.

The proportion used here is: if the total terrestrial days in a Kalpa correspond to the total revolutions in a Kalpa, then what corresponds to the given position of a planet in revolutions and signs? Through this inverse process, the *Ahargana* is derived from the mean planet. || 15 ||

Now, he explains how to find the elapsed time of a Kalpa from the *Ahargana*:
-> Multiply the desired *Ahargana* by the omitted lunar days of a Kalpa and divide by the terrestrial days of a Kalpa; add the resulting omitted days to the *Ahargana* to find the total lunar days. Separately, multiply that total by the intercalary months of a Kalpa. || 16 || <-
-> Divide by the lunar days of a Kalpa; subtract the resulting intercalary days from the total lunar days to find the total solar days. Divide that sum of days by thirty (30) to get the total months, and divide that by twelve (12) to find the elapsed years of the Kalpa. || 17 || <-

This is self-explanatory. The proof here is based on two sets of the Rule of Three <note>original: "Trairashika"; a mathematical proportion involving three known values to find a fourth</note>. Finding the elapsed time of a Kalpa through the inverse of the *Ahargana* calculation is easy to understand.

### Vernacular Commentary

Multiply the desired *Ahargana* by the omitted lunar days of a Kalpa <note>term: Avama; days omitted in the lunar calendar to sync with civil days</note> and divide by the terrestrial days of a Kalpa to get the elapsed omitted days. By adding these elapsed omitted days to the *Ahargana*, the lunar *Ahargana* is obtained. Multiply that by the intercalary months of a Kalpa <note>term: Adhimasa; extra months added to the lunar calendar to align with the solar year</note> and divide by the total lunar days of a Kalpa to find the elapsed intercalary months. Multiply the intercalary months by thirty (30) and subtract them from the lunar *Ahargana* to find the solar *Ahargana*. By dividing the solar *Ahargana* by thirty (30), the total months are found, and from that—

By dividing by twelve (12), the measure of the years elapsed in the *Kalpa* <note>A Kalpa is a vast cosmic cycle in Hindu cosmology, equivalent to 4.32 billion years.</note> is determined.

### Proof

Here, the proof proceeds in the reverse order of the calculation for the *Ahargana* <note>term: Ahargana (the total number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch)</note>. A proportion is made using the desired *Ahargana*: If the total *Avama* <note>term: Avama (intercalary omitted lunar days)</note> of a *Kalpa* are found within the total *Savana* <note>term: Savana (civil or solar days)</note> days of a *Kalpa*, then what is found in the desired *Savana* days?

   Kalpa-Avama $\times$ Desired-Savana
-------------------------------------- = Desired Avama.
       Kalpa-Savana

By subtracting this from the *Savana Ahargana*, the Lunar *Ahargana* is obtained. Again, a proportion is made: If the *Kalpa* Adhimasas <note>term: Adhimasa (intercalary or "extra" lunar months added to align the lunar and solar years)</note> are found within the *Kalpa* Lunar days, then what is found in the desired Lunar days?

   Kalpa-Adhimasa $\times$ Desired-Lunar
------------------------------------------ = Desired Adhimasa $\times$ 30 = Intercalary days.
         Kalpa-Lunar

By subtracting these from the Lunar *Ahargana*, the *Savana Ahargana* is produced. By dividing this by thirty (30), the collection of months is found, and by dividing the months by twelve (12), the years elapsed in the *Kalpa* are found. In this way, the method beginning with "From the desired day-count..." is proven. || 16–17 ||

**Now, he describes the calculation of the day-count and other factors from the start of the Kali Age—**

> Or, the collection of days may be calculated from the elapsed time of the Kali Age;
> in that case, the Lord of the Day <note>The planet ruling the first day of the epoch.</note> begins with Venus (Friday).
> When combined with the "constant" values at the beginning of the Kali Age,
> the planet resulting from that day-count is determined. || 18 ||

There is a specific detail regarding the *Ahargana* elapsed since the start of the Kali Age: the sequence of weekdays must be counted starting from Friday. This is because, based on the *Ahargana* elapsed since the start of the *Kalpa*, the day at the beginning of the Kali Age was a Friday. The positions of the planets at that moment are designated as *Dhruvaka* <note>term: Dhruvaka (epochal constants or mean positions of planets at a starting point)</note>. The planet calculated from the current day-count must be added to these Kali-epoch constants; the underlying logic (*Vasana*) here is easily understood.

Anticipating such doubts, they state this measurement of the circumference of the sky, which is joined with the light of the Lord of Day <note>The Sun</note>. ->**The Radiance**<-

The Universe itself is like a pair of shallow bowls joined together. According to the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit treatise on astronomy, c. 4th-5th century CE</note>, the joining of two such bowls forms a spherical shape. They have declared the circumference to be the binding at the seam of that shell. This means they have stated the circumference of the space bounded by the spherical universe. The mountain of the "visible and invisible" <note>Lokaloka</note> is called such because the circumference of space is bounded by the meeting of the eastern and western mountains in the north and south directions. Thus, the solar doctrine states it is "encompassed by the *Lokaloka*."

By astronomers, this circumference of the sky or space is said to be measured by the number beginning with eighteen quadrillion <note>original: 18,712,069,200,000,000</note>. This is understood by those who know the entire sphere of the universe as clearly and flawlessly as a myrobalan fruit <note>original: *Amalaka*; a common metaphor for something held clearly in the hand</note> held in the palm of the hand. All of this has been explained by us in the *Goladhyaya* <note>The "Chapter on the Sphere," a later section of the text</note>.

->**Vernacular Commentary**<-

Experts in the science of light <note>Jyotish/Astronomy</note> have accepted the measurement of the orbit of the sky to be 18,712,069,200,000,000 *Yojanas* <term>Yojana; a traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</term>. Some call this the circumference of the hemisphere of the universe. Some Puranic astronomers call this the measurement of the *Lokaloka* mountain. Those who understand the principles of the sphere <term>Golatattva</term> as completely as a fruit in the hand say that this is the measure of the circumference of the sky as far as the sun's rays spread. <margin>*</margin> || 1-2 ||

The proportion is as follows: If the total rotations in a Kalpa <note>A Kalpa is a vast cosmic cycle of 4.32 billion years</note> correspond to the total Yojanas <note>A Yojana is a traditional unit of distance, roughly 5 to 9 miles</note> of the Sky-Orbit <note>Khakaksha: the circumference of the universe</note>, then what distance corresponds to a single rotation? Therefore, by dividing the Sky-Orbit by the rotations, the planetary orbit is proven. || 4 ||

> Now, having established this, he states the orbits of the Sun, Moon, and the Stars:

> The Sun's orbit: 4,331,497½. The Moon's orbit: 324,000. The Star-orbit: 256,889,250. Here, the star-orbit is sixty (60) times the Sun's orbit. These will be relative to the Earth's center <note>Geocentric horizon</note>. Between these two altitudes—

->Here is the rationale:<-

If in the total terrestrial days of a Kalpa <term>Kudina: the number of civil days in a cosmic cycle</term> the planets travel the total yojanas of the sky's orbit, then what do they travel in one day? The result is the daily motion in yojanas. These are approximately equal to 1,185,845.

->Vernacular Commentary<-

By dividing the orbit of the sky by the terrestrial days of a Kalpa, the daily motion of the planets in yojanas is established. In their respective orbits, the planets <term>Kheta: a synonym for planet or "sky-wanderer"</term> constantly revolve at a measure of 1,185,845 yojanas.

->Rationale<-

This motion in yojanas occurs in one solar civil day. The proportion is made: if in the total civil days of a cycle the yojanas are equal to the orbit of the sky, then what is the value for one day?

1,577,916,450,000

6,621 $\times$ Desired Days
--------------------------
35,416

In this way, the method beginning with "From the sum of days..." is established. The result obtained in this manner, when subtracted from the sum of days multiplied by the approximate daily motion in <term>yojanas</term><note>A traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note>, gives the elapsed <term>yojanas</term><note>Distance traveled</note> of the planets. Here, the orbits that result for the apogee and the node are imagined only for the sake of their mathematical calculation. Otherwise, the orbit of the planet itself is the orbit for these two as well. This is because the "apogee" is simply a designation for the highest point of the planet's orbit. And the point where the planet's orbit intersects with the <term>vimandala</term><note>The ecliptic or the secondary circle</note> is called the "node"; this has been thoroughly explained in the section on the celestial sphere. 

Similarly, the two orbits for Mercury and Venus that result here as being equal to the Sun's orbit are only for the purpose of their calculation. However, they both actually revolve in their own "moving orbits" <note>epicycles</note>, but they do so at the speed of the Sun. This is what is meant: the line drawn from the center of the Earth toward the Sun—where it touches the moving orbit of Mercury, that is where Mercury is; where it touches the moving orbit of Venus, that is where Venus revolves.

## Now, the rule for Omitted Days <note>Sanskrit: *Kshayahah*; these are the "missing" lunar days required to synchronize the lunar calendar with the solar year</note> is stated—

# Mathematical Proof

Here, the first proportion <term>Anupata; a mathematical ratio or rule of three</term> was calculated—if the total omitted lunar days of a Kalpa <term>Kalpavama; the number of lunar days dropped to synchronize with solar days over a vast cosmic cycle</term> occur in the total years of a Kalpa <term>Kalpavarsha</term>, then what is the value for a single year? In this manner, the omitted days for one year were established as 5 days, 48 <term>Ghati; a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term>, 22 <term>Pala; 1/60th of a Ghati</term>, and 7.30 <term>Vipala; 1/60th of a Pala</term>. 

Now, for the purpose of calculating the total elapsed days <term>Ahargana</term>, the 48 Ghati etc. were assumed as the omitted portion and the 5 full days were set aside. Then, for the sake of simplification <term>Laghavartha</term>, the remainder 48 | 22 | 7 | 30 was subtracted from 1 (a whole unit). The result was 11 | 37 | 52 | 30. If this amount of time were added, it would complete a 6th omitted day. A proportion was then made:

If in one year a difference of 11 | 37 | 52 | 30 is found, then what is the difference in 160 years? By converting <term>Savarnana; reducing to a common fraction or form</term> with 160, the result is 31 days and 1 Ghati. If 31 | 1 is obtained in 160 years, what is obtained in the desired years? By breaking 31 into parts of 30 + 1: <insert>30v + (v + <gloss>v</gloss>/60) / 160</insert> <note>v represents the elapsed years</note>

Thus, the resulting quotient is subtracted from the elapsed years, because this operation was performed after subtracting the remainder (48 etc.) from a whole unit. ||3||

Now, he describes the omitted days <term>Kshayahaha; lunar days that are skipped in the calendar</term> by another method:

-> Multiply the days etc. by three, subtract the four-hundredth <margin>400</margin> part of the years, and add the thirtieth part of the years. <-

The "days etc." previously calculated, when tripled, decreased by the 400th part of the years, and increased by the 30th part of the years, become the omitted days.

Here is the proof: Here, in one year, the "days etc." are 0 | 15 | 30 | 22 | 30 and the "omitted days etc." are 0 | 48 | 22 | 7 | 30. When the "days etc." are tripled and subtracted from the "omitted days etc.", the remainder is 0 | 1 | 51. If this is added to the tripled "days etc.", it equals the "omitted days etc." This remainder, when multiplied by 1200 <note>original: "Khakharkai", a word-numeral where Kha=0, Kha=0, Arka=12</note>, becomes thirty-seven (37).

## Mathematical Proof

The difference between a civil day <term>Savana Din: a day measured from sunrise to sunrise</term> and a lunar day <term>Chandra Din: a thithi, or 1/30th of a lunar month</term> is the "omitted day" (Avam). and so on + Omitted days etc. Alternatively, by proportion: in 1 year, the Shuddhi is 11 <note>approximate lunar days</note>.

## Vernacular Commentary

Place the elapsed years in two separate positions. Divide them by thirty-two (32) and thirty (30) respectively. Add the resulting quotients to the product of the elapsed years multiplied by eleven. Divide this total by thirty (30); the resulting quotient is the <term>Adhimasa</term><note>Intercalary month: an extra month added to the lunar calendar to keep it in sync with the solar seasons.</note> calculated by an alternative method. Subtracting the remainder from the <term>Avama Ghatikas</term><note>Omitted lunar days or "negative" time units used to reconcile the shorter lunar day with the solar day.</note> results in what is known as <term>Shuddhi</term><note>Purification: the fractional remainder of time at the start of a solar year, used to determine the date of the first lunar month.</note>.

## Mathematical Proof

In one year, the <term>Shuddhi</term> is 11 [days], 3 [ghatikas], 51 [palas], and 30 [vipalas]. From this, we calculate the proportion: if this is the value for one year, what is it for the total elapsed years? Here, the multiplier is split into two parts. The first is 11, and the second is 0; 3, 51, 30. If we multiply this second part by 480, we get 31. Thus, it is proven that one must multiply the <term>Gatabda</term><note>Elapsed years since the beginning of the epoch.</note> by 31 and divide by 480.

Here, the Teacher <note>Referring to the original author of the Sanskrit verses, likely Bhaskara or a similar astronomer.</note> has divided the multiplier 31 into two parts according to the division of forms: the first is 15 and the second is 16. In this manner:

(Elapsed Years × 15) / 480 and (Elapsed Years × 16) / 480. By simplifying the multipliers in both positions, the denominators become 32 and 30.

Therefore: <term>Adhidina</term><note>Intercalary days.</note> = (11 × Elapsed Years) + (Elapsed Years / 32) + (Elapsed Years / 30).

By dividing the <term>Adhidina</term> by thirty (30), the <term>Adhimasa</term> is obtained. In this way, the method starting with the verse "Place the years in two places..." is proven. || 6 ||

Now, he describes the method for finding the Lord of the Year without using days and other units:

->The difference between the elapsed years and the intercalary months, increased by the omitted lunar days and divided by seven, leaves a remainder. That remainder, or the remainder after subtracting the purification and dividing by seven, indicates the Lord of the Year starting from Sunday. <- || 7 ||

This is clear.

The proof is as follows: The weekday corresponding to the total number of elapsed days <term>Ahargana: the total count of civil days elapsed from a fixed epoch</term> at the end of the solar year is the Lord of the Year <term>Abdadhipa: the planetary ruler of the current year</term>. In every year, the number of solar days is three hundred and sixty. When this is divided by seven, the remainder is three. In the days of a month <note>referring to a 30-day month</note>, when divided by seven, the remainder is two. Therefore, the number of elapsed years multiplied by three, added to the number of elapsed intercalary months <term>Adhimasa: extra lunar months added to align the lunar and solar calendars</term> multiplied by two—when this sum is divided by seven—will equal the remainder of the count of lunar dates <term>Tithi: a lunar day</term> elapsed before the start of the month of Chaitra when divided by seven. This should indeed be added to the "Correction Dates" <term>Shuddhi-tithi: the lunar date at the time of the solar new year</term>. 

From that, the previously obtained "omitted days" <term>Kshayahas: lunar days that are skipped in the civil calendar to maintain alignment</term> must be subtracted. Thus, for every year, five should be subtracted. Previously, three were to be added. Therefore, two must be subtracted <note>3 minus 5 equals -2</note>. Furthermore, the intercalary months must be added twice. Therefore, for the sake of simplification, the number of years minus the intercalary months is multiplied by two; this, combined with the obtained omitted days and divided by seven, is subtracted from the "Correction" <term>Shuddhi</term>. The remainder after dividing by seven gives the weekday at the end of the solar year. It is proven that this is the Lord of the Year.

## Vernacular Commentary

Multiply the difference between the elapsed years and the intercalary months by two, add the number of elapsed omitted days <term>Avama-sankhya: the count of dropped lunar days</term>, and divide by seven. Subtract the remainder from the "Correction" <term>Shuddhi</term> and divide by seven again. Count the final remainder starting from Sunday to determine the Lord of the Year.

## Proof

The weekday resulting from the total elapsed days at the end of the solar year is the Lord of the Year. Dividing the 360 solar days by seven leaves a remainder of three, and dividing the 30 days of a month by seven leaves a remainder of two. Therefore, the sum of three times the elapsed years and twice the elapsed months, when divided by seven, will be the same as the count of elapsed lunar days before the month of Chaitra divided by seven.

Because this result is used as a fixed value in planetary calculations, the name "constant" is appropriate. The rest is self-evident.

## Vernacular Commentary

By multiplying the elapsed years by the <term>Kalpa-Bhagana</term><note>The total number of revolutions a planet makes in a cosmic cycle or Kalpa</note> of a planet and dividing by the total years in a <term>Kalpa</term>, the resulting quotient provides the <term>Dhruvaka</term><note>A constant or mean position of a planet at a specific epoch</note> for the Nodes, the Apogees, the Sighroccas <note>conjunction zones or fast anomalies</note>, and the planets themselves at the moment the Sun completes its revolution.

The <term>Upapatti</term><note>Mathematical proof or rationale</note> is clear: in one year, the Sun completes one revolution; therefore, the end of the year is precisely the end of the Sun's revolution. The proportion is as follows: if in the total years of a Kalpa there are a certain number of revolutions, then how many revolutions occur in the elapsed years? The result, expressed in signs and degrees, constitutes the planetary constants. Since the motion of the Nodes and similar points is very subtle <note>slow-moving</note>, there is no error in calculating them annually in this manner. || 6 ||

Now, the author describes another method for finding the Moon's constant:

->That which is the remainder of the intercalary days, multiplied by twelve,<-
->becomes the constant in degrees<-
->of the Lord of the lily-wives,<-
->whose clusters of rays are drunk by the Chakora birds.<- || 10 ||

The <term>Adhimasa-shesha</term><note>The remainder of the intercalary months, expressed here in lunar days or tithis</note> multiplied by twelve results in the Moon's position in degrees.

The proof here is easy to understand. Since twelve times the lunar days <note>tithis</note> equals the angular distance between the Sun and the Moon, and at the end of the solar year the Sun's position is zero <note>at the first point of Aries</note>, the Moon's position is therefore derived directly from that difference.

## The "Prabha" (Radiance) Commentary

Based on the lexicon stating "the Kumuda and Kairava are the same," <term>Kairavini</term> refers to the night-blooming lily. She is the "wife," and the Moon is the "Lord" of her kind. This refers to the Moon because the lilies bloom specifically at the time of moonrise. "Whose clusters of rays are drunk by the <term>Chakora</term> birds"—referring to the famous birds of that name which, according to poetic tradition, live only on moonbeams. This is a poetic description of the Moon.

### Now, he describes the "Epoch Days" for the purpose of calculating the total day-count:

->**The subtractive ghatikas <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> increased by their own twentieth part**<-
->**are the "Epoch Days" for the accomplishment of the day-count.**<-

The subtractive days (Kshayahas) previously calculated—specifically the half-ghatikas beneath them—should be increased by their own twentieth part and considered as days and half-days. The ghatikas are to be taken as days, the vighatikas <note>1/60th of a ghatika, or 24 seconds</note> as ghatikas, and the sixtieth-parts below them as "water-pals" <note>paniya-pala, a small unit of time</note>. For what purpose? For the accomplishment of the day-count (Ahargana); that is, for the sake of establishing the total elapsed days.

**The Rationale here:** In the upcoming calculation of the day-count, where the "omitted lunar days" (Avamas) are determined, sixty-four is used as the divisor. This is because one omitted day occurs for every sixty-four lunar days. Therefore, the remainder of the omitted days at the end of the solar year must be added to the "Correction" (Shuddhi) tithis <note>lunar days</note>—which have been increased by their own 1/702 part—after making the denominators equal. Then, when divided by sixty-four, the quotient obtained is the number of omitted days. 

Now, the remainder of the omitted days at the end of the solar year was previously taken in the form of ghatikas (base 60), but it must be converted to a base of sixty-four. Therefore, those ghatikas should be multiplied by sixty-four and divided by sixty. In this way, the remainder of the omitted days becomes based on a sixty-four denominator. 

However, sixty-three was used instead of sixty-four. Why? It is said that the remaining lunar days of the <term>Intercalary Month</term> <note>Adhimasa: an extra month added to the lunar calendar to keep it in sync with the solar seasons</note> that were previously obtained are fit to be taken as the "Correction" (Shuddhi). This is because the lunar days starting from the month of Chaitra, decreased by those [correction days], are taken forward from the end of the year. Furthermore, due to other mathematical requirements, the Correction days are conceived as being decreased by the omitted-day ghatikas. By the Correction decreased by the omitted-day ghatikas, as many lunar days from Chaitra onwards as are decreased—

In that case, the remaining minutes of the omitted lunar days <note>original: "avama-shesha-ghatika"</note> have become additive within the remaining lunar dates of the epoch. This is because a value being subtracted as a negative becomes a positive. Since one multiple was already added, now sixty-three multiples must be added. In this calculation, sixty-three is the multiplier for the minutes of the omitted lunar days, and sixty is the divisor. Here, the multiplier and divisor are reduced by a factor of three. In place of the multiplier, we get twenty-one (21), and in place of the divisor, twenty (20). The result is expressed in days. Since the multiplier is greater than the divisor by one-twentieth, it is proven that the omitted minutes, when increased by their own twentieth part <note>literally "nakha-amsha" or "nail-part," as there are 20 nails on fingers and toes</note>, become the additive days for the epoch.

### Commentary in the Vernacular

By adding one-twentieth of their own value to the minutes of the omitted lunar days, the fractional additive days suitable for calculating the <term>Laghvahargana</term> <note>The "Small Count of Days" elapsed from a specific epoch rather than the beginning of creation</note> are established.

### Mathematical Proof

In the calculation of the <term>Laghvahargana</term> provided later, the divisor used for determining omitted lunar days is 64. At the end of the year, the remainder of omitted days has a denominator of 60, but in the subsequent calculation, a denominator of 64 is established through transmission. Thus, according to the rule of <term>Samaccheda</term> <note>finding a common denominator</note>, it becomes necessary to multiply the remainder by 64. However, in the previous verse beginning with "That which remains here shall be known as the Shuddhi, diminished by the minutes of the day," the remainder was subtracted from the Shuddhi for the purpose of the Small Count of Days. Since this Shuddhi is later subtracted in the section "The sum of lunar dates passed since the bright half of Chaitra, minus the Shuddhi," the algebraic rule "a negative value being subtracted becomes positive" <note>original: "sashodhyamanam svamrinatvameti"</note> applies, and the remainder is added. Therefore, through this algebraic dexterity, the single multiple of the remainder is added...

The result of the omitted days multiplied by sixty-four and divided by the lunar days is one unit. The remainder, when simplified, becomes one. The divisor, when simplified, becomes <gloss>702</gloss> seven hundred and two 1. This is the multiplier of the elapsed lunar days and sixty-four is the divisor; therefore, adding its own part of one-seven-hundred-and-second <note>original: "sveeyakaragraturangalavena"</note> makes everything precise and without fractions.

By subtracting that from the elapsed lunar days since Chaitra, the remainder is the <term>Ahargana</term> <note>total day count</note> from the beginning of the Lord of the Year.

The total count of days <note>Sanskrit: *ahargana*, the number of days elapsed since the beginning of an epoch</note> minus its own sixtieth part results in degrees; thus, fifty-nine minutes are taken for each day. ### Vernacular Commentary

If you subtract the sixtieth (60th) part of the **day-count** from the total day-count, and then add the result obtained by multiplying the day-count by three (3) and dividing it by twenty-two (22), the result is the **Mean Sun**.

### Mathematical Proof

The daily motions of the planets are established and recorded based on the day-count. The **mean daily motion** of the Sun is assumed to be 59' <term>minutes of arc</term>. The remaining fractional parts are 0; 8, 10, 21 <note>This is sexagesimal notation: 8/60 + 10/3600 + 21/216000</note>. These accumulate to equal one minute in 7 $\frac{1}{3}$ days. Therefore, the proportion is calculated as follows:

If in 1 day the remainder is 0; 8, 10, 21, then what is it in 7 + $\frac{1}{3}$ days? In this proportion, the "standard" is 1 and the "requisition" is 7 + $\frac{1}{3}$. Converting both to a common denominator of sixty (60), we get 60. Multiplying the mean value by the requisition of 440, we get 0; 3520; 4400; 6240. Dividing by sixty, the quotient in the first place is 59, but for simplicity, 60 is accepted. Dividing this by the standard of 60, the quotient is 1 minute.

Then the proportion is made again: If 1 minute is obtained in 7 + $\frac{1}{3}$ = $\frac{22}{3}$ days, then what is obtained in the total day-count?

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Day-count&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;3 $\times$ Day-count
$\therefore$ Day-count — ———— + —————— 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;60&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;22

In this manner, the aforementioned method is proven. || 15 ||

### Now, the method for bringing forth the Moon—

> ->The Sun, increased by degrees equal to the lunar days multiplied by twelve,<-
> ->becomes the Moon (the "cool-rayed one").<-
> ->This is further increased by minutes derived from the "remainder of the omitted days,"<-
> ->multiplied by ten and increased by its own seventh part. || 16 ||<-

The well-known <term>rationale</term><note>Sanskrit: vasana; the underlying logic or proof of a mathematical rule</note> is that the Sun, when increased by degrees equal to the <term>lunar days multiplied by twelve</term><note>Since the Moon moves approximately 12 degrees further than the Sun each lunar day (tithi)</note>, becomes the Moon. However, this calculation applies specifically to the end of a lunar day. Now, the calculation must be adjusted for the time of sunrise. Between the end of the lunar day and the moment of sunrise, there is a <term>remainder of the omitted day</term><note>Sanskrit: avama-shesha; the fractional part of a lunar day that is "lost" when aligning the lunar calendar with solar days</note>. This is measured in <term>civil time</term><note>Sanskrit: savana; time measured from sunrise to sunrise</note>. 

To convert this into lunar units, the following proportion is used: If 63 civil days correspond to 64 lunar days, then what do the civil fractions within the omitted day remainder correspond to? Previously, the omitted day remainder had a divisor of 64. Now, because the multiplier is also 64, they cancel each other out, leaving 63 as the divisor. The result is in lunar days. To convert this to degrees, one multiplies by twelve; to convert to minutes, one multiplies by sixty. Thus, the multiplier for the omitted day remainder is 720 (72 multiplied by 10) and the divisor is 63. Dividing both the multiplier and divisor by nine, the divisor becomes 7 and the multiplier becomes 80 (8 multiplied by 10). Any quantity multiplied by eight and divided by seven is equivalent to that quantity plus its own seventh part. Therefore, it is said: "increased by its own seventh part and multiplied by ten." Adding these minutes results in the Moon's position at the time of sunrise. This is proven.

---

### Vernacular Commentary

Multiply the number of elapsed lunar days by twelve and add this to the calculated degrees of the Sun. Then, add the <term>omitted day remainder</term><note>The fractional difference between solar and lunar time</note> in minutes, after multiplying it by ten and adding its own seventh part. This results in the accurate position of the Moon.

# On the Annual Correction in the Context of Intercalary Months

-> Proof <-

A lunar day <term>tithi: a 30th part of a lunar month</term> is defined by twelve degrees of separation between the Sun and the Moon. Therefore, multiplying the lunar day by twelve establishes the degrees of separation between the Sun and the Moon. The difference between the end of a lunar day and sunrise is the "omitted day" <term>avama: a lunar day that is skipped in the civil calendar</term>, which is measured in civil time <term>savana: solar or terrestrial time from sunrise to sunrise</term>. To convert this into lunar time, the following proportion is used:

If 64 omitted days are found within 63 civil days, what is the value for a fractional part of an omitted day divided by 64?

$\frac{Omitted \text{ } 64}{63 \times 64} = \frac{Omitted}{63} =$ Lunar Day. The minutes <term>kala: 1/60th of a degree</term> in 12° degrees = 720.

Now, converting the result into minutes: $\frac{Omitted \times 720}{63} = \frac{80}{7}$. Here, $\frac{8}{7}$ is separated, which is equal to $1 \frac{1}{7}$;

$\therefore$ Moon = $(\text{Sun}^\circ + 12 \times \text{Lunar Day}) + (10 \times \text{Omitted}' + \frac{Omitted'}{7})$

Thus, the aforementioned calculation is proven. || 16 ||

Now, he describes the calculation for Mars:

> Take half the total number of days <term>dinagana: the count of days elapsed since a specific epoch</term> and place it below; multiply it by the multiplier,
> then subtract the seventeenth part of the total days.
> Adding these two results in degrees and minutes
> to the constant for Mars, the current position of Mars <term>Kshitija: "Earth-born," a name for Mars</term> is found. || 17 ||

The meaning of this is clear.

Here is the proof: "Half the total days" as degrees means that 30 minutes <gloss>30</gloss> are taken daily. That, taken separately and tripled, becomes 90 <gloss>90</gloss>. These minutes, combined with the previous minutes, become 99 <gloss>99</gloss>. Since this is greater than the motion of Mars, the motion of Mars is subtracted, leaving a remainder of 0 [degrees] and 3 [minutes].

### The Radiance <note>This is the title of a Sanskrit commentary ("Prabha")</note>

The "Lord of the Water-lilies' Fall" refers to the Moon's Node <term>Chandra-pata: the ascending node of the moon, often identified with the head of the demon Rahu</term>. Because the Node moves with a westward motion <note>retrograde motion</note>, its position is calculated in reverse order—Aries, Pisces, Aquarius, and so on—according to the signs it has passed. Therefore, in the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>A foundational text of Indian astronomy</note> it is said: "The Nodes have a retrograde motion; when subtracted from the circle [12 signs], their position is determined." Thus, after subtracting from twelve signs, one should calculate in the standard order of Aries, Taurus, etc., just like other planets. This is written in the *Swagata* meter.

### Vernacular Commentary

By multiplying the *Ahargana* <term>Ahargana: the total number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch</term> by 30 and dividing by 566, the resulting degrees and units are added to the Node's constant <note>epoch position</note> to find the Moon's Node. Some teachers call this Rahu.

The mathematical derivation here is clear. According to the verse:

-> 30 × Ahargana <-
-> Moon's Node = Node Constant + —————————————— <-
-> 566 <-

Dividing the total terrestrial days in a *Kalpa* <term>Kalpa: a vast cosmic cycle of 4.32 billion years</term> by the number of revolutions of the Node in signs results in 566. Therefore, dividing the *Ahargana* by this gives the result in signs. To convert this into degrees, it is multiplied by 30. || 21 ||

Here is the proof <term>Upapatti: mathematical demonstration or rationale</term>. # Mathematical Derivation

If the total revolutions in a Kalpa <note>A Kalpa is a vast cosmic cycle of 4.32 billion years</note> are obtained in the total civil days of a Kalpa, then what is obtained in the elapsed days <term>Ahargana: the number of days elapsed since the start of the epoch</term>?

->Revolutions in a Kalpa $\times$ Elapsed Days<-
->Elapsed Revolutions = —————————————————————————————— ,<-
->Civil Days in a Kalpa<-

->Revolutions in a Kalpa $\times$ 360 $\times$ Elapsed Days<-
->Elapsed Degrees etc. = —————————————————————————————————————— .<-
->Civil Days in a Kalpa<-

Here the transformation is performed: If the divisor is equal to the civil days for the multiplier of revolutions in a Kalpa, then what is it for a multiplier of one hundred thousand <note>100,000</note>?

->Revolutions in a Kalpa $\times$ 360<-
In this way, ->———————————————————————————————————— = Divisor Constant.<-
->Civil Days in a Kalpa $\times$ 100,000<-

->100,000 $\times$ Elapsed Days<-
$\therefore$ Elapsed Degrees etc. = ->———————————————————————————— ;<-
->Divisor Constant<-

->Revolutions in a Kalpa $\times$ 360<-
And in the calculation for the Moon, ->—————————————————————————————————————————— = Divisor Constant,<-
->Civil Days in a Kalpa $\times$ 100,000 $\times$ 20<-

is established. Because of the Moon's high velocity, it is multiplied by twenty (20) to consolidate the fractional divisor constant. || 22-24 ||

Now, he describes the method for finding the daily motion:

> From the elapsed days divided by one, the results obtained are the minutes of arc.
> These are, in order, the mean daily motions of the inhabitants of the sky <note>The planets</note>. || 25 ||
> The actual speed of the inhabitants of the sky in leagues <term>Yojanas: a traditional measure of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</term> is always constant.
> It is only due to the conceptual division into minutes of arc etc. that it is considered slow or fast. || 26 ||

The derivation here is by the Rule of Three <note>A mathematical proportion: if a is to b, then c is to d</note>. Previously, the motion of the planets was stated to be equal in terms of leagues. Now it is unequal. That is due to the conceptualization of minutes of arc and other units.

These are the mean daily motions of the planets. The motion of the planets in terms of *yojanas* <note>A traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> is equal. However, due to the conceptualization of minutes, seconds, etc., it appears unequal.

### Proof

The proportion here is as follows: If in the total days of a *Kalpa* <note>A vast cosmic cycle of 4.32 billion years</note> there are a certain number of revolutions, then what will be the result for a single day of the *Ahargana* <note>The number of elapsed days since the start of the epoch</note>? The result proven by this is the planet's movement in one day, known as the mean motion.

The minutes of motion for some planets are many and for others are few; for this reason, the ancient teachers have spoken of the "slowness" and "swiftness" of motion ※. That is to say, even though the motion is equal in terms of *yojanas*, the motion is conceived as unequal in terms of minutes and other divisions.

The significance is this: while moving in their respective orbits, because of the perception of differences in minutes despite equal distance-based motion, the planets appear to move unequally. || 25-26 ||

Now, the reason for this inequality is stated:
> All the orbits of the gods of the sky <note>The planets</note> are marked with the minutes of a circle (21,600).
> In a small circle, the minutes are small; in a large circle, they are large.
> Therefore, these planets—Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—
> Appear to move slower and slower in order, starting from the Moon. || 27 ||

Since all orbits are marked with the same number of minutes of a circle, the minutes in a large circle are large, and in a small circle, they are small. For example:

---

<margin>* </margin> Shripati <note>An 11th-century Indian astronomer</note> has written: "This motion is equal in terms of the path of *yojanas*; the slowness or swiftness is due to the nature of the minutes." According to the opinion of the ancient teachers, the distance-based motion is equal and all planets move in circular paths. However, according to the modern European opinion of the present time, it is proven that the distance-based motion of planets is unequal and planets move in ellipses <term>Dirghavritta: an oval or elliptical path</term>. By accepting the elliptical path of travel, the distance-based motion does not remain equal.

<header>Annual Correction in the Chapter on Mean Motion</header>

The Moon's orbit is the lowest and smallest of all. In that orbit, one minute of arc <note>a 'kala' or 1/60th of a degree</note> is equal to fifteen *yojanas* <note>a traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note>. Saturn’s orbit is the highest and is very large. In that orbit, one minute of arc is equal to five thousand nine hundred and twenty-nine (5929) *yojanas*. A *yojana* is exactly four *kroshas* <note>about 2 miles per krosha</note>. Therefore, as one moves upward from the Moon, the planets—Mercury, Venus, and the rest—appear to move slower and slower in succession, as if they are "slow-stepping" (*mandakranta*). By using this term, the *Mandakranta* poetic meter is also hinted at.

->Thus ends the Annual Correction in the *Vasana* commentary of the *Siddhanta Shiromani*.<-

## The Light (Prabha) <note>A sub-commentary</note>

All the orbits of the Sun and other planets are epicycles and so forth. "Slow-stepping" (*mandakranta*) refers to those whose movement (*gamana*) is slow or covers little distance. The word "as if" is used as a poetic figure of speech. In reality, it is due to the smallness of the distance covered relative to the orbit's size. "In succession" means one after the other in the stated order. The rest is clear.

->Thus ends the Annual Correction in the *Prabha* commentary.<-

## Vernacular Commentary

All planetary orbits are marked with 21,600 minutes of arc <note>the total minutes in a 360-degree circle</note>. However, there is a difference between them based on the sequence of small and large circles. That is to say, for some planets, one minute of the orbit consists of many *yojanas*, while for others, it consists of fewer. For this reason, because the orbits of Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are successively further away than the Moon's orbit, they appear to move very little in terms of minutes and seconds, even though they travel at the same speed in terms of actual *yojanas*.

## Mathematical Proof (Upapatti)

There is a difference in the value of a minute of arc based on whether the planetary orbits are large or small. The proportion for this is: if the total minutes of a circle (21,600) correspond to the total *yojanas* of a specific planet's orbit, then what does one minute correspond to? In the Moon's orbit, one minute is proven to be 15 *yojanas*. In Mercury's orbit, a minute is 48 *yojanas*, and in Venus's orbit, it is 123 *yojanas*. In this same manner, for other planets as well...

# On the Calculation of Planets

Therefore, because these distances are unequal, the motion of each planet in terms of minutes of arc is also different. This is because equality in minutes cannot exist across equal yojana-distances in different orbits. Now, he describes a specific rule regarding the calculation of the total elapsed days:
->**If the total elapsed days are calculated for a desired weekday,**<-
->**Then add or subtract one; the lunar days should be treated likewise.**<-
->**Then the remainders of the intercalary months and omitted days**<-
->**Are decreased or increased by the intercalary months and omitted days of the Aeon.**<- || 1 ||

In this context, when calculating the approximate lunar day <term>Tithi: a lunar day, 1/30th of a lunar month</term>, if the weekday that occurs on a specific lunar day does not match the result of the total elapsed days <term>Ahargana: the count of days elapsed from a fixed epoch</term>, then the total elapsed days should be increased or decreased by one to calculate the planets. This is the tradition of the astronomers, and it is consistent with logic, since the weekday is the regulator of the total elapsed days. When this is done, the specific adjustment is explained by the phrase "the lunar days likewise," and so on. What is meant here is this: when the total elapsed days are increased by one for the sake of the weekday, then in the calculation of the Sun and Moon using the remainders of the intercalary months <term>Adhimasa: extra months added to align lunar and solar calendars</term> and omitted days <term>Avama: "lost" days where a lunar day ends before a sunrise</term>, the twelve-fold lunar days that are to be added to the solar positions—as in the rule "multiplied by the edge..."—should also be increased by one.

# Page 123
-> Determination of Leap Months and Related Calculations in the Chapter on Mean Motions <-

The months should be multiplied by twelve and added. When the <term>Ahargana</term><note>The total count of elapsed civil days from the beginning of a cosmic epoch.</note> is decreased by one, the calculation must be performed with that reduction. Similarly, if the total day-count is increased by one, the <term>Adhimasa-shesha</term><note>The remainder or fractional part of the leap month calculation.</note> must be increased by the total leap months of a <term>Kalpa</term><note>A vast cosmic cycle of 4.32 billion years.</note>. The same applies to the <term>Avama-shesha</term><note>The remainder of the omitted lunar days (the difference between lunar and solar days).</note> and the total omitted days. This is because when the lunar dates are increased or decreased by one, the total day-count follows suit. Furthermore, since the remainder of the leap months increases daily by the rate of the total leap months, and the omitted day remainder increases by the total omitted days, this instruction is logically sound.

### Vernacular Commentary

To obtain the desired weekday in the total day-count, one must either add or subtract one. In the same manner, one should add or subtract one from the count of lunar dates. In the context of calculating the positions of the Sun and Moon using the leap month and omitted day remainders, one must adopt the increased or decreased lunar date in accordance with the total day-count. Consequently, the leap month remainder and the omitted day remainder should be added to or subtracted from the total leap months and omitted days of the cosmic cycle.

### Mathematical Proof

To calculate the total day-count for a desired weekday, the elapsed months are multiplied by thirty. To this, the specific lunar date from the <term>Panchanga</term><note>The traditional Hindu almanac.</note> is added, treating it as a "mean" date, because the true mean date is often unknown. If this specific date, when measured by mean motion, completes exactly at the start of the next weekday, there is no difference between the specific date and the mean date. In that case, the weekday calculation is correct using the existing day-count. However, if the specific date (by mean motion) extends beyond the start of the next weekday, adding that date to the day-count is equivalent to having passed a mean lunar date. Therefore, since the weekday has advanced, one must add one (called <term>Saika</term>) to the day-count. By increasing the specific date of the desired weekday by one, it aligns with the elapsed mean dates. Conversely, if the specific date completes exactly on the desired weekday itself by mean motion, adding that date is equivalent to adding a mean date to the day following the desired day.

## Determination of Intercalary Months in the Chapter on Mean Motions

The lunar days <term>Tithis: a lunar day, approximately 1/30th of a synodic month</term> are multiplied by one and divided by sixty-four. Now, when calculating the "Small Elapsed Days" <term>Laghu-Ahargana: a simplified method for calculating the number of days passed since a specific epoch, usually within a single solar year</term>, if an intercalary month <term>Adhimasa: an extra month added to the lunar calendar to align it with the solar year</term> falls between the end of the month of Chaitra <note>The first month of the Hindu lunar calendar</note> and the desired day, then the lunar days of that intercalary month must also be included to calculate the small day-count. Here, because of the qualifier "small," these are not to be taken in the "Great Elapsed Days" <term>Brihad-Ahargana: the total count of days elapsed since the beginning of the current cosmic age or Kalpa</term>. This is because in that calculation, the intercalary months are already included through the standard mathematical derivation. However, in the calculation of the Small Elapsed Days, since there is no separate derivation for intercalary months beyond the end of the solar year, they must necessarily be added.

->Vernacular Commentary<-

In the same manner, in the calculation of the Small Elapsed Days, the elapsed lunar days should be increased or decreased by one. If an intercalary month occurs between the desired day and the start of Chaitra, one must include those lunar days as well to achieve the Small Elapsed Days.

->Mathematical Rationale<-

The addition or subtraction of one to the day-count, as previously described, is a general rule. Therefore, in the Small Elapsed Days, this adjustment should also be applied to the lunar days when calculating the position of the Moon.

The Small Elapsed Days are calculated within the span of a single solar year. Therefore, since it is impossible to derive an intercalary month beyond the solar year in this method, if an intercalary month falls in the middle and is not included, there will be an error of 30 days in the total day-count. For this reason, the intercalary lunar days must be added to the lunar days elapsed since the start of Chaitra. // 2 //

<page-num>127</page-num>
-># Determination of Intercalary Months in the Chapter on Mean Motion<-

According to the stated rule, one should add to or subtract from the intercalary remainder. Then, after adding or subtracting one from the number of elapsed months starting from Chaitra <note>The first month of the Hindu lunar calendar</note>, the positions of the Sun and the Moon should be calculated.

### Logic and Proof <note>original: "Upapatti" — a term used in Indian mathematics for demonstration or proof</note>

Planets move according to their <term>true motion (spashta-gati)</term> <note>The actual observed speed of a planet</note>, not by their <term>mean motion (madhyama-mana)</term> <note>The average speed calculated over a long period</note>. The concept of mean motion is an abstraction created only for the sake of practical calculation. The true value changes uniquely at every moment. Thus, direct observation does not always match the calculated mean value. For this reason, there is a difference between mean and true calculations.

If, at the desired time, an <term>intercalary month (adhimasa)</term> <note>An extra month added to the lunar calendar to keep it in sync with the solar year</note> occurs according to true calculations, but the <term>total elapsed days (ahargana)</term> <note>The count of days since the beginning of the current epoch</note> does not show an intercalary month by mean calculation, then the elapsed days calculated by the aforementioned method for the desired time actually belong to the previous month. This is because the true calculation establishes one additional month. Therefore, to find the elapsed days by mean calculation at the desired time, one should add one to the elapsed intercalary months found by proportion. Similarly, if an intercalary month occurs later by true calculation but has not yet occurred by mean calculation, one should subtract one from the elapsed intercalary months found by proportion.

To calculate the positions of the Sun and the Moon, the elapsed lunar days <note>tithis</note> from the start of Chaitra used in the day-count should be added to thirty (30) days to find the elapsed lunar days for the desired time. The significance is this: just as a difference of thirty days occurs in the total day-count if the "plus one" or "minus one" adjustment to the elapsed intercalary months is ignored, the Sun and Moon positions would likewise not correspond to the desired time. However, when an intercalary month occurs and is also obtained through calculation, the naturally resulting day-count is itself the correct one for the desired time. In that situation—even if there is an intercalary month—one should not add one to the elapsed months from Chaitra for the purpose of calculating the Sun and Moon. || 3-4 ||

Now, he describes a specific rule regarding the *Shuddhi* <note>The 'Shuddhi' refers to the number of days elapsed from the beginning of the lunar month to the time of the Sun's entry into a new zodiac sign; it is a corrective value used to find the current date.</note>:

> If, during the calculation of the *Shuddhi*, an intercalary month is obtained even though it has not yet actually occurred, then the total number of days (*Ahargana*) should be calculated by adding thirty (30) to the *Shuddhi*. In the calculation of the *Shuddhi*, if a "clear" <term>Spashta: the true or observed value as opposed to the mean value</term> intercalary month is obtained even though it has not yet fallen, it should not be accepted. ### Rationale

In this context, it should be understood that when a "true" Chaitra <note>The first month of the Hindu lunar calendar</note> has not become intercalary by true measurement, but is obtained as a result in the calculation of the *Shuddhi*, then that "true" Chaitra was an intercalary month by "mean" measurement <term>Madhyama-mana: calculation based on average planetary motion</term>. And from the true Chaitra, the true Vaishakha <note>The second lunar month</note> becomes Chaitra by mean measurement. Therefore, the *Shuddhi* obtained from the mathematics belongs to the beginning of Vaishakha by mean measurement. Now, to know the elapsed months from the mean Chaitra, it would be necessary to subtract one from the months obtained by the calculation of the well-known true Chaitra and others. However, instead of doing that, for the sake of brevity <term>Laghava: the principle of mathematical economy or brevity</term>, the mathematically obtained *Shuddhi* itself [is adjusted].

# Determination of Intercalary Months in the Chapter on Mean Motion

The number 30 <note>representing the days in a full lunar month</note> was added to the number of days in a single month. By subtracting the well-known dates of the lunar months starting from Chaitra <note>the first month of the Hindu calendar</note> from this "Shuddhi" <note><term>Shuddhi</term>: a correction factor representing the elapsed lunar days at the start of the solar year</note>, the dates are taken from the end of the mean solar year.

And for this reason, in the method of calculating the "Abdapa" <note><term>Abdapa</term>: the Lord of the Year or the starting day of the year</note> using the rule "the difference between elapsed years and intercalary months—" etc., it is necessary to use the aforementioned Shuddhi subtracted from thirty for the purpose of finding the elapsed intercalary months by mean motion.

In this way, it is proven that for the actual fallen intercalary month, one must subtract one <note>original: "nireka"</note> from the mathematically calculated intercalary months. However, this topic applies only when the number of intercalary months obtained in bringing forth the "clear" <note>true/corrected</note> Shuddhi is one less than the number of elapsed intercalary months obtained in the calculation of the mean Shuddhi. Thus, the time interval between the true start of Chaitra and the true Mesha Sankranti <note>the sun's entry into Aries</note> should be known as the "clear" Shuddhi.

Now, he states the definitions of the Intercalary Month and the Decayed Month:
->**A month without a transit is clearly an intercalary month; a month with two transits is sometimes called a "decayed" month. Decay occurs only in the three months starting from Kartika and not otherwise; in that case, there are two intercalary months within that year.**<-

It is well known that the lunar month in which there is no solar transit <note><term>Sankranti</term>: the moment the sun moves from one zodiac sign to the next</note> is an intercalary month <note><term>Adhimasa</term>: an extra month added to the lunar calendar to synchronize it with the solar year</note>. Likewise, the month in which two transits occur is to be known as a "decayed" month <note><term>Kshayamasa</term>: a month that is omitted because the sun passes through an entire zodiac sign without a New Moon occurring</note>. Since months are characterized by transits, when two transits occur in a single month, a pair of months has occurred <note>effectively merging them</note>. That decayed month occurs only occasionally over long periods of time. When it does occur, it happens only in the three months starting with Kartika <note>Kartika, Margashirsha, or Pausha</note>. At that time, there will be one intercalary month three months before the decayed month, and another month without a transit <note>intercalary</note> three months after it.

<note>The author explains that a "decayed" year is rare and is balanced by having two "extra" months to maintain the solar-lunar alignment.</note>

<summary>This page defines the mathematical conditions for an intercalary month (Adhimasa) and a decayed month (Kshayamasa), explaining that the former has no solar transit while the latter has two.</summary>

<header>On the Calculation of the Planets—</header>

**Here is the mathematical proof.** The duration of a lunar month is twenty-nine civil days, thirty-one *ghatikas*, and fifty *palas* <note>29d 31g 50p; a ghatika is 24 minutes and a pala is 24 seconds</note>. Similarly, a solar month is thirty days, twenty-six *ghatikas*, and seventeen *palas* (30 | 26 | 17). In this amount of time, the Sun moves through one zodiac sign <term>Rashi: a 30-degree arc of the zodiac</term> at its mean motion. When the Sun's motion is sixty-one minutes <note>arc-minutes per day</note>, it moves through a sign in twenty-nine and a half days (29 | 30). Therefore, the solar month can sometimes be shorter than the lunar month. Indeed, the absolute minimum duration of a solar month is 29 | 20 | 40; this occurs when the Sun's motion is sixty-one minutes, which happens in the three signs starting from Scorpio. When such a short solar month falls entirely within the duration of a longer lunar month, two solar entries <term>Sankranti: the moment the sun enters a new zodiac sign</term> occur within a single lunar month. Thus, it is said that a "suppressed month" <term>Kshaya-masa: a month omitted from the calendar to keep it synced with the sun</term> occurs only during the three months starting with Kartika <note>roughly October–November</note>. Previously, if the month of Bhadrapada occurred without a solar entry, and then due to the Sun's increased speed a solar entry occurred in Margashirsha, and then due to slower motion Chaitra also lacked a solar entry, then two intercalary months would occur within that year. This is thus proven.

## Vernacular Commentary

The lunar month in which no solar entry <term>Sankranti</term> occurs is called an "entry-less month" or an **intercalary month** <insert>*</insert>, and the lunar month in which two solar entries occur is called a **suppressed month**. A suppressed month occurs only during the three months of Kartika, Margashirsha, and Pausha, and not in other months. In the year that a suppressed month occurs, there are two intercalary months.

---

<margin>*</margin> The statement of Pitamaha: "A lunar month without a solar entry is proclaimed to be a 'soiled month' <note>original: *malamasa*; an impure month where religious rites are restricted</note>."
From the *Brahma-Siddhanta*: "While the Sun stays in Aries and the following signs, whichever lunar month is completed is known as Chaitra and so on. If two completions occur <note>within one solar sign</note>, the latter is the intercalary month."
The statement of Vashistha: "When, before the end of one New Moon, another New Moon occurs, and the Sun's entry is skipped <note>leaped over</note>, that is an intercalary month."

## Rationale

According to the <term>apparent motion<note>True or observed motion as opposed to mean or average motion.</note></term>, the duration of a <term>lunar month<note>The period from one new moon to the next.</note></term> is measured from one <term>Amanta<note>The ending moment of the new moon (conjunction).</note></term> to the next. If the <term>Sankranti<note>The entry of the Sun into a new zodiac sign.</note></term> of Aries occurs within that interval, it is designated as the month of Chaitra. Similarly, through the entry into Taurus, it becomes Vaishakha, and so on; thus, the twelve months from Chaitra onwards are purified <insert>validated</insert> by the power of the twelve solar transitions. That month in which no solar transition occurs is an <term>Adhimasa<note>An intercalary or "extra" month added to the lunar calendar to keep it in sync with the solar year.</note></term>, as previously noted in the commentary and the original text. Thus, it is clear that an intercalary month becomes possible when the solar month is longer than the lunar month. This occurs according to apparent motion. According to <term>mean motion<note>The average rate of movement.</note></term>, this typically happens every 32 months, 16 days, and 4 ghatis. However, this rule is only approximate.

When, according to apparent motion, the measure of the solar month is less than the measure of the lunar month, a <term>Kshayamasa<note>A "decayed" or omitted month where two solar transitions occur within a single lunar month.</note></term> occurs because two transitions are possible within one lunar month. That solar month is short when the apparent velocity of the Sun is at its maximum. This is because, with higher velocity, the passage through a zodiac sign is completed in a shorter time. Since this excess velocity can theoretically occur in almost any month, a decayed month could potentially happen in any month. However, the Teacher <note>Referring to the author of the astronomical treatise, likely Bhaskara or a similar authority.</note>, following the conventions of his own time and assuming the <term>Mandocca<note>Apogee; the point where a planet is farthest from Earth and moves slowest.</note></term> to be at 2 signs and 18 degrees, determined that a decayed month occurs only in the three months starting from Karttika, corresponding to the three zodiac signs starting from Scorpio. However, this rule is not strictly accurate <insert>in all eras</insert>.

In the year that a decayed month occurs, two intercalary months also occur. Suppose that Bhadrapada is an intercalary month; at that time, the "intercalary remainder" is very small and subsequently decreases because the Sun is near its <term>perigee<note>The point in the orbit closest to Earth where the Sun appears to move fastest.</note></term>. Thus, when it decreases to zero, a decayed month occurs, because the solar month is shorter than the lunar month. The decayed month...

It notes that while traditional authorities limited decayed months to specific times of the year, these rules vary based on the Sun's changing apogee.</summary>

# On the Calculation of Planets

...thereafter, the <term>intercalary remainder</term><note>Adhimasa-shesha: the fractional difference between solar and lunar time remaining at the end of a period.</note> approaches the value of one full lunar month. This is because "the intercalary remainder always stands before the time of the solar transition from the end of the lunar month." Subsequently, when the Sun is near its <term>apogee</term><note>Ucha: the point where the Sun appears to move slowest in its orbit.</note>, an intercalary month occurs again due to the shorter duration of the solar month. In this manner, the rule "then, within a single year, two intercalary months occur" is proven valid. || 6 ||

Now, for the conviction of the calculators <insert>astronomers</insert>, he demonstrates several past and future occurrences of the <term>lost month</term><note>Kshayamasa: a lunar month in which no solar transition (Sankranti) occurs, effectively "dropping" it from the calendar to keep lunar and solar years aligned.</note>—

->It occurred in the Shaka year 974 (1052 CE);<-
->it will be in 1115 (1193 CE), and then in 1256 (1334 CE).<-
->Likewise, it will occur in 1378 (1456 CE). Generally, this happens<-
->after 141 years, and sometimes after 19 years.<- || 7 ||

This is clear.
Here is the mathematical rationale: When the <term>residual difference</term><note>Shuddhi: the number of lunar days elapsed at the start of the solar year.</note> is exactly twenty-one, then the month of Bhadrapada becomes an intercalary month. When that happens, a lost month is possible within the three-month span starting from Kartika. Such a specific residual difference recurs after an interval of 141 years. However, it increases by six <term>ghatikas</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note> and one-third (6h 20m). Sometimes, a similar condition occurs after nineteen years. In that case, it increases by fourteen ghatikas minus one-third (13h 40m). 

From the 141-year cycle and the 19-year cycle, when the years are divided by 32 and 30 respectively <note>referring to standard algorithms for calculating intercalary cycles</note>, the remaining lunar days in the first instance result in zero at the primary position with a remainder of 6 ghatikas and 20 minutes; in the second instance, 13 ghatikas and 40 minutes. Therefore, it was said: "Generally after 141 years, and sometimes after 19 years." This refers to both past and future occurrences.

# Middle Chapter: On Planetary Mean Motions

<page-num>135</page-num>

Now, the circumference of the Earth is stated:
The circumference of the Earth, expressed in the unit of <term>Yojanas</term><note>A traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 5 to 9 miles depending on the historical period</note>, is
**four thousand nine hundred and sixty-seven (4967)**.
Its diameter is **one thousand five hundred and eighty-one (1581)**.
Now, the definition of a Yojana is explained:
The Earth's circumference is multiplied by the difference in latitude between two cities situated directly north and south of each other, and then divided by **360 degrees**.
The distance between those two cities, when divided by that result,
should be understood as the standard Yojana in this context. || 1 ||

The mathematical proof for the Earth's circumference is explained in the section on the Celestial Sphere. The definition of a Yojana has already been mentioned in the section on Calculation. Nevertheless, the reason it is discussed again here is as follows: The Earth is indeed one, yet teachers such as Aryabhata and others—despite having the consistent observation of latitude degrees as a guide—have stated its measurements differently. This is because the scriptures define a "finger-breadth" (<term>Angula</term>) as being six, seven, or eight barley-corns wide, depending on whether one measures by the pinky finger or others. Whether by that intention or another, what they have stated is clarified here. 

By knowing the degrees of latitude of two cities in the north and south through the methods to be described, a proportion is made using their difference. If, on the 360-degree circumference of the meridional circle, there is such a difference in latitude, then what is the corresponding distance on the Earth's circumference between the cities? The distance between the cities is divided by the resulting value. One such part should be known as a Yojana. The calculation of longitudinal distance (<term>Deshantara</term>) should be performed using such Yojanas.
