->On Planetary Calculations<-

In the southern hemisphere, the intersection of the diurnal circle with the prime vertical occurs below the horizon; there, the gnomon <note>original: "Samashanku"; the vertical shadow-casting pole used for measurement</note> is downward-facing, and the "retained sine" <term>Taddhriti</term> <note>The portion of the diurnal circle between the horizon and the prime vertical</note> is also below the horizon. Therefore, by adding that <term>Taddhriti</term> to the <term>Hriti</term> <note>The radius of the diurnal circle</note>, the distance from the downward prime vertical line southward along the path of the equinoctial hypotenuse to the sun is obtained. From this, a proportion is established. The result is the southern Sine of Zenith Distance <note>original: "Drig-jya"</note>. This means the sine of the degrees by which the sun is inclined from one's own zenith on the meridian circle.

### Vernacular Commentary

In the northern hemisphere, by subtracting the <term>Taddhriti</term> from the <term>Hriti</term>, and in the southern hemisphere, by adding it, then multiplying the result by the base of the local latitude figure <note>the "Palakshetra" or latitude triangle</note> and dividing by the hypotenuse, the Sine of Zenith Distance is produced.

### Mathematical Proof

The segment below the intersection—where the cord tied at the east-west intersections of the diurnal circle and prime vertical meets the <term>Hriti</term> cord tied to the meridian circle, extending to the rising-setting line—is equal to the <term>Taddhriti</term>. This is clearly visible on the armillary sphere. By subtracting it from the <term>Hriti</term>, the upper segment of the <term>Taddhriti</term> is found. That represents the diagonal line from the prime vertical southward to the solar disk.

Therefore: <term>Taddhriti</term> ± <term>Hriti</term> = Upper Segment (in the northern and southern hemispheres respectively). Now, the proportion is made:

Latitude Triangle Hypotenuse : Latitude Triangle Base :: Upper Segment : Result
Result = $\frac{Latitude Base \times (Taddhriti \pm Hriti)}{Latitude Hypotenuse}$ = Sine of Zenith Distance.

In this manner, the rule beginning with "<term>Golakramat</term>—" <note>original: "according to the order of the celestial spheres"</note> is proven.

In the southern hemisphere, because the intersection of the diurnal circle and the prime vertical is below the horizon circle, the <term>Shanku</term> <note>gnomon/vertical sine</note> is downward-facing and the <term>Taddhriti</term> is also below. Therefore, by adding the <term>Taddhriti</term> to the <term>Hriti</term>, the distance from the horizon to the <term>Arkabimba</term> <note>solar disk</note> is found.

### Now, he describes another method.

> The radius minus the versed sine of the arc of the gnomon
> becomes the sine of zenith distance; or, in the same way, the gnomon.
> Thus is the sine of zenith distance found for all cases,
> such as the intermediate directions, the prime vertical, and the six-o'clock circle. || 39 ||

The radius <note>Sanskrit: *trijya*; the radius of the standard sine-circle</note> decreased by the versed sine <note>Sanskrit: *utkrama-jya*</note> of the arc of the gnomon <note>Sanskrit: *shanku*; the vertical pillar used for astronomical observation</note> results in the sine of zenith distance. Conversely, when the radius is decreased by the versed sine of the arc of the zenith distance, the result is the gnomon. By this method, the sine of zenith distance for the midday gnomon, the gnomon on the six-o'clock circle <note>Sanskrit: *unmandala-shanku*</note>, and the gnomon on the prime vertical <note>Sanskrit: *sama-shanku*</note> can be determined. Previously, the method described was only for midday. The proof of this was already established in the section regarding the sines of the base and the upright <note>Sanskrit: *bhuja-jya* and *koti-jya*; the horizontal and vertical components of a right-angled triangle</note>.

->Vernacular Commentary<-

By subtracting the versed sine of the gnomon's arc from the radius, one obtains the sine of zenith distance; by subtracting the versed sine of the zenith distance's arc, one obtains the gnomon. In this same manner, the sine of zenith distance for the midday gnomon, the six-o'clock gnomon, and the corner gnomon <note>Sanskrit: *kona-shanku*; the gnomon at an azimuth of 45 degrees</note> is proven.

Here, the proof is clear from the geometric field of sine-derivation <note>Sanskrit: *jyotpatti-kshetra*</note> relating to the base and upright sines. || 39 ||

### Now, he describes the shadow and the hypotenuse.

> The sine of zenith distance and the radius, both multiplied by twelve
> and divided by the gnomon, become the shadow and the hypotenuse.

Both the sine of zenith distance and the radius are to be multiplied by twelve and divided by the gnomon. The result obtained in place of the sine of zenith distance is the shadow measured in digits <note>Sanskrit: *angula*; a traditional unit of length</note>. The result obtained in place of the radius is the hypotenuse <note>Sanskrit: *karna*</note> of that shadow.

The proof here is by the Rule of Three <note>A mathematical proportion: if a is to b, then c is to d</note>. If the gnomon is the vertical side, and the sine of the zenith distance and the radius are the horizontal side and the hypotenuse respectively, then what are they for a gnomon of twelve digits? The results are the shadow and the hypotenuse of the shadow. This is proven.

->**Vernacular Commentary**<-

By multiplying the sine of the zenith distance <term>drgjya: the sine of the angular distance from the zenith</term> and the radius <term>trijya: the radius of the standard sine-circle</term> by twelve and dividing by the gnomon, the shadow and the hypotenuse of the shadow are obtained.

The proof here is as follows—

Gnomon (vertical) : Sine of zenith distance (or) Radius :: 12 : (Sine of zenith distance (or) Radius $\times$ 12) / Gnomon

= Shadow and Hypotenuse of the shadow. The gnomon is the vertical side, the sine of the zenith distance is the horizontal side, and the radius is the hypotenuse; this constitutes the "Great Shadow Triangle." And where the twelve-digit gnomon is the vertical side, the shadow is the horizontal side, and the shadow-hypotenuse is the hypotenuse; this is the "Reduced Small Shadow Triangle" <note>These are similar triangles used to scale celestial measurements down to a physical gnomon</note>.

Now, he describes another method for finding the hypotenuse at midday.

## The radius multiplied by the equinoctial shadow-hypotenuse,
## Divided by the 'hriti', is the hypotenuse when the sun is at the meridian. || 40 ||

One should multiply the radius by the equinoctial shadow-hypotenuse <term>akshakarna: the hypotenuse of a 12-digit gnomon's shadow at the equinox</term> and divide by the *hriti* <term>hriti: a specific sine-segment related to the sun's altitude</term>. The result will be the midday hypotenuse. Here, the proof is through two Rules of Three. First: if the equinoctial shadow-hypotenuse gives a gnomon of twelve, then what does the *hriti* give? Here, the *hriti* multiplied by twelve is divided by the equinoctial shadow-hypotenuse. The result is the midday gnomon. Now, the second proportion: if the midday gnomon gives the radius-hypotenuse, then what does a twelve-digit gnomon give? Here, the radius is multiplied by twelve, and when the fraction representing the previously calculated gnomon is inverted, it is multiplied by the equinoctial shadow-hypotenuse and divided by twelve times the *hriti*. Here, after canceling out the twelve in both the multiplier and the divisor, the radius is to be multiplied by the equinoctial shadow-hypotenuse and divided by the *hriti*. The result is the midday hypotenuse. This is proven.

Equinoctial Hypotenuse : 12 :: Hriti : **(12 X Hriti)** / **Equinoctial Hypotenuse** = Midday Sine <note>Madhyashanku: the sine of the Sun's altitude at noon</note>.

Midday Sine : Radius :: 12 : **(Radius X 12)** / **Midday Sine** = **(Equinoctial Hypotenuse X 12 X Radius)** / **(12 X Hriti)** = **(Equinoctial Hypotenuse X Radius)** / **Hriti**

> Divide the number 101,530 by the "Great Sine" of the Sun's longitude increased by the precession of the equinoxes.
> Multiply this result, called the "Para," by the equinoctial hypotenuse and divide by the equinoctial shadow.
> This result is the hypotenuse of the shadow when the Sun reaches the equatorial horizon. || 41 ||

One should calculate the "Great Sine" <note>Brihat Bhujajya: the full sine value rather than a simplified or small-segment sine</note> of the Sun's position including the <term>precession of the equinoxes</term><note>Sayanansha: the tropical longitude of the sun</note>. This means one should not use the "Small Sines." Divide the number 101,530 (represented by the mnemonic: *Full-Fire-Lunar Day-Cipher-Moon*) by that sine. The quotient is given the name *Para*. That *Para* is to be multiplied by the <term>equinoctial hypotenuse</term><note>Palakarna</note> and divided by the <term>equinoctial shadow</term><note>Palabha</note>. The result is the <term>hypotenuse of the shadow</term><note>Chhayakarna</note> of the Sun when it is positioned on the <term>equatorial horizon</term><note>Unmandala: the six-o'clock circle</note>.

### Vernacular Commentary

Calculate the "Great Sine" of the Sun's tropical longitude and divide 101,530 by it. The result is defined as *Para*. Multiplying *Para* by the equinoctial hypotenuse and dividing by the equinoctial shadow gives the shadow-hypotenuse of the Sun when it is on the equatorial horizon. || 41 ||

->The *Para* multiplied by the equinoctial shadow<-

That same *Para* <note>A specific mathematical constant derived for these calculations</note> is to be multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse. The result is the hypotenuse of the shadow of the sun when it is positioned on the prime vertical <note>The vertical circle passing exactly East and West</note>.

The proof here is established through three sets of proportions <term>Trairashika</term> <note>The "Rule of Three" in Indian mathematics</note>. If the sine of the maximum declination is obtained by the radius, then what is obtained by the sine of the sun's longitude? Here, the sine of the longitude is multiplied by the sine of maximum declination and divided by the radius; the result is the sine of declination. Now for the second proportion: If the equinoctial shadow is obtained as the base by the equinoctial hypotenuse, then what is obtained by the sine of declination? The result is the "earth-sine" or the gnomon at the equatorial horizon <term>Unmandala-shanku</term>. Now, for the sine of longitude, the sine of maximum declination and the equinoctial shadow are the multipliers, while the radius and the equinoctial hypotenuse are the divisors.

Now for the third proportion: If the radius is the hypotenuse for this gnomon, then what is the hypotenuse for a gnomon of twelve digits? Here, the radius multiplied by twelve is the dividend, and the previous quantity is the divisor. By performing the inversion of the fraction, the square of the radius multiplied by twelve and by the equinoctial hypotenuse becomes the dividend. The sine of longitude multiplied by the sine of maximum declination and the equinoctial shadow becomes the divisor. Here, we simplify the dividend and divisor by the maximum declination. When the square of the radius multiplied by twelve is divided by the maximum declination, we obtain the value <term>ten-one-five-three-zero</term> <insert>101,530</insert> <note>original: "Kha-rama-tithy-abhra-bhuvo" using the Katapayadi system where Kha=0, Rama=3, Tithi=15, Abhra=0, Bhu=1</note>. This value, divided by the sine of longitude, is designated as the *Para*. This is done because it is useful in other calculations. Now, it is proven that this *Para* multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse and divided by the equinoctial shadow results in the hypotenuse at the equatorial horizon. Similarly, for the sake of the hypotenuse of the prime vertical, when the three proportions are applied appropriately and simplified by the maximum declination, the same *Para* results. However, in that case, the equinoctial shadow is the multiplier and the equinoctial hypotenuse is the divisor. It is thus proven that the result is the hypotenuse of the prime vertical.

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<note>The "Three Problems" refer to the determination of time, place, and direction through the shadows of a gnomon.</note>

->Vernacular Commentary<-

Multiply the previously calculated <term>Para-sadhana</term><note>A specific intermediate value used in spherical trigonometry</note> by the <term>Palabha</term><note>The equinoctial noon shadow at a specific latitude</note> and divide by the <term>Aksha-karna</term><note>The hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow triangle</note>; the result is the <term>Samavritta-karna</term><note>The hypotenuse of the shadow when the sun is on the prime vertical</note>.

->Mathematical Derivation<-

Radius : Sine of Latitude :: Sine of Declination = $\frac{\text{Sine of Latitude} \times \text{Sine of Declination}}{\text{Radius}}$ = Sine of Earth-Sine;

Hypotenuse of Latitude : Palabha :: Sine of Declination = $\frac{\text{Palabha} \times \text{Sine of Declination}}{\text{Hypotenuse of Latitude}}$ = $\frac{\text{Palabha} \times \text{Sine of Latitude} \times \text{Sine of Declination}}{\text{Radius} \times \text{Hypotenuse of Latitude}}$

This equals the <term>Unmandala-shanku</term><note>The gnomon's shadow at the equatorial horizon</note>. Then, the following proportion is made—

Unmandala-shanku : Radius :: Sine of Amplitude : = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine of Amplitude}}{\text{Unmandala-shanku}}$ = $\frac{\text{Radius}^2 \times \text{Hypotenuse of Latitude} \times \text{Sine of Amplitude}}{\text{Palabha} \times \text{Sine of Latitude} \times \text{Sine of Declination}}$

$\frac{\text{Sine of Amplitude} \times \text{Radius}^2}{\text{Sine of Latitude}}$ = 101530 ÷ Sine of Declination = <term>Para</term>;

$\frac{\text{Para} \times \text{Hypotenuse of Latitude}}{\text{Palabha}}$ = <term>Unmandala-karna</term><note>The hypotenuse of the shadow at the equatorial horizon</note>.

In the same way, by performing the three proportions above to find the <term>Samamandala-karna</term><note>Hypotenuse of the shadow on the prime vertical</note>, we get: $\frac{\text{Para} \times \text{Palabha}}{\text{Hypotenuse of Latitude}}$ = Samamandala-karna. Thus, the rule "multiplied by the indirect shadow" etc., is proven.

Now, he describes the <term>Madhya-karna</term><note>The noon-time hypotenuse of the shadow</note> derived from the Unmandala-karna.

> The Unmandala-karna multiplied by the Sine of Ascensional Difference
> and divided by the <term>Antya</term> is the hypotenuse at midday. || 42 ||
> <note>original: "उद्वृत्तकर्णश्चरशिञ्जनीघ्नो भक्तोऽन्त्यया वा श्रवणो दिनार्धे"</note>

The Unmandala-karna should be multiplied by the <term>Chara-jya</term><note>Sine of the ascensional difference</note> and divided by the <term>Antya</term><note>The sum of the radius and the sine of ascensional difference</note>. The result is the Madhya-karna. The derivation here is by the Rule of Three. If the Unmandala-karna is obtained from a portion of the Antya equal to the Chara-jya, then what is obtained from the whole Antya? This is an inverse Rule of Three.

> When an increase in the desired quantity results in a decrease in the fruit <note>the result</note>, and a decrease results in an increase,
> the experts in mathematics should know that to be an **inverse rule of three**.

Therefore, it is proven here that the sine of the ascensional difference <term>Charajya: the sine of the difference between the rising of a planet on the equator and its rising on the local horizon</term> is the multiplier, the final sine <term>Antya: the sine of the arc of the day-circle from the horizon to the meridian</term> is the divisor, and the result is the middle hypotenuse.

->**Vernacular Commentary**<-

By multiplying the hypotenuse of the equatorial circle <term>Unmandala-karna</term> by the sine of the ascensional difference and dividing by the final sine, the middle hypotenuse is obtained by an alternative method.

->**Mathematical Proof**<-

Equatorial Hypotenuse : Sine of Declination :: Radius : $\frac{\text{Sine of Declination} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Equatorial Hypotenuse}}$ = Great Sine of Altitude <term>Mahashanku</term>.

Sine of Ascensional Difference : Sine of Altitude at the Equator :: Final Sine = $\frac{\text{Sine of Altitude} \times \text{Final Sine}}{\text{Sine of Ascensional Difference}}$ = $\frac{\text{Sine of Declination} \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Final Sine}}{\text{Sine of Ascensional Difference} \times \text{Equatorial Hypotenuse}}$ = Middle Sine of Altitude. Then the proportion is made:

Middle Sine of Altitude : Radius :: Sine of Declination = $\frac{\text{Radius} \times \text{Sine of Declination}}{\text{Middle Sine of Altitude}}$ = $\frac{\text{Sine of Ascensional Difference} \times \text{Equatorial Hypotenuse} \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Sine of Declination}}{\text{Sine of Declination} \times \text{Radius} \times \text{Final Sine}}$,

= $\frac{\text{Sine of Ascensional Difference} \times \text{Equatorial Hypotenuse}}{\text{Final Sine}}$ = Middle Hypotenuse. In this way, the verse beginning with "The hypotenuse of the rising..." is also proven by the direct rule of three. || 42 ||

If the hypotenuse of the unmandala <note>the equatorial horizon</note> is obtained by a segment equal to the *kujya* <note>the sine of terrestrial latitude or "earth-sine"</note>, and the hypotenuse of the prime vertical is obtained by the *taddhriti* <note>a specific solar sine used in altitude calculations</note>, then what is obtained by the *hriti* <note>the divisor or "retained" sine</note>? These are solved by the inverse rule of three. Here, the result is the middle hypotenuse; from that hypotenuse, the middle shadow is derived as previously stated. This is thus proven.

### Vernacular Commentary

By multiplying the hypotenuse of the equatorial horizon and the hypotenuse of the prime vertical by the *kujya* and the *taddhriti* respectively, and then dividing by the *hriti*, the midday hypotenuse is established through an alternative method.

### Mathematical Proof

Equatorial Hypotenuse : Radius :: Gnomon =
  Radius $\times$ Gnomon
------------------------- = Great Sine of Altitude.
  Equatorial Hypotenuse

*Kujya* : Equatorial Sine of Altitude :: *Hriti* =
  Equatorial Sine of Altitude $\times$ *Hriti*
---------------------------------------------- = Midday Sine of Altitude.
  *Kujya*

Then, the proportion is made:

Midday Sine of Altitude : Gnomon :: Radius =
  Gnomon $\times$ Radius   *Kujya* $\times$ Radius $\times$ Gnomon $\times$ Equatorial Hypotenuse
------------------------ = ---------------------------------------------------------------------- ;
  Midday Sine of Altitude           Radius $\times$ Gnomon $\times$ *Hriti*

  *Kujya* $\times$ Equatorial Hypotenuse
= -------------------------------------- = Midday Hypotenuse.
  *Hriti*

Then, for the alternative method, the proportion is:

Prime Vertical Hypotenuse : Radius :: Gnomon =
  Radius $\times$ Gnomon
------------------------- = Great Sine of Altitude.
  Prime Vertical Hypotenuse

*Taddhriti* : Prime Vertical Sine of Altitude :: *Hriti* =
  Prime Vertical Sine of Altitude $\times$ *Hriti*   Gnomon $\times$ Radius $\times$ *Hriti*
-------------------------------------------------- = ------------------------------------------------- = Middle Sine of Altitude.
  *Taddhriti*                                        *Taddhriti* $\times$ Prime Vertical Hypotenuse

Middle Sine of Altitude : Radius :: Gnomon =
  Radius $\times$ Gnomon   *Taddhriti* $\times$ Prime Vertical Hypotenuse $\times$ Radius $\times$ Gnomon
------------------------ = ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ ,
  Middle Sine of Altitude                      *Hriti* $\times$ Radius $\times$ Gnomon

  Prime Vertical Hypotenuse $\times$ *Taddhriti*
= ---------------------------------------------- = Midday Hypotenuse.
  *Hriti*

In this manner, the verse beginning with "The hypotenuse of the equatorial horizon, the hypotenuse of the prime vertical..." is also proven by the direct rule of three. || 43 ||

<note>Technical Vocabulary:

- <term>Taddhriti</term>: A specific sine related to the sun's position on the diurnal circle.

- <term>Dinardha-karna</term>: The hypotenuse of the shadow at midday.</note>

Now, wishing to describe the shadow in any desired direction, the author speaks in the form of a challenge, while describing the superior wisdom of one who understands this:

The shadows of the north-south line, the prime vertical <note>the east-west line</note>, and the corners <note>intermediate directions like Northeast or Southwest</note> were indeed calculated by the ancient teachers using separate methods. But he who can calculate all of these—as well as those falling in the intervals between those directions according to the inquirer's wish—using only a single unified method, I consider him to be another Sun <note>original: "Bhaskara"</note> upon this earth, causing the lotus-buds of the astronomers' faces to blossom. || 44 ||

In this context, the ancient teachers brought forth only three types of shadows without regard to time: one for the east-west, another for the north-south, and another for the corners. These were derived through separate methods. The method by which the midday shadow is obtained does not yield the corner shadow or the prime vertical shadow. In other words, one method does not result in the other. This refers to those shadows and those falling in the intervals between those directions according to the inquirer's wish.

The meaning is this: He who calculates these shadows, but by only one single method—not by various different procedures—I consider him to be another Sun on earth. Indeed, there is one Sun in the heavens; this man is a Sun on earth. In what respect? In the "blossoming of the lotus-buds of the astronomers' faces," which is to say, in causing the bud-like faces of the calculators <term>Ganaka: an astronomer or mathematician</term> to open in realization.

### Vernacular Commentary

The ancient teachers have calculated the north-south, prime vertical, and corner shadows using separate methods. However, he who can establish all those shadows—including those in the middle of said directions or at any desired spot according to the inquirer's wish—using the same single method, I consider him to be a second Sun on earth for the purpose of blossoming the lotus-like faces of the calculators. || 44 ||

# On the Calculation of Planets

The sine of declination <note>original: "krāntijyā"; the angular distance of a planet north or south of the celestial equator</note> should be multiplied by the sine of the latitude <note>original: "akṣajyā"</note> brought forth here, and divided by the sine of the latitude of one's own location. The result is the desired sine of declination. From these two, the increase or decrease of the midday light is determined. This is what is meant:

The arc of the desired sine of latitude is the desired latitude <note>original: "iṣṭapalo"</note>. The arc of the desired sine of declination is the desired declination. When the latitude and its complement are adjusted by the declination, the resulting midday shadow is the shadow produced when the sun <note>literally "the jewel of the sky"</note> is situated in the desired direction.

**The Proof:**
On the day of the equinox, the sun moves along the equatorial circle. The shadow produced when the sun, moving there, reaches a desired direction is what is being calculated here. When a gnomon <note>a vertical pillar used for measuring shadows</note> of twelve digits is placed such that the tip of its shadow falls in the middle of a specific direction, its distance from the east-west line is exactly equal to the equinoctial shadow. That is the base of the gnomon. In the absence of "agra" <note>amplitude at the horizon</note>, that itself is the "bhujā" <note>the side or polar distance</note>. The shadow is the sine of the zenith distance <note>original: "dṛgjyā"</note>.

Now, the circle drawn from the center of the directions with a compass set to the radius is indeed the horizon. There, the sine of the amplitude <note>original: "digjyā"</note> on the horizon is the "bhujā". The radius going from the end of that sine to the center of the directions is the sine of the zenith distance. Now, the proportion: If a sine of zenith distance equal to the radius is obtained from a "bhujā" measured by the sine of amplitude, then what is obtained from a "bhujā" measured by the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "palabhā"</note>?

Here, the radius should be multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by the sine of amplitude. The result is the shadow of the sun in the desired direction when it is on the equatorial circle. Now, treating that equinoctial shadow as a premise, the "desired sine of latitude" is to be calculated. One must calculate the sine of the degrees of interval between the zenith and the sun located on the visibility circle <note>original: "dṛṅmaṇḍala"</note>. Taking this shadow that has been brought forth as the equinoctial shadow, and having calculated its hypotenuse, that equinoctial shadow should be multiplied by the radius and divided by that hypotenuse. The result is the desired sine of latitude. The sine of latitude of one's own place resides on the meridian circle <note>the north-south circle</note>; however, this one resides on the visibility circle.

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<page-num>275</page-num>
->**The Authority on the Three Problems**<-

Because of the oblique position, the value becomes greater. Now, the <term>sine of declination</term><note>original: "krāntijyā"; the angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator</note> is also being projected onto the <term>vertical circle</term><note>original: "dṛṅmaṇḍala"; the circle passing through the zenith and the celestial object</note>. In this regard, the proportion is as follows: If the local <term>sine of latitude</term><note>original: "akṣajyā"</note> yields a corresponding projected latitude on the vertical circle, then what will the sine of declination yield on that same vertical circle? Thus it was said: "Multiply by that and divide by the local sine of latitude."

The result here is the sine of the degrees of interval between the equatorial circle and the Sun on the vertical circle. This is the "desired sine of declination." Then, one should proceed with these two values as one does with the midday calculation. The arc of the "desired sine of latitude" projected on the vertical circle is the "desired latitude." The arc of the "desired sine of declination" is the "desired declination" on the vertical circle. In the southern hemisphere, their sum—and in the northern hemisphere, their difference—results in the Sun's zenith distance degrees on the vertical circle. The sine of those degrees is the <term>sine of zenith distance</term><note>original: "dṛgjyā"</note>. The sine of those degrees subtracted from ninety is the <term>sine of altitude</term><note>original: "unnatjyā"</note>, which is the <term>gnomon</term><note>original: "śaṅku"</note>. By using the formula "the sine of zenith distance and the radius multiplied by the Sun's position," the shadow and the hypotenuse are derived; thus, it is proven.

### Vernacular Commentary

Multiply the <term>equinoctial shadow</term><note>original: "palabhā"; the shadow cast by a gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox</note> by the radius and divide by the sine of zenith distance; take the result as the equinoctial shadow to determine the sine of latitude. Multiply the sine of declination by that sine of latitude and divide by the local sine of latitude to find the "desired sine of declination." Then, using the desired sine of latitude and the desired sine of declination according to the previously stated method, the shadow of the Sun at its current position in the desired direction is established.

<header>On the Calculation of Planets—</header>

A vertical circle <note>original: "drungmandala"; the circle passing through the zenith and the celestial object</note> is drawn over the Sun. The distance from the point where this circle meets the horizon to the East-West marker is the sine of the amplitude <note>original: "digjya"; the angular distance along the horizon</note>. A gnomon of twelve digits <note>term: "dvadashangula shanku" — a standard 12-unit vertical rod used for astronomical measurements</note> was placed in the center of the circle such that its shadow fell exactly at the center. At that time, the distance between the base of the gnomon and the East-West line was equal to the equinoctial shadow <note>term: "palabha" — the shadow cast by a vertical gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox</note>. Due to the absence of the sine of amplitude <note>original: "agra"</note> on that day, that distance itself became the base <note>original: "bhuja"</note>; it is named the "base of the gnomon" <note>original: "shankutala"</note>. In this manner, two triangles are produced here: one with the radius as the hypotenuse, the sine of amplitude as the base, and the East-West line as the upright. The second has a segment of the radius as the hypotenuse, the equinoctial shadow as the base, and the East-West line as the upright. Now, a proportion is made from these:

-> If Sine of Amplitude : Radius :: Equinoctial Shadow : $\frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow } \times \text{ Radius}}{\text{Sine of Amplitude}}$ = Desired Directional Shadow. <-

Taking this as the equinoctial shadow, the proportion for the sine of latitude <note>original: "akshajya"</note> is:

-> 12 : Equinoctial Shadow :: Sine of Co-latitude : $\frac{\text{Equinoctial Shadow } \times \text{ Sine of Co-latitude}}{\text{12}}$ = Sine of Latitude. <-

This is the sine of latitude relative to the vertical circle, therefore it is named the "Desired Sine of Latitude" <note>original: "ishtakshajya"</note>. This is because the local sine of latitude is always situated only in the North-South circle <note>the meridian</note>. To also bring the sine of declination <note>original: "krantijya"</note> into the plane of the vertical circle, the proportion is:

-> Local Sine of Latitude : Desired Sine of Latitude :: Sine of Declination : $\frac{\text{Desired Sine of Latitude } \times \text{ Sine of Declination}}{\text{Local Sine of Latitude}}$ = Declination in the Vertical Circle. <-

This distance exists from the celestial equator to the solar disk. In this way, the rule **"Multiplied by that and by its own sine of latitude, the sine of declination..."** <note>original: "taya vinighni svakshajyayatapamashinjini cha"</note> is proven.

The arc of the Desired Sine of Latitude is the "Desired Latitude," and the arc of the Desired Sine of Declination is the "Desired Declination." By adding these two if they are in the same direction, or taking their difference if in opposite directions, the zenith distance <note>original: "natansha"</note> from the zenith to the solar disk is obtained. By subtracting these from 90°, the altitude <note>original: "unnatansha"</note> is found. Its sine is the gnomon-upright, the sine of zenith distance is the base, and the radius is the hypotenuse. From these, according to the rule **"The sine of zenith distance and the radius..."**, the calculation of the shadow in the desired direction and the hypotenuse of the shadow is easily accomplished.

In the northern hemisphere <term>Saumya-gola</term>, when the vertical circle is placed at the tip of the sine of the desired northern direction, it intersects the diurnal circle <term>Ahoratra-vritta</term> <note>the daily path of the sun</note> at two points, once in the morning and once in the afternoon. If you ask how that is, it is explained thus: In this manner, whatever the desired latitude degrees are, subtract them from one hundred and eighty (180). Taking the remaining degrees as the assumed latitude, the desired shadow should be calculated in two ways, where possible. This occurs only when the sine of the direction is less than the amplitude <insert>distance of the sun from the east-west line at rising</insert> in the northern hemisphere. In the southern hemisphere <term>Yamya-gola</term>, however, the sun does not enter above the horizon in that specific direction. Therefore, there is a total absence of shadow there.

The degrees by which it occurs are indeed the desired degrees of latitude <note>Sanskrit: *palāṃśāḥ*; the angular distance from the equator</note>. Another point, which is at a distance from one's own zenith in the other direction, is also considered as degrees of latitude. From the tip of those latitudes and the tip of the others, the desired circle of day and night <note>the diurnal circle</note> meets at the end of the desired visibility. Now, an example for calculating the shadow of the prime vertical <note>the east-west vertical circle</note> using this method: In a place where the equinoctial shadow <note>*palabhā*; the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</note> is five digits, and when the sine of declination is seven hundred and eighty (780), then the gnomon of the prime vertical <note>*samaśaṅku*</note> is two thousand and twenty-eight (2028). For example: In that country, the sine of latitude <note>*akṣajyā*</note> is measured as one thousand three hundred and twenty-two and eighteen seconds (1322;18). Dividing by this, the "own divisor" becomes 17160. Taking this as the equinoctial shadow, the sine of latitude is to be calculated. From the square of this, added to the square of twelve (144) with a common denominator that has become zero, the square root is the hypotenuse, which is equal to the equinoctial shadow itself: 17160. The radius should be multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by that same hypotenuse. Thus the sine of latitude is found. Here, because the multiplier and divisor are equal, and the zeros and equal equinoctial shadows are canceled out, the radius itself becomes the sine of latitude. Its arc-degrees are ninety (90) for the latitude. The colatitude <note>*lamba*; the complement of latitude</note>, subtracted from ninety, is zero (0). 

Then, "multiplied by that," and so on: the sine of declination (780) is multiplied by that sine of latitude which is equal to the radius (3438), and divided by the sine of latitude of one's own country (1322;18). By doing this, the gnomon of the prime vertical...

## Vernacular Commentary

In this manner, subtract the established degrees of latitude <term>Palansha: degrees of latitude derived from the equinoctial shadow</term> from 180°. Taking the remainder as the latitude, calculate the two types of desired shadows. In the Northern Hemisphere <term>Uttaragola</term>, the two types of shadows will only be established when the sine of amplitude <term>Agra: the distance of the rising sun from the east point</term> is greater than the sine of the azimuth <term>Digjya</term>. In the Southern Hemisphere <term>Dakshinagola</term>, there will be an absence of shadow because the sun does not rise above the horizon <note>This refers to specific high-latitude conditions or specific solar positions where the sun remains below the horizon of the observer</note>.

## Mathematical Proof

Because the Sun moves North or South of the prime vertical, the azimuth and the amplitude belong to the same direction. Due to the rotation of the visible vertical circle <term>Drigvritta</term>, in regions where the latitude is less than the declination, the azimuth at sunrise is equal to the amplitude in the Northern Hemisphere. After that, for a certain period, two shadows are possible. Similar conditions exist for other positions of the sphere. The calculation is described in two ways for the sake of the difference in shadows, because shadows are not equal at different times within the same half of the celestial sphere <term>Kapala: literally 'bowl', referring to the eastern or western hemisphere</term>.

In a region where the latitude exceeds the declination, when a planet is north of the prime vertical, the intersection of the celestial equator and the visible vertical circle occurs at azimuths less than the degrees of amplitude—one intersection being near the zenith <term>Khasvastika</term> and the other far from it. The desired latitude on the vertical circle at the intersection near the zenith, and the latitude at the second intersection...

One should set down the first value. Then, the product of the three—the radius, the equinoctial shadow <note>The shadow cast by a vertical gnomon at noon on the equinox</note>, and the sine of the solar amplitude <note>The angular distance of the sun from the east or west point at sunrise/sunset</note>—should be set down and designated as the "other" value. Then, both the "first" and "other" values should be divided by the difference between the squares of the sine of the azimuth and the sine of the amplitude. 

From that first quantity, take the square root of the sum of its square and the square of the other quantity; that root, when decreased by the other quantity in the Northern Hemisphere <note>original: "uttara-gole"</note>, or increased by it in the Southern Hemisphere <note>original: "dakshina-gole"</note>, results in the hypotenuse of the shadow <term>Chāyā-karṇa: the distance from the tip of the gnomon to the tip of its shadow</term> when the sun has reached the desired direction. 

Now, in the Northern Hemisphere, if the sine of the azimuth is less than the sine of the amplitude, then the square root of the difference between the square of the "other" quantity and the "first" quantity should be taken. That root, once subtracted from and once added to the "other" quantity, gives two possible values for the hypotenuse. Where it is added, the sun is understood to be north of the prime vertical <note>The east-west circle passing through the zenith</note>; where it is subtracted, it is south. Sometimes, even in the north, there are two possible hypotenuses.

### The Proof

The proof here is by the method of algebra <term>Bījagaṇita: literally "seed-calculation," the Indian term for algebra</term>. There, the unknown quantity is represented by the syllable *yā* <note>Short for "yāvattāvat," meaning "as much as" or "x"</note>, and the knowns like the radius and amplitude are represented by their initial syllables. The algebraic process is demonstrated as follows:

Let the measure of the shadow-hypotenuse be *yā* 1. From this, the "base" <note>The north-south component of the shadow</note> is to be calculated. By the rule "the solar amplitude multiplied by the hypotenuse and divided by the radius," the amplitude on the hypotenuse-circle in the Southern Hemisphere (and conversely in the North) is: 
(yā · a) / r <gloss>radius</gloss>

This amplitude on the hypotenuse-circle, processed with the equinoctial shadow <gloss>radius 1</gloss>, results in the "base": 
(yā · a ± r · v) / r <note>original: "v" for "viṣuvat," the equinoctial shadow</note>

From this, the sine of the azimuth is to be calculated by the rule "this [base] multiplied by the radius and divided by the shadow." This [base] multiplied by the radius is: (yā · a ± r · v). When the square of twelve <note>The standard height of the gnomon</note> is subtracted from the square of the hypotenuse, the result is the square of the shadow: yā² - 144. According to the rule "multiply or divide a square by a square," the square of the previous quantity is the dividend. When the square of the previous quantity is calculated, it is first the square of the amplitude multiplied by the square of the unknown (*yā*). Then, the product of the unknown, the amplitude, the radius, and the equinoctial shadow...

# Chapter on the Three Problems

Subtracting in one place and adding in the other results in two values for the shadow's hypotenuse <note>original: 'chayakarna'; the distance from the top of a gnomon to the tip of its shadow</note>. Where the addition is performed, it represents the shadow's hypotenuse when the sun is north of the prime vertical; where subtraction is performed, it represents the shadow's hypotenuse when the sun is in the southern direction. Occasionally, even in the Northern Hemisphere <note>original: 'uttara gola'</note>, two shadow hypotenuses can occur.

### Mathematical Proof

Here, the proof is established through the methods of algebra <note>original: 'bijaganita'</note> using equations. Let the shadow's hypotenuse = *ya* <note>original: 'ya', an abbreviation for 'yavat-tavat', the standard algebraic unknown or 'x'</note>.

->(*ya* $\times$ *a*) / *tri* = Hypotenuse-Amplitude<-
->Base = [(*ya* $\times$ *a*) / *tri*] + *vi*<-
<margin>The 'Base' (bhuja) here refers to the distance from the east-west line. 'a' represents the latitude (aksha), 'tri' is the radius (trijya), and 'vi' is the equinoctial shadow (vishuva).</margin>

From this, following the rule "the base is to be accomplished from the hypotenuse-amplitude," the sine of the azimuth <term>digjya: the horizontal angle of a celestial body from the cardinal points</term> is to be calculated. Since the shadow itself is unknown, the square of the shadow is calculated by an alternative method:

Shadow$^2$ = *ya*$^2$ - 12$^2$ <note>The gnomon is traditionally 12 units high; by the Pythagorean theorem, shadow squared equals hypotenuse squared minus gnomon squared</note>. By dividing the previously determined Base (multiplied by the radius) by this, and following the rule "multiply or divide a square by a square," we get:

->Sine of Azimuth$^2$ = [(*ya*$^2 \times a^2$) + (2 $\times ya \times a \times vi \times tri$) + (*vi*$^2 \times tri^2$)] / (*ya*$^2$ - 12$^2$)<-

To solve the equation, the terms are placed for clearing the fractions and reducing the sides:
->(*ya*$^2 \times a^2$) + (2 $\times ya \times a \times vi \times tri$) + (*vi*$^2 \times tri^2$) = (*ya*$^2 \times$ Sine of Azimuth$^2$) - (12$^2 \times$ Sine of Azimuth$^2$)<-

$\therefore$ *ya*$^2$ (Sine of Azimuth$^2$ - $a^2$) - (2 $\times ya \times a \times vi \times tri$) = (12$^2 \times$ Sine of Azimuth$^2$) + (*vi*$^2 \times tri^2$).

By applying the divisor (Sine of Azimuth$^2$ - $a^2$) to both sides:

->Final Term = (*a* $\times$ *vi* $\times$ *tri*) / (Sine of Azimuth$^2$ - $a^2$)<-

-> $\frac{\text{Square of the gnomon}^2 \times \text{Square of the sine of the day-radius}^2 + \text{Square of the equinoctial shadow}^2 \times \text{Square of the radius}^2}{\text{Square of the sine of the day-radius}^2 - \text{Square of the sine of the amplitude}^2}$ <-

This subject is already clear here in the *Vāsanābhāṣya* <note>The author's own explanatory commentary on the mathematical verses</note>. || 46-51 ||

Now, the teacher has stated a single, well-known method for bringing forth the shadows of all directions. To remove the doubt of the slow-witted as to what the proof therein might be, he says:

> The "arm" <note>the sine of the altitude or a specific side of the triangle</note> should be calculated here by the <term>hypotenuse-tip</term> <note>karṇāgrā; the distance from the rising-setting line to the tip of the shadow</note>.

> and that sine will be exactly the same for both hypotenuses. || 52 ||

This is understood by the wise as soon as it is spoken. Now, for the conviction of those who are dull-witted, the "arm" should be calculated by the <term>hypotenuse-tip</term> in the manner to be described. That arm, multiplied by the radius and divided by the shadow, becomes the <term>sine of the direction</term>. This is because the direction of that shadow is the point where the string from the base of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>śaṅku; a vertical pillar used for astronomical measurement</note> to the tip of the shadow touches the <term>radius-circle</term>. However, it is in the opposite direction of the Sun. In this way, conviction should be produced in the slow-witted.

# Chapter on the Three Problems
<note>original: "Triprasna-adhikara"; the three problems refer to the determination of direction, place, and time using a gnomon's shadow.</note>

->Vernacular Commentary<-

The base <term>bhuja; the horizontal side of a right-angled triangle</term> that was established using the amplitude of the hypotenuse circle should be multiplied by the radius and divided by the shadow; the result is the sine of the amplitude <term>dig-jya; the sine of the angular distance from the east-west line</term>. One must develop confidence through mathematics that this sine of amplitude is identical to the one calculated previously. This sine of amplitude remains equal across both hypotenuses.
The proportion is as follows:
If this base, derived from the amplitude of the hypotenuse circle, is found within the hypotenuse of the shadow, then what would it be within the hypotenuse of the radius? The result will be the sine of the amplitude. In this manner, even if there are differences in the hypotenuse and the shadow, the same sine of amplitude is established through the aforementioned method. || 52 ||

Thus, having described the method for determining the shadow by the rule of direction, the author now speaks on the rule of time.

> The shadow has been described according to the rule of the desired direction;
> Now I shall speak of that same shadow again according to the rule of time.
> Whichever is less between the time passed since sunrise and the time remaining until sunset is known as the "elevated" time <term>unnata</term>.
> The midday half-day length minus that "elevated" time is designated as the "bent" time <term>nata; the hour angle</term>. || 53 ||
> Then, from the "elevated" time, subtract or add the ascensional difference <term>chara; the variation in the length of the day from the equinox</term>
> Respectively for the Northern and Southern hemispheres, and take the sine.
> This is called the "chord" <term>sutra</term>; when multiplied by the radius of the diurnal circle
> And divided by the radius of the sphere, it is named the "digit" <term>kala</term>. || 54 ||

Whichever is the lesser between the time elapsed in the day and the time remaining is to be known by the name "elevated" <insert>unnata</insert>. The measure of the half-day <note>midday</note> reduced by that elevated time becomes known as the "bent" <insert>nata</insert> time. Now, from that elevated time, in the Northern hemisphere <note>uttara-gola</note> subtract the ascensional difference, and in the Southern hemisphere <note>dakshina-gola</note> add it; the sine of that result is the "chord" <insert>sutra</insert>. This means it is designated as the *Sutra*. That *Sutra* multiplied by the radius of the diurnal circle <note>dyujya</note> and divided by the radius of the sphere <note>trijya</note> becomes the value named the "digit" <insert>kala</insert>.

<header>On Planetary Mathematics</header>

Here is the proof <note>Sanskrit: *atropapattiḥ*; the logical derivation of the formula</note>. At the time when the shadow is to be calculated, the number of ghatikas <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> the sun has risen above the horizon on its own diurnal circle is called the "elevated time" <term>unnata-kala</term>. The time elapsed since noon is called the "inclined time" <term>nata-kala</term>. Now, the sine of the elevated time, subtracted from or added to the ascensional difference <term>cara</term>, must be calculated. That sine is measured from the midpoint. This midpoint of the diurnal circle occurs at the intersection with the equatorial horizon <term>unmandala</term>. This is because half of the diurnal circle is above the equatorial horizon intersection and half is below. Therefore, the sine must be calculated from the equatorial horizon. The interval between the true horizon and the equatorial horizon is the half-ascensional difference <term>carardha</term>. Thus, the half-ascensional difference is subtracted from the elevated time in the northern hemisphere <term>uttara-gola</term>, but added in the southern hemisphere <term>dakshina-gola</term>. This is because in the northern hemisphere, the equatorial horizon is above the true horizon, and in the southern, it is below. The sine calculated from that resulting time, when scaled to the radius of the circle, is termed the "chord" <term>sutra</term>. Then, by proportion—if the value is this much in a circle of total radius <term>trijya</term>, what would it be in the diurnal circle <term>dyujya</term>?—it is converted to the diurnal circle. That result is termed the "digit-sine" <term>kala</term>.

->The Shadow<-

The shadow <term>prabha</term> in relation to a desired direction was explained previously. Now, I shall state and describe that same shadow according to the rule of time, in relation to the specific time of day. The idea is that the shadow remains consistent whether calculated by direction or by time.

->Vernacular Commentary<-

The calculation of the shadow according to the desired direction has been stated through the aforementioned methods. Now I describe that same shadow calculation through the rule of time. Of the elapsed or remaining time of the day, whichever is less is the "elevated time" <term>unnata-kala</term>; subtracting that from half the day gives the "inclined time" <term>nata-kala</term>.
In the northern hemisphere, subtracting the ascensional difference from the elevated time, and in the southern hemisphere, adding it, gives the "elevated sine," which is called the "chord" <term>sutra</term>. Multiplying the chord by the diurnal radius and dividing by the total radius gives the result known as the "digit-sine" <term>kala</term>.

## Mathematical Proof

At the time when the shadow is to be determined, by subtracting the ascensional difference <note>Sanskrit: *cara*; the difference between the time of sunrise on the equator and at a specific latitude</note> from the elapsed time since sunrise in the northern hemisphere, and adding it in the southern hemisphere, the time elapsed from the equatorial horizon <note>Sanskrit: *unmaṇḍala*</note> to the solar disk is found. The sine of this time is the "sine of the altitude above the equatorial horizon." When this is calculated within the radius-circle, it is designated as the *sūtra* <note>literally "thread" or "chord"</note>. To transform this into the diurnal circle <note>the path the sun travels on a specific day</note>, the following proportion is used:

If the *sūtra* is in the radius-circle, what is it in the diurnal circle? = (*sūtra* × radius of the diurnal circle) / radius = *kalā* <note>the sine of the altitude adjusted to the sun's specific path</note>;

That is to say, the *sūtra* of the radius-circle, when transformed into the diurnal circle, is designated as the *kalā* <note>arc-sine</note>. || 53-54 ||

Now, he describes another method for finding the *kalā* and from that, the "desired pole" <note>Sanskrit: *iṣṭayaṣṭi*; a specific vertical segment used in shadow calculation</note>.

->The *sūtra* multiplied by the earth-sine <note>Sanskrit: *kujīvā*</note> and divided by the sine of the ascensional difference <note>Sanskrit: *carajyā*</note> results in the *kalā*. That *kalā*, multiplied by the "base" of the local latitude-triangle <note>Sanskrit: *palakṣetra-koṭi*</note> and divided by its hypotenuse, becomes the "desired pole." || 55 ||<-

Alternatively, that *sūtra* multiplied by the earth-sine and divided by the sine of the ascensional difference becomes the *kalā*. That *kalā* is multiplied by the eight types of latitude-triangle bases and divided by their respective hypotenuses; the eight resulting values are the "desired poles."

Here is the proof: Here, the sine of the ascensional difference and the earth-sine are transformations of the radius and the diurnal radius. Therefore, the proportion is derived from them: If the earth-sine is obtained from the sine of the ascensional difference, then what is obtained from the *sūtra*? The result is the *kalā*. That *kalā* is a sine in the diurnal circle. Due to the local latitude, it becomes slanted like the latitude-hypotenuse <note>Sanskrit: *akṣakarṇa*</note>. Now, the measure of its vertical segment <note>Sanskrit: *koṭisūtra*</note> must be calculated. The proportion is: If the "base" is obtained from the hypotenuse of the latitude-triangle, then what is obtained from the *kalā*-hypotenuse? The result is a vertical segment extending from the solar disk down to the level of the equatorial horizon's gnomon-tip. This is designated as the *iṣṭayaṣṭi* <note>the "desired pole" or "calculated vertical"</note>.

## Vernacular Commentary

Multiply the *sutra* <note>a specific chord or sine value used in these calculations</note> by the *earth-sine* <term>Kujya: the sine of the terrestrial latitude's effect on the diurnal circle</term> and divide by the *ascensional difference sine* <term>Charajya: the sine of the difference between the local and equatorial rising times</term> to find the minutes of arc. Multiply those minutes by the *cosine* <note>koti</note> of a given latitude-triangle and divide by its *hypotenuse* <note>karna</note> to find the *desired rod* <term>Ishtayashti: a vertical measure or gnomon-like calculation for a specific time</term>.

### Mathematical Proof

The *ascensional difference sine* and the *earth-sine* are transformed into the radius and the *day-radius* <term>Dyujya: the radius of the diurnal circle of a planet</term> circles respectively. Therefore, the proportion is made:

-> *sutra* × *earth-sine* <-
-> *ascensional sine* : *earth-sine* :: *sutra* = —————————————— = minutes of arc, <-
-> *ascensional sine* <-

which is derived through this alternative method.

-> *latitude-cosine* × minutes <-
-> *hypotenuse* : *latitude-cosine* :: minutes = ————————— = *desired rod*. <-
-> *hypotenuse* <-

The minutes of arc represent the sine of the diurnal circle, and therefore act as a slanted hypotenuse. The proportion is calculated from that. The *desired rod* acts as the vertical side <note>koti</note> from the *unmandala-gnomon* <term>Unmandala Shanku: the gnomon or sine of altitude when the sun is on the six-o'clock circle</term> up to the solar disk. Because it pertains to the desired time, it is named the *desired rod* <note>Ishtayashti</note>. || 55 ||

> Now he describes the *desired rod* through another method:
> If the *unmandala-gnomon* is multiplied by the *sutra*
> and divided by the *ascensional difference sine*, it is the *desired rod*.
> This is clear. Here is the proof: If the *unmandala-gnomon* is the rod for the *ascensional difference sine*, then what will it be for the value called *sutra*? By this rule of three <note>trairashika</note>, the rod is proven.

## Vernacular Commentary

Alternatively—multiply the *unmandala-gnomon* by the *sutra* and divide by the *ascensional difference sine*; this is another way to find the *desired rod*.

-> *unmandala-gnomon* × *sutra* <-
-> *ascensional sine* : *unmandala-gnomon* :: *sutra* = ————————— = *desired rod*. <-
-> *ascensional sine* <-

# Section on the Three Problems of Direction, Place, and Time

Because when the <term>Sine of terrestrial latitude</term> <note>original: "charajya"</note> is the hypotenuse, the <term>Unmandala-Gnomon</term> <note>the gnomon on the equatorial horizon</note> acts as the upright staff.

Now, the author explains the method for bringing forth the <term>Desired Last Sine</term> <note>istāntyaka</note> and the <term>Desired Divisor</term> <note>istahrti</note>:

->When the sun moves into the Northern or Southern hemispheres,<-
->The "Sutra" added to or subtracted from the Sine of terrestrial latitude becomes the Last Sine. || 56 ||<-
->Similarly, the "Kala" added to or subtracted from the Earth-Sine<-
->Becomes the Desired Divisor at the intended time.<-

The "Sutra" <note>a specific chord or sine value</note> previously calculated, when added to the <term>Sine of terrestrial latitude</term> in the Northern hemisphere and subtracted in the Southern hemisphere, is called the <term>Desired Last Sine</term>. In the same manner, following the order of the hemispheres, the <term>Earth-Sine</term> <note>kujya</note> added to or subtracted from the <term>Kala</term> <note>the sine of the time elapsed since sunrise</note> is called the <term>Desired Divisor</term> <note>istahrti</note>.

Here is the rationale: The sine in the diurnal circle representing the time above the <term>Equatorial Horizon</term> <note>unmandala</note> is the <term>Kala</term>. The sine below it is the <term>Earth-Sine</term>. In the Northern hemisphere, when these two are added, the result is a transverse line following the path of the <term>Equinoctial Hypotenuse</term> from the solar disc to the rising-setting line. This is the <term>Desired Divisor</term>. When that same value is transformed to the scale of the <term>Radius</term> <note>trijya</note>, it becomes the <term>Desired Last Sine</term>. Therefore, the Sutra is added to the Sine of terrestrial latitude. In the Southern hemisphere, because the Equatorial Horizon stays below the horizon, the Kala must be decreased by the Earth-Sine, and the Sutra by the Sine of terrestrial latitude; thus it is proven.

# Vernacular Commentary

When the sun is in the Northern and Southern hemispheres respectively, adding and subtracting the "Sutra" to the <term>Sine of terrestrial latitude</term> results in the <term>Desired Last Sine</term>. Similarly, adding and subtracting the <term>Kala</term> to the <term>Earth-Sine</term> results in the <term>Desired Divisor</term>.

# Rationale

The sine of the desired time in the diurnal circle above the Equatorial Horizon is the <term>Kala</term>. Below the Equatorial Horizon is the <term>Earth-Sine</term>.

Therefore: Kala ± Earth-Sine = Desired Divisor, in both hemispheres. This is measured from the solar disc...

# Chapter on the Three Problems

> The sine of the declination circle <note>original: "dyujya"</note> multiplied by the Versine of the hour angle <note>original: "shara"</note> and divided by the radius <note>original: "vyasadala"</note>,
> or the earth-sine <note>original: "kujya"</note> multiplied by the same and divided by the sine of the ascensional difference <note>original: "charashinjini" — the difference between right and oblique ascension</note>; || 58 ||
> When the resulting quotient is subtracted from the total divisor <note>original: "hriti"</note>,
> it becomes the specific divisor for the desired time <note>original: "ishta-hriti"</note>.

At the desired time, the Versine <note>original: "utkramajya"</note> of the hour angle <note>original: "nata"</note> is known by the name "arrow" <note>original: "shara"</note>. When the previously calculated "final chord" <note>original: "antya"</note> is diminished by this "arrow," it becomes the "specific final chord" <note>original: "ishtantya"</note> for that moment. Now, this arrow is multiplied by the sine of the declination circle and divided by the radius. Alternatively, it is multiplied by the earth-sine and divided by the sine of the ascensional difference. The result should be set aside. When the previously calculated total divisor <note>original: "hriti"</note> is diminished by this result, it becomes the "specific divisor" <note>original: "ishta-hriti"</note> for the desired time.

Here is the rationale <note>original: "upapatti"</note>: According to the mechanics of the celestial sphere, the radius increased or decreased by the sine of the ascensional difference is indeed the "final chord." The "chord of the day" <note>original: "sutra"</note> increased or decreased by the sine of the ascensional difference becomes the "specific final chord." To the extent that the radius is diminished by the Versine of the hour angle (the "arrow"), it becomes the "chord of the day." Therefore, it is said that the "final chord" diminished by the "arrow" is the "specific final chord." 

Now, this "arrow," which is scaled to the radius, is converted to the scale of the declination circle through proportion: If the radius gives the sine of the declination circle, then what does the "arrow" give? Alternatively, if the sine of the ascensional difference gives the earth-sine, then what does the "arrow" give? From these two rules of three <note>original: "trairashika" — a mathematical method to find an unknown fourth value from three knowns</note>, the resulting quotient is the Versine of the hour angle converted to the scale of the declination circle. The sine of the declination circle increased or decreased by the earth-sine is the total divisor <note>original: "hriti"</note>. The "chord of the day" increased or decreased by the earth-sine is the "specific divisor." Now, when the sine of the declination circle is diminished by the Versine of the hour angle (converted to that scale), it becomes the "chord of the day." If the total divisor is thus diminished, it becomes the "specific divisor" for the desired time; this is proven.

Now, on the diurnal circle <note>original: "svahoratra-vritta"</note>, having fixed one end of a string at the intersection of the meridian and the other at the lower intersection... of that string, from the rise—

->Now, the method for finding the desired sine of altitude is stated:<-

> Or, the sine of altitude at the sub-vertical circle multiplied by the <term>Shara</term><note>The arrow or versed sine</note>

The previously calculated <term>Phala</term>, which was kept aside, is multiplied eightfold by the uprights of the latitude triangles and divided by their respective hypotenuses; this becomes the "Upper Segment" in eight ways. Alternatively, the previously calculated <term>Shara</term> multiplied by the <term>Unmandala-shanku</term><note>The sine of altitude when the sun is on the six-o'clock circle</note> and divided by the <term>Charajya</term> results in the Upper Segment. Why labor through the calculation of the <term>Phala</term>? By subtracting that Upper Segment from the midday sine of altitude, the <term>Ishta-shanku</term><note>The sine of altitude for the desired time</note> is obtained.

Here is the <term>Upapatti</term><note>Mathematical proof or rationale</note>: The horizontal segment previously shown as the upper portion of the <term>Hriti</term> is called the <term>Phala</term>. To convert this into a vertical upright, a proportion is used: If the hypotenuse of the latitude triangle gives its upright, then what does this <term>Phala</term> give? The result is the "Upper" vertical segment. When this is subtracted from the midday sine of altitude, the remainder is equal to the desired sine of altitude. This is because the Sun's disk resides on the <term>Ahoratra-vritta</term><note>The diurnal circle of the sun's path</note> along that very same coordinate line. Furthermore, if the <term>Charajya</term> (converted to the radius scale) yields a height equal to the <term>Unmandala-shanku</term>, then what height does the <term>Shara</term> (converted to the radius scale) yield? This also results in the Upper Segment. Thus, all is proven.

## Vernacular Commentary

The result previously established should be multiplied by the cosine <note>original: "koti" - the adjacent side of a right triangle</note> of a given latitude-triangle and divided by its hypotenuse <note>original: "karna"</note>—this produces the result known as the "Vertical Result" <note>Urdhva-sangyaka</note>. Alternatively, multiply the Unmandala-Gnomon <note>the gnomon at the equatorial horizon</note> by the "Arrow" <note>Shara - the versed sine</note> and divide by the Sine of Ascensional Difference <note>Charajya</note> to obtain the Vertical Result. By subtracting this from the Midday Gnomon, the Desired Gnomon <note>Ishta-shanku - the altitude of the sun at a specific time</note> is determined from the hour angle <note>Natakala - time from noon</note>.

## Mathematical Proof

The result transformed into the diurnal circle was written previously. That value acts as a hypotenuse; to convert it into a cosine form, we use the following proportion:

-> Latitude-Hypotenuse : Latitude-Cosine :: Result : (Result X Latitude-Cosine) / Latitude-Hypotenuse = Vertical Result. <-

Midday Gnomon — Vertical Result = Desired Gnomon.
Alternatively, using a different method of proportion:

-> Sine of Ascensional Difference : Unmandala-Gnomon :: Arrow : (Arrow X Unmandala-Gnomon) / Sine of Ascensional Difference = Vertical Result. <-

In this manner, everything is mathematically proven. || 56-60 ||

Now, he describes the Gnomon using the "Desired End-portion" <note>Ishta-antyaka</note> and the "Divisor" <note>Hriti</note>.

> Or, from the Desired End-portion and the Divisor,
> the Desired Gnomon is found just as the Midday Gnomon was described.
> From that Gnomon, the Sine of Amplitude, the Hypotenuse, and the Shadow are found;
> the wise should not calculate the Sine of Zenith Distance from the Divisor here. || 61 ||

Just as the Midday Gnomon was derived using the method "The End-portion multiplied by the Unmandala-Gnomon etc.," and similarly as the Divisor was multiplied by the cosine of the latitude-triangle, so too should the Desired Gnomon be calculated from the Desired End-portion and the Desired Divisor. Furthermore, from the Gnomon comes the Sine of Zenith Distance <note>Drigjya</note>, and from that, the Shadow-Hypotenuse—

# Chapter on the Three Problems

The shadow is to be calculated. The meaning is that it should be calculated in the same manner as the midday calculation previously described. However, in this specific case, the <term>Drigjya</term><note>The sine of the zenith distance</note> should not be calculated using the <term>Hriti</term><note>A specific hypotenuse used in spherical trigonometry</note> by multiplying it by the side of the local latitude field, and so on. This point was also mentioned there.

The underlying logic <insert>rationale</insert> is as follows: The <term>Hriti</term> is situated in the meridian circle <note>the north-south circle</note>. The <term>Drigjya</term> calculated by it can only belong to the meridian circle at midday. This is because, at that moment, the meridian circle itself serves as the vertical circle <note>the circle passing through the zenith and the celestial object</note>. But here, at any other desired time, the vertical circle is different. Therefore, it is stated that the <term>Drigjya</term> should not be calculated via the <term>Hriti</term>.

## Vernacular Commentary

Alternatively—following the method for calculating the midday gnomon, one should calculate the desired gnomon <note>Shanku</note> using the desired <term>Antya</term><note>The sum of the radius and the sine of the amplitude</note> and the desired <term>Hriti</term>. From that gnomon, the <term>Drigjya</term> is found, and from that, the shadow and the hypotenuse of the shadow are established. However, one must not calculate the <term>Drigjya</term> directly from the <term>Hriti</term> here.

## Rationale

The logic here is clear from the previous method. The specific distinction is that in the calculation of the desired gnomon, the <term>Drigjya</term> should not be derived from the <term>Hriti</term>. The significance is that the <term>Hriti</term> exists in the meridian circle, and any <term>Drigjya</term> proven by it will be restricted to the north-south direction. At midday, the vertical circle and the meridian circle are identical. However, at any other desired time, the vertical circle is different. || 61 ||

### Now, another method for finding the hypotenuse of the shadow is stated:

-> From the hypotenuse of the equatorial circle multiplied by the earth-sine, or from the hypotenuse of the prime vertical multiplied by its corresponding <term>Hriti</term>, or from the midday hypotenuse multiplied by the <term>Hriti</term>—if these are divided by the desired <term>Hriti</term>, the result is the desired hypotenuse of the shadow. || 62 || <-

That which was previously calculated as the hypotenuse of the unmandala <note>the six-o'clock circle or equatorial horizon</note> should be multiplied by the <term>Kujya</term><note>the earth-sine</note>.

The hypotenuse <note>the term used here is 'Karna', referring to the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle formed by the gnomon and its shadow</note> produced from the gnomon of the prime vertical should be multiplied by the *Taddhriti* <note>a specific sine used in Indian trigonometry related to the sun's position on the prime vertical</note>. The hypotenuse of the midday shadow should be multiplied by the *Hriti* <note>the divisor or the sine of the amplitude at a given time</note>. By dividing these three products separately by the desired *Hriti*, the desired hypotenuse is obtained in three ways.

The proof here is by the inverse rule of three <note>a mathematical proportion where one value increases as the other decreases</note>. If, by a *Hriti* equal to the *Kujya* <note>the sine of the terrestrial latitude or earth-sine</note>, the equatorial hypotenuse is obtained; by the *Taddhriti*, the prime vertical hypotenuse is obtained; and by the *Hriti*, the midday hypotenuse is obtained; then what would be obtained by the desired *Hriti*? The result is the desired hypotenuse; thus, it is proven.

->**Vernacular Commentary**<-

By multiplying the equatorial hypotenuse by the *Kujya*, the prime vertical hypotenuse by the *Taddhriti*, and the midday hypotenuse by the *Hriti*, and then dividing in all three instances by the desired *Hriti*, the desired hypotenuse is found by an alternative method.

->**Proof**<-

Here, the Teacher <note>referring to the original author of the Sanskrit verses, likely Bhaskara II</note> has written the proof using the inverse rule of three. It can also be demonstrated using the direct rule of three:

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Equatorial Hypotenuse : Gnomon :: Radius : | (Gnomon $\times$ Radius) / Equatorial Hypotenuse = Equatorial Gnomon |
| *Kujya* : Equatorial Gnomon :: Desired *Hriti* : | (Equatorial Gnomon $\times$ Desired *Hriti*) / *Kujya* = (Gnomon $\times$ Radius $\times$ Desired *Hriti*) / (*Kujya* $\times$ Equatorial Hypotenuse) |

= Desired Gnomon.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Desired Gnomon : Radius :: Gnomon : | (Radius $\times$ Gnomon) / Desired Gnomon = Shadow Hypotenuse |

(Radius $\times$ Gnomon $\times$ *Kujya* $\times$ Equatorial Hypotenuse) / (Gnomon $\times$ Radius $\times$ Desired *Hriti*) = (Equatorial Hypotenuse $\times$ *Kujya*) / Desired *Hriti* = Shadow Hypotenuse.

It is proven.

->**The procedure is as previously stated, but**<-
->**the wise should perform subtraction where addition is indicated. || 63 ||**<-

Now, in any instance where a subtraction must be performed and the quantity to be subtracted is greater than the quantity it is being subtracted from, the wise mathematician should subtract the smaller from the larger and proceed with the remaining operations. However, when this "inverse subtraction" is performed, if the rule subsequently calls for addition, one must instead perform subtraction.

The mathematical rationale <note>Sanskrit: upapatti; the logical proof or derivation of a formula</note> is as follows: In the rule beginning with "from the altitude increased or decreased by the ascensional difference," if in the Northern Hemisphere the ascensional difference <note>The difference between right and oblique ascension</note> cannot be subtracted from the altitude-time, then one must subtract the altitude-time from the ascensional difference. The sine of the remainder then represents a segment of the "string" <note>Sanskrit: sutra; here referring to a specific chord in the celestial sphere</note> located below the equatorial horizon <note>Sanskrit: unmandala; the six-o'clock circle</note>. When the "portion" <note>Sanskrit: kala</note> is calculated from this, it becomes a segment of the earth-sine <note>Sanskrit: kujya</note> below the equatorial horizon. When the "desired pole" <note>Sanskrit: ishtayashti</note> is calculated from that portion, it becomes a segment above the equatorial gnomon. Now, according to the rule "when the sun has moved to the north or south," the "string" should normally be added to the sine of the ascensional difference. But here, that must not be done. Instead, the "string" which is directed downwards below the equatorial horizon must be subtracted from the sine of the ascensional difference. The remainder is the "desired last" <note>Sanskrit: ishtantya; a specific chord used in shadow calculation</note>. Likewise, the "portion" directed below the equatorial horizon is subtracted from the earth-sine; the remainder is the segment below the earth-sine known as the "desired circle" <note>Sanskrit: ishtavriti</note>. Finally, the "desired pole" directed below the equatorial horizon is subtracted from the equatorial gnomon; the remainder is the "desired gnomon" <note>Sanskrit: ishtashanku; the sine of the altitude of the sun</note>. Thus, the instruction was correctly stated.

### Vernacular Commentary

When at any place during subtraction the quantity to be subtracted cannot be taken away, then the other quantity should be subtracted from it. In that case, perform all calculations according to the rules, except that wherever an occasion for addition arises, one must subtract, and in place of subtraction, one must add.

This inverse method of correction should be understood as follows: just as it is written in the verse beginning with "**Then, by the rising-difference (char) added or subtracted from the altitude-time...**" <note>original: "athounnatadunayutacharena"</note>—if the altitude-time is less than the rising-difference, then it should be subtracted from the rising-difference itself. Now, he describes another special case:

> When the hour-angle is greater than fifteen <note>literally "arrow-moon" (15) in the numerical code system</note> ghatikas <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>, the R-sine of the remainder added to the Radius is the versed sine of that hour-angle. The gnomon-shadow of the equatorial circle is not visible in the southern hemisphere, yet it must be calculated for the sake of further proportions. || 64 ||

When the hour-angle <note>the time elapsed since the sun was on the meridian</note> is greater than fifteen ghatikas, one should understand that in calculating the versed sine <note>the "reversed" sine or sagitta</note>, one must subtract fifteen ghatikas from the hour-angle; the R-sine of the remainder added to the Radius becomes the versed sine. Furthermore, in the southern hemisphere, because it is located below the horizon, the equatorial gnomon-shadow <note>unmandala-shanku</note> is invisible; nevertheless, this must be calculated for the purpose of other mathematical proportions.

**The Proof here:** The versed sine is essentially in the form of an "arrow" <note>the segment of a chord</note>. When the hour-angle exceeds fifteen ghatikas, the versed sine of those fifteen ghatikas is equal to the Radius. Then, for the time exceeding fifteen ghatikas, the R-sine is vertical. When that is added to the Radius, it becomes the versed sine in the form of an arrow. In the celestial sphere, on the diurnal circle, if one end of a string is tied at the end of the hour-angle ghatikas to the east of the meridian and the second end is tied at the end of the hour-angle ghatikas to the west, the distance between that string and the intersection of the meridian and the diurnal circle is the "arrow." In this way, one should demonstrate their versed sine.

As long as the northern declination <note>original: "kranti"</note> of the Sun is greater than the local latitude <note>original: "pala"</note>, the Sun remains north of the prime vertical even at midday. It is visible only in the northern hemisphere. Therefore, only there should its shadow be given a name.

<page-num>303</page-num>
-># Chapter on the Three Problems<-
<note>The "Three Problems" refer to the determination of time, direction, and place through gnomon shadows.</note>

The equinoctial shadow <note>the shadow cast by a vertical pole at noon on the equinox</note> serves as the basis for the "prime vertical gnomon" <term>Samashanku: the vertical sine of the Sun's altitude when it is exactly due east or west</term> that is produced. The horizontal line <note>the distance from the center to the rising/setting line</note> produces the corresponding "amplitude-shadow" <term>Taddhriti: a specific trigonometric segment used in spherical astronomy</term>. In that context, the "amplitude" <term>Agra: the distance of the Sun at rising from the east-west line</term> acts as the "base" <term>Bhuja: the side of a right-angled triangle</term>. This constitutes the "latitude-triangle" <term>Akshakshetra: a right-angled triangle whose sides are related to the local latitude</term>. Therefore, this model is valid for the calculations of others. Even in the Southern Hemisphere, where the prime vertical gnomon is invisible <note>because the Sun does not cross the prime vertical above the horizon</note>, it is still valid for the sake of mathematical proportion; this is the meaning of the text.

### Vernacular Commentary

In the Northern Hemisphere, when the declination <term>Kranti: the angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator</term> is greater than the latitude <term>Akshansha</term>, midday will occur to the north of the prime vertical. Similarly, when the declination is less than the latitude, midday will occur to the south of the prime vertical, and the Sun will enter the prime vertical <note>meaning it will pass directly through the east or west points</note>. However, the entry into the prime vertical is only visible in the Northern Hemisphere, and only then will the "prime shadow" and other measurements occur. This does not happen in the Southern Hemisphere. In a region where the Sun does not enter the prime vertical but a "prime vertical gnomon" is proven through calculation, that value is still consistent for the purpose of mathematical proportion.

### Mathematical Proof

In the meridian circle, the distance from the celestial equator to the solar disk is the declination, and the distance to the zenith <term>Khasvastika: the point directly overhead</term> is the latitude. Therefore, when the declination is greater than the latitude, the Sun is north of the zenith at midday. For this reason, there will be an absence of prime vertical entry. When the declination is less than the latitude, the Sun is south of the prime vertical, and thus entry into the prime vertical must occur. This is the situation in the Northern Hemisphere.

In the Southern Hemisphere, because the intersection of the diurnal circle <term>Ahoratravritta: the daily path of the Sun</term> and the prime vertical occurs below the horizon, the entry into the prime vertical will not be visible there. However, the prime vertical gnomon produced there will still be useful for mathematical proportions. || 65 ||
