# In the Calculation of Days—

From the southern mark, if it is toward the north, then from the northern mark. How is this to be known? He says: "Clockwise and counter-clockwise are indeed south and north." If the <term>deflection</term><note>original: "valana"; the angle between the local vertical/horizontal and the celestial equator/ecliptic</note> is southern, then it is clockwise: from the eastern mark to the south, from the southern mark to the west, from the western mark to the north, and from the northern mark to the east—this is clockwise. Anything other than this is counter-clockwise. And that deflection should be applied as a sine-chord, not as an arc. Having thus applied the deflections, lines should be marked from the center reaching the ends of the deflection. Then, from the end of the deflection at contact, the <term>latitude</term><note>original: "vikshepa"; the angular distance of the planet from the ecliptic</note> at contact should be applied; and from the end of the deflection at separation, the latitude at separation. This too is applied as a sine-chord. Then the middle latitude should be applied from the center on the deflection line. From those marks at the ends of the latitudes, circles should be drawn with a cord the size of half the <term>eclipsing body</term><note>original: "grahaka"; the body that covers the other, such as the Moon covering the Sun</note>, and thus the contact, separation, and middle eclipse are to be understood.

Here is the <term>rationale</term><note>original: "vasana"; the underlying physical or geometric logic</note>. When the center of the eclipsing circle is on the circle of the half-sum of the radii, then the edges of the eclipsed and eclipsing disks are touching. Therefore, the circle of the half-sum of the radii is drawn externally and marked with the directions. There, the "East" is the East of the <term>prime vertical</term><note>original: "samamandala"; the great circle passing through the zenith and the east/west points</note>. When the deflection is applied to that, the line going from the center to the end of the deflection is the East of the <term>ecliptic</term><note>original: "krantivritta"; the sun's apparent path</note>. In this way, the deflection of all directions is found. Now, the latitude is applied as a sine-chord from the deflection line, because the latitude is north-south relative to the East of the ecliptic. This is indeed the case for contact and separation. Now, the middle latitude is applied from the center on the deflection line because "middle deflection" is the name for the north-south direction relative to the East of the ecliptic at that time. The center of the eclipsing circle is at the end of the latitude; therefore, by the circles made there, the contact, separation, and middle positions are established.

->Vernacular Commentary<-

Having drawn a circle on level ground with a radius equal to half the eclipsed disk, draw a second circle from the same point with the value of the half-sum of the radii. Then on that...

Establish the directions by drawing East-West <term>Purvapara; the horizontal line</term> and North-South <term>Yamyottara; the meridian line</term> lines through a central point. In this circle of the "half-sum of the diameters" <term>Manaikyardha-vritta; a circle whose radius equals the sum of the radii of the eclipsed and eclipsing bodies</term>, apply the lunar deflection <term>Valana; the angle between the ecliptic and the local horizon</term>. From the East mark, apply the deflection for the contact <note>the beginning of the eclipse</note>, and from the West mark, apply it for the separation <note>the end of the eclipse</note>, according to the sine. If the deflection is South, it should be applied in a clockwise direction—that is, from the East mark toward the South, from South to West, from West to North, and from North to East. If it is North, apply it in the opposite direction within the diagram <term>Parilekha; the graphical projection</term>. In a solar eclipse, apply the deflection for contact from the West mark and for separation from the East mark in the same manner. Then, draw lines from the center to the ends of these deflection marks. From the end of the contact deflection, apply the celestial latitude <term>Shara; literally 'arrow', representing the angular distance from the ecliptic</term> at the time of contact, and from the end of the separation deflection, apply the latitude at the time of separation, each from its respective deflection point according to its direction and sine. The middle latitude <note>at the moment of maximum eclipse</note> should be applied from the center along the deflection line. By drawing circles with a radius equal to half the diameter of the eclipsing body <term>Grahakardha</term> from these latitude endpoints, the contact, middle, and separation points are determined.

### Proof / Rationale

When the center of the eclipsing circle <note>the Earth's shadow in a lunar eclipse</note> is on the circle of the half-sum of the diameters, the edges of the eclipsed and eclipsing disks meet. For this reason, the circle of the half-sum of the diameters is drawn on the outside. Having marked the directions within it, the deflection is applied from the East point of the prime vertical <term>Samamandala; the great circle passing through the East, West, and Zenith</term>. The line drawn from the center of the circle to the end of the deflection is known as the East point of the Ecliptic <term>Kranti-vritta</term>. The North-South distance from the East of the prime vertical to the East of the ecliptic is the latitude. Since the eclipsing body remains at the end of this latitude, drawing a circle there allows one to know the magnitude of the contact, middle, and separation.

In the circle of the half-sum of the diameters, wherever the center of the eclipsing body is located, if a circle is drawn with a radius of half the eclipsing body's diameter, the point where it touches the eclipsed circle is the point of contact or separation. Where the line from the latitude of contact meets the eclipsed circle, contact occurs; where the line from the latitude of separation meets it, separation occurs.

Now, he describes the projection for the total immersion, the beginning of emergence, and the desired obscuration at any given time.

> From the center, extend the <term>sine of the base</term> <note>bhujā: the horizontal side of a right triangle</note> along the line of the <term>deflection</term> <note>valana: the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator</note>. From the tip of that base, extend the <term>latitude</term> <note>śara: literally 'arrow', the celestial latitude of the moon</note>, and from the center, extend the <term>hypotenuse</term> <note>śravaṇa: the distance between the centers of the two bodies</note>. From the point where the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>koṭi: the vertical side of the triangle</note> and the hypotenuse meet, draw a circle using the radius of the obscuring body. || 30 || Thus, the <term>total immersion</term> <note>sammīlana: the moment the eclipsed body is fully covered</note>, the <term>emergence</term> <note>unmīlana: the moment the body begins to reappear</note>, and the <term>obscuration</term> <note>grāsa: literally 'the bite', the portion of the disk eclipsed</note> at a desired time are to be known; or else, these may be found by another method.

At the time of <term>total immersion</term>, having calculated the <term>deflection</term>, mark it from the eastern point as before. Draw a line from the center to the end of that deflection. On that line, the <term>base</term> should be marked eastward from the center. From the tip of the base, extend a pointer equal to the <term>latitude</term> at that time, and from the center, extend a pointer equal to the <term>hypotenuse</term>. From the point where the tips of these pointers meet, draw a circle with the radius of the obscuring body to determine the point of <term>total immersion</term>.

In the same way, by applying the deflection for the <term>emergence</term> from the western side, the point of emergence is known. Similarly, by applying the deflection for a desired time from either the east or west as appropriate, the <term>obscuration</term> at that desired time is known. The phrase "or else, these..." connects to what follows.

<note>The author is providing a geometric method for visualizing an eclipse. By constructing a right-angled triangle using the calculated astronomical values (latitude, deflection, and distance), the astronomer can physically draw the positions of the sun/moon and the shadow on a board to predict exactly where and when the eclipse will appear.</note>

### Rationale
The logic here is as follows: The "base" <term>bhujā; the horizontal side of a right-angled triangle</term> is a segment of the path of the eclipsing body (the Earth's shadow). In this construction, the "latitude" <term>śara; literally 'arrow', representing the celestial latitude</term> is the "upright" <term>koṭi; the vertical side of a right-angled triangle</term>. The square root of the sum of their squares is the "hypotenuse" <term>karṇa</term>. It is correctly stated that when the eclipsing body is drawn from the tip of this hypotenuse, the "total immersion" <term>sammīlana; the moment the moon is fully covered</term> and other phases occur. 

Now, an objection might be raised: the "base" is marked along the line of "deflection" <term>valana; the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator</term> from the center of the eclipsed body (the Moon); how then can it be called a segment of the path of the eclipsing body? This is true, but wherever a triangle is formed by a base, an upright, and a hypotenuse, it must necessarily be half of a rectangle. Here, the latitude (the upright) is drawn from the tip of the base. The same applies to the root of the base. The distance between the tips of the two latitude lines is the same as the distance between their roots. Therefore, calling the segment of the eclipsing body's path the "base" is perfectly accurate.

### Vernacular Commentary
From the center, draw a line to the tip of the deflection. On that line, mark the "base" <gloss>bhujā</gloss> toward the East from the center. From the tip of that base, apply the instantaneous latitude <gloss>śara</gloss>, and from the center, apply the hypotenuse <gloss>karṇa</gloss>. Taking the point where the upright and hypotenuse meet as the center, draw a circle with a radius equal to half the sum of the diameters <note>original: "mānāntarārdha", referring to the sum of the radii of the Moon and the Shadow</note> to determine the magnitude of the total immersion. Similarly, by marking the base toward the West, one can determine the "emergence" <term>unmīlana; the moment the moon begins to exit the shadow</term> in the same manner. Depending on the desired time, the "partial eclipse" <term>iṣṭagrāsa; literally 'desired bite'</term> toward the East or West can also be known.

### Geometric Proof
The base is the segment of the eclipsing body's path and the instantaneous latitude is the upright; the square root of the sum of their squares is the hypotenuse. At the moment of total immersion, the distance between the centers of the eclipsed and eclipsing bodies is the hypotenuse, which is equal to the difference of their semi-diameters <note>The text uses "mānāntarārdha" which technically refers to the half-sum or half-difference of diameters depending on the eclipse phase being calculated</note>. From the center of the eclipsed body, in the direction of contact, the center of the eclipsing body lies at the tip of the hypotenuse. When the eclipsing body has entered the disk of the eclipsed body at the desired time, the value of the immersion is found. This is clear from the diagram. || 30 ||

Now, he describes another method for the graphical representation of the total immersion and emersion.

> From the two points at the ends of the latitudes for the first and last contact,
> draw separate lines reaching to the end of the middle latitude. || 31 ||
> These lines are indeed the paths of the first contact and the clearing;
> their magnitudes should be calculated and known.
> Having drawn a circle from the center with a radius equal to
> half the sum of the diameters <note>Sanskrit: bimbāntarārdha; the distance between the centers of the two bodies at the moment of internal contact</note>, || 32 ||

A line should be drawn from the end of the latitude at first contact to the end of the middle latitude. That is to be known as the path of first contact <note>Sanskrit: pragraha-mārga</note>. Then, another separate line should be drawn from the end of the middle latitude to the end of the latitude at the moment of clearing. That is to be known as the path of clearing <note>Sanskrit: mukti-mārga</note>. Having measured the lengths of those two paths with a <term>finger-staff</term> <note>angula-śalākā; a graduated measuring rod used in astronomical diagrams</note>, they should be set aside carefully. Now, having produced a circle at the center with a cord of the length of <term>half the sum of the diameters</term>, the two points where that circle intersects the two paths are the locations from which—by drawing circles with a radius of half the Earth's shadow—the total immersion and the beginning of emersion are to be understood.

**The Rationale:** As the center of the obscuring body <note>the Earth's shadow in a lunar eclipse</note> moves along its own path, the total immersion and emersion occur at the points where the hypotenuse <note>the distance between centers</note> is equal to half the difference of the diameters. Therefore, by drawing a circle with <term>half the sum of the diameters</term> <note>Note: The text uses bimbāntarārdha, which in the context of total obscuration refers to the distance between centers when the moon is just fully inside the shadow</note>, those two positions are determined.

"Desired" refers to the chosen time in units such as ghatikas <note>a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. This should be multiplied by the "path units" <note>the spatial length of the eclipse path</note> and divided by the ghatikas of the half-duration of the eclipse. If the desired time is after the first contact, the units should be marked forward from the tip of the latitude at contact. If the desired time is before the middle of the eclipse, they should be marked toward the east from the tip of the middle latitude. Similarly, on the path of emergence, according to the desired time, one should draw a circle with the radius of the eclipsing body at the end of those desired units to find the desired obscuration. This is a simplified geometric projection for the sake of convenience.

The proof here is by the Rule of Three <note>A mathematical proportion: if A gives B, what does C give?</note>. If the total number of fingers <note>angulas, a traditional unit of measurement</note> on the path of the eclipse is obtained during the half-duration of the eclipse, then what is obtained at the desired elapsed time? The result is the "desired fingers." This indicates the position of the center of the eclipsing body <note>the "graha" or planet causing the eclipse</note> at that moment. It is no wonder then, that by drawing a circle with the radius of the eclipsing body at that point, the desired amount of the eclipse is revealed.

->Vernacular Commentary<-

Multiply the previously calculated desired time <note>time elapsed since the start of the eclipse</note> by the value of the fingers on the path, and divide by your own half-duration time. The result will be the desired fingers. By marking these fingers along the path according to the desired time, and drawing a circle with the radius of the eclipsing body from that point, one can know the value of the eclipse at that moment. In this way, the graphical representation <term>parilekha: a geometric diagram or projection used in Indian astronomy</term> is established through these rough values.

The ratio for the desired eclipse—

Half-duration : Path-fingers :: Desired-time = (Path-fingers $\times$ Desired-time) / Half-duration = Desired-fingers.

The center of the eclipsing body lies at the end of these desired fingers. By drawing a circle there with the radius of the eclipsing body, the desired eclipse is clearly known. The situation here is as follows: the hypotenuse formed by the half-sum of the diameters minus the desired eclipse represents the distance between the centers of the eclipsed and eclipsing bodies. This is because the center of the eclipsing body is located where the distance is applied along the previously calculated path-line from the center of the eclipsed body. The portion of the eclipsed circle enclosed by the eclipsing circle from that point is the desired eclipse. || 34 ||

# Chapter on the Computation of Lunar Eclipses

The two segments of the path <note>the orbital path of the Moon during the eclipse</note> are multiplied by their respective half-duration segments <term>sthitikhanda: the time from the start or end to the maximum eclipse</term> and divided by the total digits of the path. The result is the desired time <term>ishtakala: the specific moment of observation</term> forward from the first contact, or backward from the moment of clearance.

The mathematical rationale <term>upapatti: proof or demonstration</term> is as follows: At the desired time, the difference between the sum of the radii and the amount of obscuration <term>grasa: the portion of the Moon covered by the shadow</term> is the hypotenuse—meaning the distance between the centers of the eclipsed body and the eclipsing body. This has been stated previously. Using that hypotenuse as a radius, a circle is drawn from the center; the segments of the path that lie outside this circle are used for the proportion. If the total digits of the path correspond to the half-duration in minutes, then what time corresponds to the digits of the segments lying outside? Thus, the desired time is calculated, and all is flawless.

->Vernacular Commentary<-

Subtract the obscuration from the sum of the radii; with the remaining value, draw a circle from the center. Multiply the segments of the path lying outside that circle by their respective half-duration segments and divide by the total digits of the path. The result is the value of the desired time after the first contact and before the final clearance.

The rationale here is clear from the previous method. || 35 ||

Now, the color of the Moon during the eclipse is described:

> When the obscuration is slight, the Moon <note>original: "Sudhanshu," literally 'the nectar-rayed one'</note> is **smoke-colored**;
> When half-obscured, it is **black**; when more than half, it is **blackish-red**.
> When fully obscured, the color is said to be **tawny** <note>original: "pishanga," a reddish-yellow or brown</note>;
> In an eclipse of the Sun, the obscured part is always **black**. || 36 ||

The meaning is clear.

->Vernacular Commentary<-

The color of the Moon during an eclipse is stated—when there is a small amount of obscuration, the Moon has a smoky color. In a half-eclipse, it is black, and in more than that, it is black...

### Vernacular Commentary

In the <term>Ecliptic</term> which takes the form of the observer's vertical circle, when the Sun is at the <term>Zenith</term> <note>The point directly overhead</note>, the <term>deflection</term> at the <term>horizon</term> is equal to the Sun's <term>amplitude</term> <note>Agrā: the angular distance of the rising sun from the true east</note> increased by three signs <note>90 degrees</note>. If you can prove that same deflection using the <term>versed sine</term>, then I would accept the deflection described in texts such as the *Dhivridhida* as being without error. In a country at 66° latitude, during the sunrise of Aries, Taurus, or Gemini, the contact occurs in the southern direction of the Sun due to the absence of celestial latitude. There, the <term>Ecliptic</term> takes the shape of the horizon, and the maximum <term>apparent deflection</term> is equal to the <term>radius</term>. However, this cannot be proven using the <term>versed sine</term>. Therefore, the calculation of deflection should always be performed using the <term>sine</term> <note>original: "kramajyā"</note> only.

The expansion of this subject has already taken place in the <term>Goladhyaya</term> <note>The section of the text concerning the Celestial Sphere</note>. || 38-39 ||

# Now, the Chapter on Solar Eclipses is Explained.

---

First, the author states the purpose for beginning this topic:

> Even at the moment of the new moon's end, when the Sun and Moon are at equal longitudes,
>     the observer, being elevated on the Earth's surface, does not see them on a single line of sight
> because they are in different orbits and are inclined from the zenith.
>     Therefore, I shall explain "Parallax in Longitude" <term>lambana: the difference in observed longitudinal position due to the observer's viewpoint</term> and "Parallax in Latitude" <term>nati: the difference in observed latitudinal position</term>. || 1 ||

At the conclusion of the new moon <note>Amavasya</note>, even when the Sun and Moon are at the same degree and minute, an observer elevated by the Earth's radius from the center does not see them on a single line of sight if they are inclined <note>nata: positioned away from the zenith/overhead point</note>. This is because they occupy different orbits. The Moon's orbit is small, while the Sun's is large. In a lunar eclipse, the Moon's orbit and the Earth's shadow are effectively the same distance. There, at the end of the lunar day, an observer—even if elevated—sees the Moon and the Earth's shadow on a single line of sight. However, in a solar eclipse, one does not see the Sun and Moon on the same line because of their differing orbits. For that reason, I describe the difference called "Longitude Parallax" <gloss>lambana</gloss> and "Latitude Parallax" <gloss>nati</gloss>.

->Vernacular Commentary<-

At the end of the new moon, the Sun and Moon—equal in their signs, degrees, and minutes—are not seen on a single line of sight by an observer living on the Earth's surface (elevated by the measure of the Earth's radius) when they are inclined from the zenith, because their orbits are distinct. Therefore, I state the differences known as Longitude Parallax and Latitude Parallax. || 1 ||

Now, to explain the presence or absence of parallax and its addition or subtraction, he describes the procedure:

> Having first calculated the Ascendant <term>lagna: the rising point of the zodiac on the eastern horizon</term> for the end of the new moon,
>     there is no Longitude Parallax when that point is equal to the Nonagesimal <term>vitribhalagna: the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the Ascendant, representing the highest point of the ecliptic</term>.

<summary>This text introduces the concept of solar eclipses, explaining that parallax occurs because the observer sits on the Earth's surface rather than at its center, causing a visual displacement of the Sun and Moon.</summary>
<keywords>solar eclipse, parallax, longitude parallax, latitude parallax, celestial orbits, new moon, astronomy, observation</keywords>

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

-> If the Sun is less than or greater than that point, parallax occurs; <-
-> thus, addition and subtraction should be understood respectively. || 2 || <-

To determine the parallax <note>parallax (lambana) refers to the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body as viewed from the Earth's surface versus its center</note> at the moment of the end of the lunar month (conjunction), one must calculate the ascendant <note>the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note> and subtract three signs from it. When the Sun is exactly equal to this "nonagesimal" point <note>the point 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note>, there is no parallax. It should be understood that parallax occurs only when the Sun is less than or greater than that point. Furthermore, when the Sun is less than the nonagesimal, the resulting parallax is designated as "positive" (additive); this means it should be added to the time of the end of the lunar day. When the Sun is greater, it is "negative" (subtractive), meaning it should be subtracted from the time of the end of the lunar day.

Now, the geometric derivation of parallax is explained. Here, the horizon is the circle bound like a rim by the intersection of the prime vertical and the meridian circles. An observer at the center of the Earth sees a planet situated there. However, an observer on the surface of the Earth does not even see that true horizon due to the Earth's curvature <note>literally "the Earth's umbrella"</note>. Instead, because of the Earth's radius of roughly 800 leagues <note>yojanas</note>, he perceives another horizon all around, slightly above that true horizon. This is because he sees from an elevated position. He cannot see the horizon below that, which is "dropped" from his line of sight. Therefore, the minutes of arc <note>liptas</note> corresponding to those leagues on the planet's orbit within the vertical circle are the "Earth-shadowed minutes"; these are the maximum longitudinal parallax and maximum latitudinal parallax <note>avanati</note>. These are equal to one-fifteenth of the planet's daily motion. This is because the Earth's radius is one-fifteenth of the distance traveled by a planet in one day <note>according to the specific cosmological model used here</note>. When the planet is on the horizon, it appears lowered by these "Earth-shadowed minutes." But when the Sun is at the zenith <note>directly overhead</note>, both the observer at the Earth's center and the observer on the surface see it exactly at the zenith. It is not lowered in any direction, and thus there is an absence of parallax. At the horizon, however, the maximum parallax is equal to the Earth-shadowed minutes. Thus, it is known that parallax arises when the planet is below the zenith. This applies to the Moon as well. At the end of the lunar month...

When the minutes of the Sun's parallax are subtracted from the minutes of the Moon's parallax, the remainder is 48' 46" <note>This represents the maximum relative parallax between the Sun and Moon</note>. These are the maximum minutes of parallax for the Moon, which is situated below the Sun's line of sight. Now, when the ecliptic <term>Krāntivṛtta: the apparent path of the Sun</term> coincides with the vertical circle <term>Dṛṅmaṇḍala: the circle passing through the zenith and the planet</term>, the following proportion is used to convert the maximum parallax minutes into units of time <term>Ghaṭīs: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term>:

If sixty *ghatīs* are obtained from the difference in daily motion <note>The relative speed between the Sun and Moon</note>, then what is obtained from a fifteenth part of that difference? The result is four *ghatīs*, which is the maximum parallax. Therefore, it is appropriate to calculate the parallax using a proportion based on four *ghatīs*, provided the ecliptic is vertical. However, if the ecliptic is slanted, then a double proportion is required.

Parallax is produced along the line of the vertical circle, and that is the "mean" parallax. This acts as the hypotenuse. When it is transformed into the direction of the ecliptic's east-west line, it becomes the "corrected" <term>Sphuṭa: clear or calculated value</term> parallax, acting as the base of a triangle. When the vertical circle is itself the ecliptic, then the mean parallax is the corrected one. Since the corrected state of parallax depends on the east-west orientation of the ecliptic, the parallax is at its maximum at the lowest point of the ecliptic.

There is a total absence of parallax at the highest point. This highest point occurs at the "Nonagesimal" <term>Vitribhalagna: the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point or Ascendant</term> when that point is at the zenith. At that time, its sine-altitude <term>Śaṅku: the gnomon or sine of the altitude</term> is equal to the radius <term>Trijyā</term>. In that case, the mean parallax is itself the corrected parallax. When that Nonagesimal point is tilted away from the zenith, its sine-altitude becomes less than the radius; then the corrected parallax becomes smaller than the mean parallax, following the relationship of the base to the hypotenuse. Therefore, the decrease in parallax follows the decrease in the sine-altitude of the Nonagesimal. Thus, it is proper to use a proportion with the sine-altitude of the Nonagesimal to determine the corrected value of the mean parallax.

When the Sun is exactly at the zenith, there is an absence of <term>parallax</term> <note>original: "lamban"; the apparent displacement of a celestial object when viewed from different positions</note>. If the Sun is less than or greater than this position, parallax is produced. When the Sun is at a lower longitude than the <term>Nonagesimal</term> <note>original: "vitribhalagna"; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note>, the parallax is designated as additive (positive), and when it is greater, it is subtractive (negative).

## Geometric Derivation

The derivation written here by the Teacher <note>referring to the original author of the astronomical treatise</note> is being explained clearly. At the moment of the new moon conjunction, an observer at the center of the Earth sees the Sun, inclined from the zenith, covered by the Moon. However, at that same moment, an observer on the surface of the Earth does not see this; from their line of sight, the Moon remains "dropped" or displaced. This occurs because the orbits of the Moon and the Sun are different. Both the observer at the center and the observer on the surface see the Sun at the zenith at the same time, because there, the central line of sight and the surface line of sight are identical. Therefore, there is an absence of parallax at the zenith.

One must understand the Moon's position to be where the line drawn from the Earth's surface to the solar disk touches the solar orbit, and the Sun's position to be where the line drawn from the Earth's center to the Sun touches the lunar orbit. The difference between these two on the Moon's vertical circle is the parallax. This is because the observer on the surface sees the Moon displaced from their line of sight. For this reason, it is written in the <term>Goladhyaya</term> <note>The "Chapter on the Sphere" from the Siddhanta Shiromani</note>:

> "The Moon is displaced from the line of sight; therefore, that displacement is known as parallax." <note>original Sanskrit: "drksutralambitashchandrastena tallambanam smrtam"</note>

In the ecliptic, which takes the form of the observational circle, this constitutes the "clear" or true parallax. From this, it is also understood that for those at the center of the Earth, there is an absence of parallax in a solar eclipse due to the unity of the central lines of sight. Thus, parallax is produced due to the difference in the orbits of the Sun and Moon and the position of the observer on the Earth's surface. This state of parallax occurs when the planet is inclined from the zenith.

An observer at the center sees a planet situated on the central horizon, but the surface observer does not see it, because it remains "above" by the measure of the Earth's radius; the surface observer has a different surface horizon. From the central horizon's line of sight, the planet is displaced by an amount equal to the Earth's radius in <term>yojanas</term> <note>an ancient unit of distance</note>. Therefore, the minutes of arc <note>kala</note> that these yojanas represent on the observational circle...

This is what is called the <term>Kullambanakala</term> <note>Total parallax in minutes</note>, or <term>Paramalambanakala</term> <note>Maximum parallax in minutes</note>. That is to say, the maximum difference between the lines of sight from the Earth's surface and the Earth's center occurs at the horizon. That difference is equal to the fifteenth part of the difference between the daily motions of the Sun and the Moon. In this way, it is understood that there is an absence of parallax at the zenith <note>the point directly overhead</note>, it is at its maximum at the horizon, and in between, it decreases or increases according to the desired position. Similarly, the Moon also has parallax.

In the <term>Drigmandala</term> <note>the vertical circle passing through the planet and the zenith</note> shaped ecliptic, the <term>Sphutalambana</term> <note>corrected or true parallax</note> is established by a single proportion; however, when it is slanted, it is established by two proportions. This takes the form of a "side" <note>koti</note> and the mean hypotenuse of the vertical circle. The ecliptic is only clear when it is oriented toward the east. The highest point of the ecliptic is the <term>Vitribha</term> <note>the nonagesimal, or the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon</note>; when this is at the zenith, the sine of the nonagesimal <note>Vitribhalagna Shanku</note> is equal to the radius. # Chapter on Solar Eclipses

Now, having considered this very matter, the author explains the calculation of parallax <note>parallax in time, or 'lambana', refers to the difference in the time of the eclipse's appearance due to the observer's position on Earth</note> using two proportions.

> Having designated the point ninety degrees behind the rising sign as the Sun,
> the time interval between that point and the rising sign
> shall be the time elapsed since sunrise for that point.
> From that, the gnomon and other values are found using the ascensional differences. || 3 ||
> The sine of the difference between the Sun and the point ninety degrees behind the rising sign,
> multiplied by four and divided by the radius,
> then multiplied by the gnomon of that point and
> divided by the radius, gives the parallax in ghatikas <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> and its fractions. || 4 ||

At the moment of the end of the new moon <note>the conjunction of the Sun and Moon</note>, one should calculate the rising sign <term>Lagna: the point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon</term> and, keeping that fixed, determine the point ninety degrees behind it <term>Vitribha-lagna: the nonagesimal or the highest point of the ecliptic</term>.
The time elapsed since the rising of this nonagesimal point is found by adding the portion of the nonagesimal yet to rise, the portion of the rising sign already risen, and the intervening signs. With that time, and using the earth-sine, the radius of the diurnal circle, and the final sine <note>technical components of spherical trigonometry</note> as explained in the "Three Problems" chapter, the gnomon <term>Shanku: the sine of the altitude</term> is to be calculated. From the gnomon, the sine of the zenith distance and the hypotenuse of the shadow are also to be determined.
Then, the sine of the difference between the nonagesimal and the Sun must be calculated. Now, the proportion for the sake of parallax: If, when the sine of the difference between the nonagesimal and the Sun is equal to the radius, the parallax is four ghatikas, then what will it be for this desired sine? The result is the "mean parallax." Then, for the sake of making it "clear" <note>spherical correction</note>, a second proportion is used: If such parallax is obtained when the gnomon of the nonagesimal is equal to the radius, then what is obtained for the gnomon calculated just now? Thus, the "clear" <note>corrected</note> parallax is found.

->The Commentary (Prabha)<-

"Between those two signs" means between the nonagesimal and the rising sign. "The sine of the difference" refers to the sine of the interval between the nonagesimal and the Sun.

# Commentary in the Vernacular

Now the method for calculating parallax <note>Sanskrit: *lambana*; the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body as seen from the Earth's surface versus its center</note> is described—At the end of the new moon, consider the "Nonagesimal" <note>Sanskrit: *tribhonalagna*; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising sign</note> as the Sun. By finding the difference between that and the Ascendant, the elapsed time of the Nonagesimal is determined. From that, calculate the sine-altitude <note>Sanskrit: *shanku*; the vertical gnomon-shadow equivalent</note> of the Nonagesimal using the methods of the "Three Problems" <note>Sanskrit: *tri-prashna*; involving earth-sine, day-sine, and ascensional difference</note>. Then, multiply the sine of the difference between the Nonagesimal and the Sun by four, divide by the radius <note>Sanskrit: *trijya*</note>, multiply the result by the aforementioned sine-altitude, and divide again by the radius. This will yield the parallax in *ghatikas* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> and its fractions.

## Mathematical Proof

The proportion is made as follows: If the maximum parallax is obtained when the sine of the difference between the Nonagesimal and the Sun is equal to the radius, what is obtained for the desired sine-difference? The result is the mean parallax. Then, for the true parallax in the form of a cosine: If this parallax exists when the sine-altitude is equal to the radius, what is it for the calculated sine-altitude?

-> ∴ Parallax in Ghatikas = $\frac{4 \times \text{sine (Sun - Nonagesimal)}}{\text{Radius}} \times \frac{\text{Sine-altitude of Nonagesimal}}{\text{Radius}}$ ||3-4|| <-

Now, another method for the correction <note>Sanskrit: *sphutikarana*</note> is stated:

> Or, the parallax is indeed obtained from the result
> multiplied by twelve and divided by the hypotenuse
> of the shadow of the Nonagesimal.

"From the result multiplied by twelve" etc. Twelve times the mean parallax, divided by the hypotenuse of the shadow <note>Sanskrit: *chhaya-karna*</note> generated by the Nonagesimal, results in the true parallax. The proof here is by the rule of three <note>Sanskrit: *trairashika*</note>. There, by using the twelfth part of the sine-altitude of the Nonagesimal, the sine-altitude and the radius are reduced; twelve becomes the multiplier and the hypotenuse of the Nonagesimal becomes the divisor. Thus, it is proven.

That indeed is the mean <term>parallax</term><note>original: "lambana"; the apparent displacement of a celestial object when viewed from different positions</note>. That same value becomes the corrected parallax because the ecliptic is positioned upright. Now, when the <term>nonagesimal</term><note>original: "vintribhalagna"; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</note> is tilted from the zenith, the ecliptic is in an oblique position. Then, that corrected parallax, which acts as the "longitude" component <note>original: "koti"; the vertical or adjacent side of a right-angled triangle</note> along the east-west line, is determined. This is made into the corrected longitude component by the falling of the sine of the altitude of the nonagesimal. If you ask how that is done, the explanation follows:

In the calculation of mean parallax, the radius itself is the <term>gnomon</term><note>original: "shanku"; here referring to the sine of the altitude</note> of the nonagesimal. Then, for the sake of accuracy, the sine of the altitude of the nonagesimal which was calculated becomes the "longitude" component in the circle of the <term>ecliptic zenith distance</term><note>original: "drikkshepa-mandala"</note>. In that context, the sine of the zenith distance is the "base" component <note>original: "bhuja"; the horizontal or opposite side</note> and the radius is the hypotenuse. It is stated in the study of the celestial sphere that the vertical circle of the nonagesimal is the same as the circle of the ecliptic zenith distance. Therefore, that which is derived from the sine of the zenith distance (scaled by the radius) results in the form of a hypotenuse. It is logical that this is converted into the "longitude" component by a proportion using the sine of the altitude of the nonagesimal.

The same reasoning for the corrected parallax acting as a "longitude" component is now explained by another method. The sine of the zenith distance of the Sun in its own vertical circle acts as the hypotenuse. The sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal is the "ecliptic zenith distance" itself, and that is the "base" component. This is because the circle of the ecliptic zenith distance passes from the zenith through the nonagesimal, exactly north-south relative to the east of the ecliptic. There, the sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal is the ecliptic zenith distance. The minutes of <term>latitude parallax</term><note>original: "nati"; the northward or southward displacement</note> produced by that are seen by the observer to be equal everywhere in the interval between the orbits of the Moon and the Sun. As stated in the *Sphere*:

> The distance between the two orbits that exists at the nonagesimal is the same everywhere. Therefore:
> The minutes of latitude parallax are the "base," and the minutes of total parallax are the hypotenuse.
> The square root of the difference of their squares is the "longitude" component, which is the minutes of corrected <term>longitude parallax</term>.

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

The parallax in latitude <note>original: "drignati"</note> ought to be equal to the result of the calculation. However, as the celestial sphere is currently situated, it is not seen this way upon the diagram. This is because the parallax in latitude is formed when the sine of the distance between the nonagesimal <note>the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note> and the Sun is transformed by the radius and the sine of the altitude of the nonagesimal. Therefore, by this method as well, when the Sun is on the horizon, the maximum parallax in latitude is equal to the sine of the altitude of the nonagesimal. Thus, this method is identical to the previous one. 

However, if one places two sticks on level ground representing the sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal <note>original: "drikkshepa"</note> and the sine of the zenith distance of the Sun as the base and the hypotenuse, the difference between them will show the parallax in latitude as the upright side <note>original: "koti"</note> of the triangle. In this way, the noble teachers <note>original: "aryas"</note> conclude their mathematical demonstrations <note>original: "dhulikarma," literally "dust-work," referring to calculations done in sand</note> after devising various diagrams according to the underlying principles.

Now, the present topic is explained. Here, the square root of the difference between the squares of the sines of the zenith distances of the nonagesimal and the Sun is the same as the difference between their sines of altitude <note>original: "shanku"</note>. If you ask how this is so, it is explained: Here, the squares of the sines of the zenith distances are equal to the square of the radius minus the squares of their respective sines of altitude. When the difference between those two is taken, since the squares of the radius are equal, they cancel out, and only the difference between the squares of the sines of altitude remains. Thus, for any given radius, the difference between the squares of the two "base-sines" <note>sines</note> is equal to the difference between the squares of their "upright-sines" <note>cosines</note>. Therefore, it is said: "of the sines of altitude, or of the sines of the zenith distances, of the nonagesimal and the Sun." The conversion of this parallax into the measure of ghatis <note>units of time equal to 24 minutes</note> of parallax in longitude <note>original: "lambana"</note> is done by a proportion with the radius.

-> Light <-

"Of the two sines of the zenith distances" means of the sines of the zenith distances of the nonagesimal and the Sun. The rest is clear.

### Vernacular Commentary

The square root of the difference between the squares of the sines of altitude of the nonagesimal and the Sun—or of both their sines of zenith distance—is called the parallax in latitude <note>drignati</note>. By multiplying this parallax in latitude by the maximum parallax and dividing by the radius, one obtains, by an alternative method, the ghatis of parallax in longitude <note>lambana</note>.

It explains that the difference between the squares of sines of zenith distances is equivalent to the difference between the squares of sines of altitude.</summary>

## ->Proof / Rationale<-

When the Nonagesimal <note>the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note> is at the zenith, the ecliptic takes the form of the vertical circle; therefore, the mean parallax is itself the apparent parallax. Now, in the situation where the Nonagesimal is inclined from the zenith, the calculation of parallax is performed by another method. The vertical circle of the Nonagesimal is called the *Drkshepa-mandala* <note>the vertical circle of the nonagesimal</note> and its sine is called the *Drkshepa* <note>the ecliptic zenith distance</note>.

In the diagram described below, the north-south difference along the pole-star string <note>the secondary to the ecliptic</note> from the Moon's position to the disk is the minutes of latitude (*nati*), and from there to the Sun's disk along the vertical circle, the mean east-west difference is the minutes of parallax (*lambana*). The square root of the difference of their squares <note>applying the Pythagorean theorem</note> is the apparent parallax in the east-west direction on the original ecliptic; this is the opinion of the ancients. In reality, this parallax occurs on a small circle of the ecliptic produced by the cosine of the latitude. By the proportion: "If this is the parallax in the cosine of the latitude, what would it be in the radius of the circle?", the apparent parallax is converted to the ecliptic; this is the opinion of the moderns. Here, the Teacher has written extensively in the original text regarding the means of achieving the "vertical latitude" (*drng-nati*). That vertical latitude is equal to the square root of the difference between the squares of the *Drkshepa* and the sine of the Sun's zenith distance. However, it is not easily seen in the diagram as it stands. The sine of the difference between the Nonagesimal and the Sun, converted into the radius of the Nonagesimal's gnomon, takes the form of the vertical latitude. This should be understood through measurement. The *Drkshepa* is the base, the sine of the Sun's zenith distance is the hypotenuse, and the vertical latitude is the upright side.

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

The difference of the squares of the sine of the arcs <term>bhujajyā; the sine of an angle</term> is equal to the difference of the squares of the sine of their complements <term>koṭijyā; cosine</term>. Therefore, the difference between the squares of the sines of the zenith distances <term>dṛgjyā</term> of the nonagesimal <term>vitribhalagna; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</term> and the Sun <term>ravi</term> is the same as the difference of the squares of their respective gnomons <term>śaṅku; the sine of the altitude</term>. According to this rule:

(Sun's Sine Zenith Distance)$^2$ — (Nonagesimal Sine Zenith Distance)$^2$ = (Sine Parallax in Latitude)$^2$ = (Nonagesimal Gnomon)$^2$ — (Sun's Gnomon)$^2$.

$\therefore$ (Radius)$^2$ — (Nonagesimal Gnomon)$^2$ = (Nonagesimal Sine Zenith Distance)$^2$
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;(Radius)$^2$ — (Sun's Gnomon)$^2$ = (Sun's Sine Zenith Distance)$^2$
(Sun's Sine Zenith Distance)$^2$ — (Nonagesimal Sine Zenith Distance)$^2$ = (Radius)$^2$ — (Sun's Gnomon)$^2$ — (Radius)$^2$ + (Nonagesimal Gnomon)$^2$;
$\therefore$ Sine Parallax in Latitude = (Nonagesimal Gnomon)$^2$ — (Sun's Gnomon)$^2$.

The parallax in time <term>ghaṭikātmaka lambana; parallax expressed in units of 24 minutes</term> is derived from the Sine Parallax in Latitude using the ratio of the Radius <term>trijyā</term>:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;4 $\times$ $\sqrt{\text{(Nonagesimal Gnomon)}^2 - \text{(Sun's Gnomon)}^2}$
Parallax = ———————————————————————————————————————— .
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Radius

In this manner, everything is proven. || 5 ||

**Now, he describes another method for calculating parallax.**
> **The square root of the difference of the squares of those two gnomons,**
> **or of those two sines of zenith distance,**
> **when divided by one-fourth of the Radius,**
> **results in the parallax in units of time (ghatika) and so on. || 6 ||**
<note>original: "शङ्कोस्तयोर्हग्गुणयोस्तयोर्वा..." This verse provides a simplified computational shortcut.</note>

The square root of the difference of the squares of the previously mentioned gnomons of the nonagesimal and the Sun, when reduced by one-fourth of the Radius, becomes the parallax. Alternatively, the square root of the difference of the squares of the sines of the zenith distances of those two, divided by one-fourth of the Radius, also results in the parallax.

**Here is the rationale <term>upapatti</term>:** Here, the resulting Sine Parallax in Latitude (which takes the form of a "cosine" or upright side in this geometric context) is calculated using a proportion involving four *ghatikas* <note>4 ghatikas = 96 minutes, a standard constant in these calculations</note> and the Radius. If that calculation is applied to the gnomons or the sines of zenith distances—which serve as the components—to simplify the operation <term>kriyālāghava</term>, then the Sine Parallax in Latitude is produced directly in the form of time. That itself is the parallax <term>lambana</term>. Thus, by doing so, two other methods are established.

# Commentary in the Common Language

Regarding the <term>Shanku</term><note>The gnomon or the sine of the altitude</note> or the <term>Drig-jya</term><note>The sine of the zenith distance</note> mentioned previously: by dividing them by one-fourth of the radius and taking the square root of the difference of their squares, the <term>Lambana</term><note>Parallax in longitude</note> is established in two different ways.

## Mathematical Proof

The parallax is derived using the method starting with "From the gnomon of the Sun and the point ninety degrees behind the ascendant..." and so on:

$\frac{\sqrt{(Vih^2 - Rah^2)} \times 4}{Radius}$ = $\frac{\sqrt{16 Vih^2 - 16 Rah^2}}{Radius}$ = Parallax.

Taking the square root and applying the division by one-fourth of the radius:

$\therefore \frac{4 Vih - 4 Rah}{Radius} = \frac{Vih - Rah}{\frac{Radius}{4}} = Parallax.$

In this same manner, the parallax is also proven using the sines of altitude. || 6 ||

Now, the purpose of parallax is stated:

> The end of the lunar month, when corrected by that parallax,
> becomes the true time of the middle of the eclipse, found through iteration. || 7 ||

Thus, the parallax generated at the time of the new moon is additive to the hours of the new moon if the Sun is less than the <term>Vitribha-lagna</term><note>The point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point; the nonagesimal</note>. If the Sun is greater than the nonagesimal, the parallax is subtractive and should be removed from the hours of the new moon. In this way, by repeatedly calculating the ascendant and the nonagesimal from the time of the new moon corrected by parallax, the parallax should be calculated again using the stated method. The mathematically calculated end of the new moon must be corrected again. This process is repeated until the value remains constant <note>original: "avishesa" - meaning no further difference occurs through iteration</note>. The end of the new moon thus corrected becomes the time of the middle of the eclipse.

The logic here is as follows: Because the orbit of the Moon is near and the orbit of the Sun is distant, and because the observer is elevated on the surface of the Earth, the line of sight to the solar disk...

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

The distance by which the Moon appears to hang down <note>original: *avalambita*, meaning suspended or shifted downwards due to parallax</note> from the line of sight is called **Parallax** <term>Lambana: the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body as viewed from the Earth's surface versus its center</term>. When the Sun is less than the position of the Nonagesimal <term>Vipribha: the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point or Ascendant</term>, the Moon appears shifted behind the Sun. Since the Moon is faster in motion, and the faster body is behind, the conjunction is yet to occur. Therefore, the parallax must be **added** to the time of the New Moon. 

When the Sun is greater than the Nonagesimal, the Moon appears shifted ahead of the Sun. Since the faster body is already ahead, the conjunction has already passed by a time equal to the parallax; therefore, the parallax is **subtracted**. Thus, the end of the New Moon day, adjusted by parallax, becomes the true middle of the eclipse. This is logically established.

If, by the Sun's Sine of Zenith Distance <term>Drigjya: the sine of the angular distance from the zenith</term> equal to the Radius, we obtain 48 minutes and 46 seconds of parallax <note>This value represents the maximum possible parallax in the Hindu astronomical system</note> (which is one-fifteenth of the difference between the daily motions of the Sun and Moon), then what would it be for a given Sine of Zenith Distance? The result is the **Parallax in Altitude**. 

By this same proportion, the parallax minutes produced from the Sine of Ecliptic Zenith Distance <term>Drikkshepa: the sine of the zenith distance of the highest point of the ecliptic</term> are called the **Minutes of Latitudinal Parallax** <term>Avanati: the vertical component of parallax affecting the latitude</term>. These represent the "base" <term>Bhuja</term> of a right-angled triangle. The Parallax in Altitude acts as the "hypotenuse" <term>Karna</term>. The square root of the difference of their squares is the **True Longitudinal Parallax** <term>Sphuta-lambana</term>, which acts as the "upright" <term>Koti</term>. This is because in the calculation of zenith distance, the Sun's Sine of Zenith Distance is the hypotenuse and the Sine of Ecliptic Zenith Distance is the base. Therefore, the Latitudinal Parallax derived from the latter is the base, and the True Longitudinal Parallax is the upright. All of this has been explained in the section on the Sphere regarding the logic of parallax, as follows:

-> Since the observer, raised by the height of half the Earth's diameter, sees the Moon shifted downwards, both the **Longitudinal Parallax** and **Latitudinal Parallax** are calculated using the Earth's radius. <-

-> Having drawn the Earth and the orbits of the Moon and Sun to scale on a wall, one should draw a horizontal line and a vertical line through the center. <-

-> Where the horizontal line meets the orbit, one should imagine the horizon; where the vertical line meets it, the zenith. Having marked the Sun and Moon at their positions according to the degrees of their zenith distance, one should demonstrate the origin of parallax. One line should be drawn from the center of the Earth to the disk of the Sun... <-

# On the Calculation of the Planets
<page-num>424</page-num>

The line of sight from an observer situated on the Earth's surface is distinct from the line originating at the Earth's center. The difference between these two lines, measured upon the celestial orbit, is called the <term>parallax</term> <note>original: "lambana"; literally "hanging down" or "lagging," referring to the apparent displacement of a celestial body</note> in minutes of arc.

In the line originating from the Earth's center <note>the geocentric line</note>, the Moon and the Sun are always at the same longitude during a conjunction. However, because the Moon is displaced as seen from the surface-based line of sight, it is known as "parallax."

Because the geocentric line and the surface line of sight coincide at the zenith <note>the point directly overhead</note>, there is no parallax in the middle of the sky. Now, one should draw the previously mentioned diagram on a north-south wall.

Those two orbital circles should be understood as the circles of the <term>ecliptic zenith</term> <note>original: "drkshepa-mandala"; the vertical circle passing through the pole of the ecliptic</note>. The sine of the zenith distance of the <term>nonagesimal</term> <note>original: "tribhonalagna"; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</note> is the "ecliptic zenith sine" for both.

By marking two points at the degrees of the arc of that sine, they are designated as the "nonagesimal" points. Just as before, the "latitude parallax" <note>original: "nati"</note> is the downward displacement of the Moon's nonagesimal from the line of sight.

The distance between the two orbits at the nonagesimal point remains constant in all directions. That north-south difference is the "latitude parallax" here, and it is calculated from the ecliptic zenith sine.

Wherever the Moon is suspended below the Sun due to its zenith distance, that distance between the Moon and the Sun on the vertical circle is resolved into eastern-western and northern-southern components.

The eastern-western component is the longitudinal difference, and the north-south component creates a second difference. Here, the ecliptic is considered the "East" and the line perpendicular to it is "North-South."

The difference known as "parallax" is that which exists in the east-west direction. That which exists in the north-south direction is called "latitude parallax" <note>original: "nati"</note>.

The minutes of latitude parallax form the base of a triangle, and the minutes of total parallax form the hypotenuse. The square root of the difference of their squares is the perpendicular side, which represents the "corrected longitudinal parallax" in minutes.

The maximum parallax in minutes multiplied by 48 and divided by the radius (3438) equals the sine of the Sun's zenith distance.

-> 46 <-

These are the minutes of total parallax; similarly, the latitude parallax is derived from the ecliptic zenith sine.

One-fifteenth of the difference in daily motion (731) is 48 minutes and 46 seconds, which is the maximum parallax.

-> 46 <-

The motion in leagues <note>yojana</note> is 1185; the portion of the lunar day <note>tithi</note> is 780, which is the measure of the earth's semi-diameter.

The minutes of longitude parallax <note>lambana</note> converted into hours <note>nadis</note> are obtained by dividing by the difference in the speeds of the sun and moon. When the moon is ahead of the sun in the east, or behind it in the west, it is said to be "suspended" <note>parallaxed</note>.
Because the conjunction has already passed when the faster body is ahead, and is yet to come when it is behind, the parallax is added to the lunar day <note>tithi</note> for an eclipse in the east and subtracted for one in the west.
The latitude <note>shara</note> is the north-south distance between the moon and the sun. Similarly, the "latitude parallax" <note>nati</note> is calculated, and when the latitude is adjusted by that, the result is the "corrected latitude" <note>sphuta shara</note>.

# Vernacular Commentary

In this manner, the longitude parallax <term>Lambana: the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body as seen from the Earth's surface versus its center</term> established at the end of the lunar month <note>darshanta-kala</note> is applied to the hours of the conjunction. If the Sun's position is less than the "Nonagesimal" <term>Vitibhra-lagna: the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</term>, the parallax is added; if it is greater, it is subtracted. By performing this calculation repeatedly <note>asakrit</note>, the corrected midpoint of the eclipse is found.

# Mathematical Proof

At the moment of the conjunction's end, the Moon appears "suspended" (displaced by parallax) from the line connecting the Earth's surface to the Sun. When the Sun is less than the Nonagesimal, the displaced Moon remains behind the Sun—therefore, the parallax is added to the hours of the conjunction. Conversely, when the Sun is greater than the Nonagesimal, the Moon is ahead of the Sun by an amount equal to the parallax time; thus, by subtracting the parallax, the midpoint of the eclipse is determined.

However, during the time of parallax, the Sun also moves along the ecliptic. Therefore, at the parallax-adjusted conjunction time, the Moon will certainly still be displaced from the line connecting the Earth's surface to the Sun. Thus, the initial midpoint of the eclipse is only an approximation. Because the Sun and Moon are not stationary at the moment the lunar month ends, the time of conjunction is not immediately precise. For this reason, one must calculate the instantaneous parallax again from the adjusted time and apply the correction to the conjunction repeatedly <note>asakrit sanskara</note> to arrive at the precise midpoint. Here, the "Commentary on Spiritual Realization" <note>Vasana-bhashya</note> states...

->In the Calculation of the Planets<-

The verses written here regarding the proofs have been explained in detail in the *Chapter on the Sphere* <note>Golādhyāya: the section of the Siddhānta Śiromaṇi dealing with celestial cosmology and spherical trigonometry</note>. || 7 ||

Now, he describes the method for calculating parallax <term>lambana: the difference in the observed position of a celestial body due to the observer's position on Earth</term> in a single step.

> The sine of the altitude of the meridian ecliptic point <note>tribhonalagna: the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising sign</note> multiplied by thirteen and divided by thirty-two shall be called the "Maximum Value" <term>para: a specific constant used in this calculation</term>. 
> Having determined the sine of the base and the sine of the upright <note>dorjyā and koṭijyā: the horizontal and vertical components of an arc</note> from the difference between the rising sign and the Sun, 
> take the difference between the sine of the base and the "Maximum Value." || 8 ||
> Add the square of that difference to the square of the sine of the upright; 
> the square root of this sum is the hypotenuse <term>karṇa</term>. Multiply the sine of the upright by the "Maximum Value" and divide by that hypotenuse. 
> The arc of the resulting value, in minutes, provides the seconds of time for the parallax in a single calculation. || 9 ||

The sine of the altitude <note>śaṅku: literally 'gnomon', here referring to the sine of the vertical angle</note> of the meridian ecliptic point is multiplied by 13 and divided by 32; the result is designated as the *Para*. At the moment of the new moon <term>darśāntakāla</term>, one should calculate the sine of the base and the sine of the upright from the longitude of the Sun subtracted from the rising sign. Take the difference between that sine of the base and the previously calculated *Para*. The square root of the sum of the square of that difference and the square of the sine of the upright is the hypotenuse. From the product of the sine of the upright and the *Para*, divided by that hypotenuse, the resulting arc in minutes represents the respiration-measures <note>asavaḥ: units of time equivalent to 4 seconds</note> of parallax produced in a single step.

Here is the proof <term>upapatti</term>: If the maximum sine of parallax is obtained when the sine of the altitude of the meridian ecliptic point is equal to the radius, then what would it be for a given altitude? The calculation is as follows: If the divisor is the radius and the multiplier is the maximum sine of parallax, then what is the result for a multiplier of thirteen? The result is thirty-two. This is given the name *Para*. To simplify the operations for the Moon and Sun, which are situated one below the other, the field of parallax <note>lambanakṣetra: the geometric representation of parallax</note> is conceived differently. In that context, the maximum parallax is stated. Indeed, the maximum parallax is four ghatikas <note>approximately 96 minutes of time</note>.

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

<page-num>427</page-num>

->**Parallax**<-

Parallax <note>Sanskrit: *lambana*; the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body viewed along two different lines of sight</note> occurs when the sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal <note>The *vintribhalagna* is the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point; its sine of zenith distance is the *driggati*</note> is equal to the radius. 

The number of respirations <note>*asu*; a unit of time equal to 4 seconds</note> in those ghatikas <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> is exactly equal to the minutes of arc of twenty-four degrees. Therefore, the maximum parallax in respirations is equal to the minutes of the declination produced by the radius. 

When the gnomon-shadow of the nonagesimal is less than the radius, the parallax is equal to the minutes of the declination produced by that specific value. Thus, it should be understood that the sine of declination produced by the gnomon of the nonagesimal is the sine of the maximum parallax in respirations.

Now, on the north side of a wall extending east-west, draw a circle with a compass <term>karkatrena</term> <note>A pair of compasses or a divider tool</note> set to the measure of the radius. In the center of that, draw a horizontal line and a vertical line. That should be imagined as the orbit of the Moon. 

From the center of that, mark a point designated as "Earth" at a distance equal to the sine of the maximum parallax in respirations. At that point, draw another circle with the same compass setting. In the center of that one also, a horizontal line should be made. The vertical line should be extended from the one above. That is imagined as the orbit of the Sun. 

Both circles should be marked with the degrees of a circle and with sixty ghatikas. At the junction of the vertical line, mark the points designated as the "nonagesimal" in both circles. Then, at a distance from the nonagesimal in the Sun's orbit equal to the degrees of the interval between the Sun and the nonagesimal, mark a point designated as the "Sun." 

Similarly, in the Moon's orbit, mark the "Moon" point at the same degrees from the Moon's nonagesimal. Then, extend a string from the Earth-point passing over the Moon-point. The number of ghatikas between where that string touches the Sun's orbit and the Sun-point itself are to be known as the ghatikas of parallax at that time. 

In such a diagram, the proof of the calculation of this parallax is produced in the same manner as the "fast-correction" <note>*shighraphala*; the correction for the planet's orbital position relative to the Sun</note> of a planet. In this context, the Sun's orbit is the "eccentric circle," the Moon's orbit is the "deferent circle," the sine of the maximum parallax is the "sine of the maximum correction," and the nonagesimal plus six signs is the "apex of fast motion" <term>shighrochcha</term>.

By assuming the remainder, the process should be carried out. This method of calculation is somewhat approximate <note>original: "sthulam" - meaning a simplified or gross calculation rather than a precise infinitesimal one</note>.

## Vernacular Commentary

Multiply the gnomon <term>Shanku: the vertical shadow-caster used here as the sine of the altitude</term> of the meridian ecliptic point <term>Tribhonalagna: the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</term> by thirteen, divide by thirty-two, and designate the result as the "Par" <note>a specific mathematical variable used in this local algorithm</note>. Then, at the moment of the new moon conjunction <term>Darshanta: the end of the lunar month</term>, calculate the ascendant. Determine the sine of the difference between that and the Sun (the sine of the longitude difference) and the cosine <term>Kotijya</term>. Find the difference between the sine <term>Dorjya</term> and the previously calculated "Par." Add the square of this result to the square of the cosine; the square root of this sum is the hypotenuse <term>Karna</term>. By dividing the product of the cosine and the "Par" by this hypotenuse, the result in arc-minutes—the parallax in time <term>Lambanasu: parallax expressed in units of time/respiration</term>—is established by this single-step method.

## Mathematical Proof

The geometric configuration of the parallax here is similar to the previously described positions. It is merely a variation in the calculation through mathematical transformation <term>Sanchara</term>.

### Proportion—

->Radius : Equinoctial Shadow :: Sine of the Altitude of the Meridian Ecliptic Point : [X]<-

->Parallax relative to the Gnomon = (Equinoctial Shadow × Sine of the Altitude of the Meridian Ecliptic Point) / Radius<-

### Mathematical Transformation—

->Equinoctial Shadow : Radius :: 13 : 32<-
->Therefore, the Sine of the Latitude (Palajya) = 13 and Radius = 32.<-
->Therefore, Par = (13 × Sine of the Altitude of the Meridian Ecliptic Point) / 32.<-

The maximum parallax = 4. Its equivalent in time units <note>Asu: a unit of time equal to 4 seconds or the time taken for one breath</note> = 4 × 60 × 60 = 14400.
The maximum declination = 24 × 60 = 1440. These two are considered proportional. The first half is easy to understand and has been explained previously. Whether that solar <term>Drikkshepa</term> is North or South is now stated for clarity. There, when the northern declination of the <term>Vitribhalagna</term> <note>The nonagesimal point; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</note> is greater than the degrees of local latitude, it is known as North. Otherwise, it is South. Then, the arc of that <term>Drikkshepa</term> must be calculated. Treating the nonagesimal as the Moon's position, the <term>Vikshepa</term> <note>Celestial latitude</note> should be calculated using the sine of the distance from the node at that moment. The arc of the <term>Drikkshepa</term> should be adjusted by that nonagesimal latitude. This means addition if they are in the same direction, and subtraction if they are in different directions. The direction of the Moon's <term>Drikkshepa</term> depends on this adjustment. Its sine is the <term>Drikkshepa</term> of the Moon—this connects to the following section.

Here is the rationale: The nonagesimal <note>the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note> lies on the ecliptic. Due to its rotation, it is sometimes to the east and sometimes to the west of the meridian <note>the north-south line</note>. If the rising sign <term>Udayalagna: the point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon</term> is in the northern hemisphere, then the nonagesimal is to the east. Otherwise, it is to the west. The arc of the ecliptic's zenith distance <note>the distance from the zenith to the nonagesimal</note> is measured on the vertical circle passing through the zenith and the nonagesimal. Where this circle meets the ecliptic, that distance from the zenith represents the degrees of the Sun's ecliptic zenith distance. Where it meets the secondary circle <term>Vimandala: the orbit of the moon or a planet inclined to the ecliptic</term>, that distance represents the degrees of the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance. The sines of those arcs are their respective "Drigkshepa" <term>Drigkshepa: the sine of the zenith distance of the highest point of the ecliptic</term>. As the illustrious Brahmagupta <note>a famous 7th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> said:

> When the vertical circle of the nonagesimal is joined with the ecliptic for the Sun, and with the secondary circle for the Moon.

When the orbital circle is at the zenith, it takes the form of a vertical circle; therefore, a planet situated anywhere there, even if subjected to parallax, does not leave the orbital circle. Thus, in this case, there is an absence of latitude parallax <term>Avanati: the difference in celestial latitude caused by parallax</term>. When the nonagesimal is tilted to the south from the zenith, the ecliptic becomes slanted. A Sun situated there, pulled down by the force of the vertical circle, appears at a certain distance south of the ecliptic; that distance is its latitude parallax <term>Nati: specifically the parallax in latitude</term>. Similarly, if the nonagesimal is tilted to the north from the zenith, the latitude parallax is northern. The same applies to the Moon's latitude parallax. However, the Moon's orbital circle should be considered as the secondary circle <insert>the inclined orbit</insert>, because the Moon moves along that secondary circle. Therefore, the arc of the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance is the amount by which the secondary circle is tilted from the zenith. Its sine is the Moon's "Drigkshepa." Thus, because of this sine, when the secondary circle is in a slanted position, the distance between the secondary circle and the Moon—which has been pulled down by the force of the vertical circle—is...

## This lunar parallax in latitude arises from the Drigkshepa (ecliptic zenith distance).

->The Radiance (Commentary)<-

When the declination of the <term>Vitribha-lagna</term> <note>The point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point; the nonagesimal</note> is northerly and greater than the local latitude, the <term>Drigkshepa</term> <note>The sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal</note> is North. This is calculated using the celestial latitude of the nonagesimal.

->Vernacular Exposition<-

The <term>Drig-jya</term> <note>Sine of the zenith distance</note> of the gnomon at the <term>Vitribha-lagna</term> is the <term>Drigkshepa</term> of the Sun. If the northern declination of the <term>Vitribha-lagna</term> is greater than the latitude, the <term>Drigkshepa</term> is North; otherwise, it is South. By taking the arc of this <term>Drigkshepa</term> and treating the <term>Vitribha-lagna</term> as the Moon's position, one should calculate the <term>Shara</term> <note>Celestial latitude</note>. By applying the correction of that latitude to the aforementioned <term>Drigkshepa</term>, the Moon's <term>Drigkshepa</term> is obtained.

->Mathematical Rationale<-

The <term>Dring-mandala</term> <note>Vertical circle</note> passing from the zenith through the <term>Vitribha-lagna</term> marks the Sun's <term>Drigkshepa</term> at the point where it meets the ecliptic. Where it meets the <term>Vi-mandala</term> <note>The Moon's orbit or secondary circle</note>, that arc from the zenith constitutes the Moon's <term>Drigkshepa</term> degrees. In the <term>Dring-mandala</term> shaped ecliptic, there is an absence of <term>Nati</term> <note>Parallax in latitude</note> <note>original: "नति" (Nati)</note>; however, when there is a tilt North or South from the zenith, parallax occurs in that direction. Similarly, when the <term>Vi-mandala</term> is tilted, the Moon's parallax in latitude occurs in that direction.

From the point where the <term>Drigkshepa-mandala</term> <note>The vertical circle of the nonagesimal</note> meets the <term>Kranti-vritta</term> <note>Ecliptic</note>, the arc of the Moon's latitude at the nonagesimal lies along that same vertical circle. If both the parallax and the latitude are North, the Moon's <term>Drigkshepa</term> is found by their sum; otherwise, by their difference.

Therefore: Moon's Drigkshepa = Solar Drigkshepa ± Moon's Latitude at the nonagesimal.

The <term>Drigkshepa-mandala</term> is perpendicular to the <term>Kranti-vritta</term> (ecliptic), but not to the <term>Vi-mandala</term> (Moon's orbit). Therefore, the <term>Nati</term> derived from the Moon's <term>Drigkshepa</term> is not the "true" or "clear" <term>Nati</term> because it does not lie on the <term>Kadamba-prota-vritta</term> <note>The circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic</note>. For this reason, the <term>Acharya</term> <note>The lead teacher/author, likely Bhaskara II</note> has refuted the opinion of <term>Brahmagupta</term> at the end of this chapter, specifically regarding the verse beginning with "For the sake of the Moon's Drigkshepa..." etc.

Now, he describes the method for determining the parallax in latitude <term>Nati: the latitudinal shift caused by the observer's position on Earth</term> from the sine of the zenith distance of the ecliptic <term>Drigkshepa: the sine of the arc between the zenith and the highest point of the ecliptic</term>.

->The moon's *Drigkshepa* multiplied by its own mean daily motion<-
->and divided by fifteen, then divided by the radius, gives the result. || 11 ||<-
->The *Nati* of the Sun and Moon, if in the same or different directions,<-
->their difference or sum, respectively, is the true *Nati* here.<-

Those two *Drigkshepas* of the Moon and the Sun, multiplied by one-fifteenth of their respective mean daily motions and divided by the radius <note>original: "Trijya"</note>, result in their respective latitudinal parallaxes. The difference between these two parallaxes if they are in the same direction, or their sum if they are in opposite directions, becomes the true parallax in latitude <note>Nati</note> during a solar eclipse.

The mathematical proof <note>original: "Upapatti"</note> here is by the rule of three: If a *Drigkshepa* equal to the radius yields a maximum parallax equal to one-fifteenth of the daily motion, then what will the desired *Drigkshepa* yield? The result is the minutes of parallax. Now, the reason for the addition or subtraction of these two parallaxes is explained: If the Sun is in the same direction in which the Moon is deflected, then the distance between the Moon and Sun is known by the difference of the parallaxes. When the parallaxes are in different directions, the distance between the Moon and Sun is produced by their sum.

## Vernacular Commentary

Multiplying the *Drigkshepas* of the Sun and Moon by one-fifteenth of the difference in their motions <insert>or their respective motions</insert> and dividing by the radius gives the parallax <note>Nati</note> of the Sun and Moon. In a solar eclipse, the true parallax is found by taking the difference if they are in the same direction, and the sum if they are in different directions.

## Mathematical Proof

It has been stated previously that in the ecliptic <note>original: "Kranti-vritta"</note> which takes the form of the visible vertical circle, there is an absence of parallax when there is an absence of *Drigkshepa*. At the horizon, the maximum parallax in minutes is equal to one-fifteenth of the difference in motion. When the *Drigkshepa* is equal to the radius, the Sun's motion...
