# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

The line from the Earth's surface remains perpendicular in the north-south direction, equal to the maximum minutes of the Moon's parallax. From this, the desired parallax <note>nati: the latitudinal component of parallax</note> is determined by proportion.

Therefore: Parallax = $\frac{\left( \frac{\text{Daily Motion Difference}}{15} \right) \times \text{Ecliptic Zenith Distance}}{\text{Radius}}$ . In this same manner, by calculating the Moon's parallax from the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance <note>drkshepa: the sine of the arc between the zenith and the highest point of the ecliptic</note> and applying the correction to both, the north-south difference between the Sun and Moon is known. || 11 ||

Now, he describes the calculation of the corrected parallax:

->The Moon's ecliptic zenith distance multiplied by two and divided<-
->by 141 <note>original: kindra</note> results in the corrected parallax. || 12 ||<-
->Or, if derived from the small sines, multiplied by two and divided by five,<-
->increased by its own sixtieth part, is the corrected parallax.<-

The Moon's ecliptic zenith distance multiplied by two and divided by 141 <note>represented by the word-numeral 'Earth-Arrows'</note> results in the corrected parallax. If the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance is derived from the "small sines" <note>a simplified trigonometric table</note>, then it should be multiplied by two and divided by five; the result, when increased by its own sixtieth part, becomes the corrected parallax.

Here is the rationale <note>upapatti: mathematical proof or demonstration</note>: Because the difference is very small, the Sun's ecliptic zenith distance is assumed to be equal to the Moon's, and the proportion is made using one-fifteenth of the difference in their daily motions. If, for an ecliptic zenith distance equal to the Radius, the corrected parallax is equal to one-fifteenth of the daily motion difference, then what will it be for this desired distance? Here, one-fifteenth of the daily motion difference is the multiplier and the Radius is the divisor. The multiplier and divisor are both reduced by half of the multiplier. The result is 2 in the place of the multiplier and 141 in the place of the divisor. This is for the "Great Sines." For the "Small Sines," the multiplier is 2 and the divisor is slightly less than five (4:55); for ease of calculation, it is treated as 5. Therefore, that result is increased by its own sixtieth part <note>to compensate for the rounding of the divisor from 4:55 to 5</note>.

# Vernacular Commentary

By multiplying the Moon's <term>Drigkshepa</term> <note>the sine of the zenith distance of the ecliptic point</note> by two and dividing by 141, the result is the "Clear Parallax in Latitude" (<term>Sphuta-nati</term>). If the <term>Drigkshepa</term> was calculated using the "Small Sine" method <note>a simplified trigonometric system where the radius is 120 instead of 3438</note>, then multiply by two and divide by five, then add one-sixtieth of that result to the quotient; the result is the Clear Parallax in Latitude.

# On the Calculation of the Planets
<page-num>436</page-num>

Having performed the previous steps, the <term>latitude</term><note>Sanskrit: vikṣepa; the angular distance of the Moon north or south of the ecliptic</note> must be calculated. Then, from the <term>nonagesimal</term><note>Sanskrit: vitribhalagna; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</note> at the time of the fixed parallax, the <term>parallax in latitude</term><note>Sanskrit: avanati or nati; the downward shift of the Moon relative to the Sun due to the observer's position on Earth's surface</note> is to be determined. The latitude is then adjusted by that parallax. It should be understood that this becomes the "clear" or <term>corrected latitude</term><note>Sanskrit: sphuṭa-vikṣepa</note> at the middle of the eclipse. Subsequently, the durations of the half-totality and half-duration of the eclipse are to be calculated using the squares of the sum and difference of the semi-diameters, and so forth.

The underlying logic <note>Sanskrit: upapatti</note> is as follows: At the Moon's position, the interval between the ecliptic and the Moon's orbit is the latitude. The Moon is in its own orbit and the Sun is in the ecliptic; therefore, their latitude is their north-south distance. However, this is only if the observer is at the center of the Earth. When the observer is situated on the Earth's surface, elevated by the Earth's semi-radius, the Moon's orbital plane appears depressed below the Sun's orbital plane due to the power of the <term>zenith parallax</term><note>Sanskrit: dṛkkṣepa</note>. The amount by which it is lowered in the north-south direction is the parallax in latitude. Since the celestial latitude starts from the end of that parallax, the corrected distance between the Sun and Moon is found by adjusting the latitude with that parallax. This is the corrected latitude. As stated in the section on the Celestial Sphere <note>Sanskrit: Gola</note>:

> The latitude is the north-south distance between the Moon and the Sun.
> The parallax in latitude is likewise; therefore, when adjusted by that, the latitude becomes corrected.

The explanation for the half-duration and half-totality is the same as previously stated.

---

-> Vernacular Commentary <-

By applying the correction of the parallax in latitude to the latitude derived through the previous method, the corrected latitude for a solar eclipse is obtained. Then, using the rule "from the squares of the sum and difference of the semi-diameters," one should calculate the segments for the duration and totality.

Due to the line of sight from the Earth's surface, the Moon's orbit appears suspended below the Sun's orbit. The extent to which it is suspended in the north-south direction is the parallax in latitude. Since the latitude extends beyond the parallax, the corrected latitude—representing the true distance between the Sun and Moon—is found by adding them if they are in the same direction or subtracting them if they are in different directions.

The time of the first contact <note>original: "sparśakāla"; the moment the eclipse begins</note>. This process is to be repeated. The difference between the time of first contact and the time of the middle of the eclipse is to be known as the "half-duration of contact" <note>original: "spārśika sthityardha"</note>. Having again calculated the parallax in longitude <term>lambana: the difference in the apparent positions of the sun and moon due to the observer's location on Earth</term> from the time of contact, it should be set aside. From the moon's latitude, corrected by that parallax in latitude, the half-duration is calculated again. Thus, the corrected time of first contact is found. This "repeatedly" <note>iterative calculation</note> continues until the difference disappears.

In the same way, the time of separation <note>original: "mokṣakāla"; the end of the eclipse</note> is found by adding the half-duration to the calculated time. In that case, when adjusting the moon's node to the current time, the result is additive. Thus, the difference between the time of separation and the middle of the eclipse is the "half-duration of separation." Similarly, the time of total immersion <note>original: "saṃmīlana"</note> is found by subtracting the half-duration of total eclipse <note>original: "mardadala"</note> from the calculated time. The time of the beginning of emergence <note>original: "unmīlana"</note> is found by adding the half-duration of total eclipse. The difference between the immersion and the middle of the eclipse is the first corrected half-duration of totality; the difference between the emergence and the middle is the second. This is the method if parallax is applied repeatedly. Alternatively, if parallax is applied only once, the times of contact and separation are corrected in a single step. However, there is a distinction: at the time of contact or separation, the nonagesimal must be recalculated to find the parallax in latitude. The moon's latitude at that moment, when corrected by that parallax, becomes the corrected latitude for contact or separation. If this is not done, the result is merely an approximation.

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

The time of separation <note>The end of the eclipse</note>. Furthermore, because the observer is situated at a certain height <note>literally "elevation," referring to the observer's position on the surface of the sphere</note>, parallax is produced. Therefore, the end of the conjunction <note>the moment of the new moon</note> corrected by that parallax becomes the true time of the middle of the eclipse. In the same way, the time of first contact also deserves to be corrected by the parallax generated at that specific moment to become true. The same logic applied to the parallax correction for the middle of the eclipse applies to the times of first contact, separation, total immersion, and emergence. 

However, when the parallax correction for the time of contact is performed, the celestial latitude <term>Shara: the angular distance of the moon north or south of the ecliptic</term> becomes slightly different due to the change in time. The latitudinal parallax <term>Nati: the difference in apparent latitude due to the observer's position</term> is also slightly different. Consequently, the half-duration <term>Sthityardha: half the total time from first contact to the end of the eclipse</term> resulting from those corrections is also slightly different. Therefore, it is appropriate to add or subtract that parallax to the calculated end of the conjunction. Thus it is said: "The half-duration, increased or decreased by the corrections, arises from the latitudinal parallax of that time," and so on. 

If the parallax is calculated by the iterative method <note>repeated calculation to reach a precise value</note>, then the parallax and latitudinal parallax are calculated again and again. By that, the celestial latitude of that moment is made true for the sake of the half-duration. Then the half-duration becomes true, and the celestial latitude of that moment also becomes true. That itself should be understood as the celestial latitude at the moment of contact. However, when parallax is calculated by the single-step method, because the latitude and latitudinal parallax are not recalculated repeatedly, it is proper to calculate the latitude at contact again. Hence it is said: "But here, the latitude and latitudinal parallax are calculated again from the moon's position and the 'three-sign' point <note>the Vitribha, or the point 90 degrees behind the meridian</note> of that specific time."

One must perform the calculation. In this manner, perform the <term>Asakrit-karma</term> <note>Iterative calculation or successive approximation</note>. The meaning is that first, by means of the <term>Spashta-shara</term> <note>True celestial latitude of the moon</note> at the mean time, one should calculate the <term>Sthityardha</term> <note>Half-duration of the eclipse</note>. Subtracting that from the <term>Sphuta Tithyanta</term> <note>True end of the lunar day/moment of conjunction</note>, one must calculate the <term>Lambana</term> <note>Parallax in longitude</note> and <term>Nati</term> <note>Parallax in latitude</note>. Then, calculate the latitude from the moon's position relative to its node at that specific moment, and derive the <term>Spashta-shara</term> <note>True latitude</note> by applying the correction for <term>Nati</term>. From that, derive the <term>Sthityardha</term> as is done in lunar eclipses, subtract it from the mathematically calculated end of the lunar day, and again establish the <term>Lambana</term>, <term>Nati</term>, and <term>Sphuta Sthityardha</term> <note>True half-duration</note>. In this way—by calculating the <term>Lambana</term> through <term>Asakrit-karma</term>—the <term>Sphuta Sparshakala</term> <note>True time of first contact</note> is determined by applying the resulting positive or negative correction to the calculated <term>Darshanta</term> <note>End of the New Moon period</note> diminished by the <term>Sthityardha</term>. Similarly, the <term>Mokshakala</term> <note>Time of separation/end of eclipse</note> is found by adding the <term>Sthityardha</term> to the end of the lunar day.

In this manner, the difference between the <term>Sphuta Sparshakala</term> (True Contact Time) or <term>Mokshakala</term> (Separation Time) and the <term>Madhyagrahakala</term> <note>Middle of the eclipse</note>—that is, the <term>Spashta-darshantakala</term> <note>True moment of conjunction</note>—becomes the <term>Sparshika</term> <note>Contact-related</note> and <term>Maukhika</term> <note>Separation-related</note> <term>Spashta Sthitikhanda</term> <note>True duration segments</note>. Likewise, by calculating the <term>Sphuta Sammilana</term> <note>True total obscuration</note> and <term>Unmilana</term> <note>True emergence from totality</note> times through <term>Asakrit-karma</term>, the difference between those and the <term>Madhyakala</term> (Middle Time) is established as the <term>Spashta Mardakhanda</term> <note>True duration of totality</note>.

This method applies when the <term>Lambana</term> (Parallax) has been established through the <term>Asakrit</term> (Iterative) method. If the <term>Lambana</term> was calculated using the <term>Sakrit-vidhi</term> <note>Single-step or non-iterative method</note>, then the <term>Sparshakala</term> and <term>Mokshakala</term> are also established as <term>Sakrit</term> (Single-step results). The specific detail here is that at the time of contact or separation, one must calculate the <term>Nati</term> from the <term>Vitribha Lagna</term> <note>The 90th degree point or Nonagesimal</note>, apply the correction to the <term>Shara</term> (Latitude) of that moment, and thus make the <term>Sparshika</term> or <term>Maukhika Shara</term> "True" (<term>Sphuta</term>).

By applying corrections to the calculated time of the New Moon <note>The moment of conjunction in longitude</note>, the approximate middle of the eclipse is determined. Following this, one must calculate the "Nonagesimal" <note>The point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note> using the Sun's position at that specific moment. Then, calculate the parallax <term>Lambana: the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body as seen from the Earth's center versus its surface</term> and apply it to the calculated New Moon time. Through this process of successive approximation <note>iteration</note>, the true middle of the eclipse for observers on the Earth's surface is established. In other words, the true middle of the eclipse for those on the surface corresponds to the specific time when the Sun's position, the Nonagesimal, and the resulting parallax are all synchronized to yield the true moment of conjunction.

In this manner, at the chosen time, the positions of the Sun, Moon, and the Node <note>The point where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> are calculated. From the Node and the Moon, the latitude <term>Shara: the celestial latitude of the Moon</term> is derived, and from the Sun, the Nonagesimal is derived. Using the "visual projections" <note>Drigkshepa</note> of the Sun and Moon and the formula "multiplied by the difference of their daily motions and divided by the degrees of a lunar day," one calculates the parallax in latitude <term>Nati</term>. By combining the latitude and the parallax in latitude, the true latitude is found. From this true latitude, using the formula "from the squares of the difference of the sum of the radii," the duration of the eclipse <term>Sthitikhanda</term> is produced. Subtract this from the middle of the eclipse and apply the parallax correction corresponding to that earlier time to find the true moment of first contact <note>Sparshakala</note>. The difference between this and the true middle of the eclipse is the true half-duration of the beginning phase. Similarly, the moments of total immersion and the half-duration of totality are determined.

-> When calculating the time from the magnitude of the eclipse <note>Grasa</note>, the resulting value is multiplied by the true duration and divided by the duration produced by the true latitude. By repeating this process, the result, when subtracted from the half-duration, becomes the desired time. (19) <-

In this context, regarding a solar eclipse <note>original: "ravi-grahana"</note>, the calculation of the disk's deflection <term>valana: the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator</term>, the base <term>bhuja: the horizontal side of a right triangle</term>, the perpendicular <term>koti</term>, and so forth, should be understood as previously described for lunar eclipses. This means it is divided by the interval between the time of contact and the middle of the eclipse. The resulting quotient is the corrected base.

Now, regarding the calculation of the time for a specific magnitude of eclipse: the square root of the difference between the square of the sum of the radii minus the eclipsed portion and the square of the latitude—that result which is divided by the difference in daily motions—must be corrected. That result is multiplied by the corrected half-duration (the interval between contact and middle) and divided by the half-duration generated by the corrected latitude of that moment; this yields the corrected value. When this is subtracted from its own half-duration, it gives the desired time. This time is measured forward from the start of contact and backward from the end of the eclipse. At that specific time, having again calculated the latitude adjusted by parallax <term>nati: the latitudinal component of solar parallax</term>, one should calculate the result using the formula "the square of the sum of the radii minus the eclipsed portion..." and so on. This result must again be corrected. This iterative process <note>original: "asakrit-karma"</note> should be repeated until the desired time becomes stable and accurate.

The rationale <note>original: "upapatti"</note> for this is as follows: The method for bringing out the base is the same as stated before. Its correction is now explained. Just as in a lunar eclipse, the half-duration is derived from the difference of the squares of the latitude and the sum of the radii; the same is brought forth here. However, that is uncorrected. When the parallax adjustment <term>lambana: the longitudinal component of solar parallax</term> is applied, the interval between the contact and the middle of the eclipse becomes the corrected half-duration. This means it is adjusted by the difference in parallax. Indeed, the base is derived in relation to the half-duration. Just as in a lunar eclipse where the half-duration is mean, the base that arrives there in relation to it must be of the same nature here as well, because the underlying theory <note>original: "vasana"</note> is identical. # Chapter on Solar Eclipses | 443

When the mathematician calculates the desired half-duration <note>Sanskrit: sthityardha; the time from the start or end of the eclipse to its maximum point</note>, the resulting "arm" <note>Sanskrit: bhuja; the horizontal side of the eclipse projection triangle</note> is related to that specific half-duration. However, this is inaccurate. Therefore, a proportion <note>Sanskrit: anupāta; the rule of three</note> is applied to align it with the half-duration produced by the corrected latitude <note>Sanskrit: śara; the celestial latitude of the Moon</note> at that specific moment.

The logic follows: If the corrected half-duration yields this much of an "arm," then what will the half-duration produced by the instantaneous corrected latitude yield? The result is the "corrected arm." This same process is reversed when calculating the time elapsed since the start of the eclipse <note>Sanskrit: grāsa-kāla</note>. Because the result obtained from the rule "From the square of half the sum of the diameters minus the eclipsed portion..." is only a mean or approximate desired half-duration. As long as this is subtracted from the corrected half-duration, the "desired time" remains inaccurate. Therefore, a proportion is used to transform that result into the corrected half-duration: If the mean half-duration yields this much, what does the corrected half-duration yield? The result obtained here is the corrected value; when this is subtracted from the corrected half-duration, the true "desired time" remains.

->Vernacular Commentary<-

In this chapter, the calculation of the remaining disk, the "arm" <term>bhuja: the base of the right-angled triangle formed during an eclipse</term>, the "perpendicular" <term>koṭi: the vertical side of the triangle</term>, etc., should be performed as in the section on lunar eclipses. The only distinction is as follows: The "arm" established by the previous method should be multiplied by the half-duration produced by the instantaneous corrected latitude and divided by the corrected half-duration itself; the result is the "corrected arm."

According to the rule "From the square of half the sum of the diameters minus the eclipsed portion...", the desired time derived from the eclipse magnitude should be multiplied by the corrected half-duration and divided by the half-duration produced by the instantaneous corrected latitude to make it "corrected." By subtracting this from its own half-duration, the remainder is the desired time before the start <note>contact</note> or after the end <note>separation</note> of the eclipse. From this, one should calculate the instantaneous corrected latitude and then, using the rule "From the square of half the sum of the diameters..." etc., establish the true desired time through iterative calculation <note>Sanskrit: asakṛt-karma; a process of repeated approximation until the value stabilizes</note>.

### Proof

The proof for calculating the "arm" <note>term: Bhujasadhana; the calculation of the side of a right-angled triangle used in eclipse geometry</note> has been stated previously; now the method for clarifying it is described. According to the rules of lunar eclipses, the "mean half-duration" <note>term: Madhyama-sthityardha; the theoretical half-duration of an eclipse without accounting for parallax</note> becomes the "corrected half-duration" through the processing of parallax <note>term: Lambana; the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body viewed from different points</note>. Now, regarding the rule: "The difference in motion multiplied by the desired half-duration is the arm"—to make the arm calculated here applicable to the desired time, the following proportion is used: If this calculated arm is obtained within the corrected half-duration, then what would it be within the corrected half-duration produced by the specific latitude at the desired time? Thus, the corrected arm is found. Furthermore, regarding the rule: "From the square of half the sum of the diameters minus the eclipsed portion"—the mean half-duration which is calculated as less than the desired time is converted into the corrected half-duration by proportion. If this calculated result is obtained in the mean half-duration, then what is it in the corrected half-duration? By subtracting the resulting value from the corrected half-duration, the corrected desired time remains. || 18-19 ||

Now, a specific distinction is mentioned and explained through the gateway of the previous statement:

-> The correction of the Moon’s ecliptic zenith distance <note>term: Shashi-drikkshepa; the arc between the zenith and the highest point of the ecliptic for the Moon</note> by the latitude of the nonagesimal <note>term: Vitribha-lagna; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</note> is the opinion of Brahmagupta <note>note: original: "Jishnuja-matam"; referring to Brahmagupta, son of Jishnu</note>. I shall state why that opinion is not correct here through logic. || 1 || <-

-> Where the latitude is twenty-four degrees, and the Sun and Moon are at the beginning of Libra at sunrise, and the ascending node is at six signs <note>180 degrees</note>, then the ecliptic would coincide with the prime vertical <note>the east-west circle passing through the zenith</note>. || 2 || <-

-> The Moon, though deflected from the Sun by parallax, does not leave the ecliptic even when possessed of celestial latitude. Due to the correction of the nonagesimal's latitude, a parallax in latitude <note>term: Nati</note> arises here, but it is useless. || 3 || <-

Here, it was stated that the arc of the Sun’s ecliptic zenith distance, when corrected by the latitude arising from the nonagesimal, becomes the arc of the Moon’s ecliptic zenith distance; this is the opinion of Brahmagupta, but it is not a sound opinion. The intent is that it only *appears* to be logical. To show how it is illogical, he says: "I shall state the logic here." In a solar eclipse, the north-south difference between the Sun and the Moon is the celestial latitude <note>term: Vikshepa</note>. Latitude is defined as—

# Chapter on Solar Eclipses

The distance between the orbit <term>kakṣā-maṇḍala; the mean orbit of a planet</term> and the eccentric or inclined orbit <term>vimaṇḍala; the actual path of the moon inclined to the ecliptic</term> is the north-south difference. Now, when the Moon is suspended downward along the path of the vertical circle <term>dṛṅ-maṇḍala; the circle passing through the zenith and the planet</term>, the distance between that Moon and the Sun's orbit is the north-south interval between the Moon and the Sun; this is what is meant by the "corrected latitude" <term>sphuṭa-vikṣepa</term>. The difference between this and the previously calculated latitude is the "parallax in latitude" <term>nati; the latitudinal shift caused by the observer's position on Earth</term>. This is indeed the nature of parallax in latitude in a solar eclipse.

Now, the underlying logic is explained. Suppose a place where the latitude <unclear>of the observer</unclear> is twenty-four degrees. When the Sun is at the beginning of the sign Libra <note>6 signs or 180 degrees</note>, and the Moon is at the same position, and the ascending node <term>pāta; the point where the moon crosses the ecliptic</term> is also there, the Moon's latitude is zero. At that place, at the time of sunrise, the Sun itself is the rising point <term>lagna; the ascendant</term>. The point ninety degrees behind the ascendant <term>vitribha-lagna; the nonagesimal or the highest point of the ecliptic</term> is three signs away.

Sun: 6s 0° | Moon: 6s 0° | Node: 6s 0° | Ascendant: 6s 0°
The Nonagesimal: 3s 0° <note>The beginning of Cancer</note>.

Its northern declination is twenty-four degrees; when this is adjusted by the local latitude, the zenith distance becomes zero. Therefore, the nonagesimal is at the zenith, and the Sun is at the East point. At this moment, the prime vertical is the same as the ecliptic. That itself is the vertical circle. The Moon, suspended downward by the motion of the vertical circle, does not leave its orbital circle. Therefore, here the corrected latitude is also zero. Thus, there is an absence of parallax in latitude <gloss>nati</gloss> here. However, if one applies the correction for the latitude of the nonagesimal, a parallax of four minutes is produced here, which is useless <note>The author is pointing out a potential error in standard calculations where a value appears despite the geometry dictating it should be zero</note>.

The method by which Brahmagupta <note>A famous 7th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> calculated the parallax in latitude by assuming the inclined orbit itself to be the orbital circle is also logical. However, that result arrives at the limit of the inclined orbit, not the limit of the ecliptic orbit. Therefore, one must take the difference between the Moon's latitude as moved by the time of longitudinal parallax <term>lambana</term> and the initial latitude; that difference must be applied inversely to the parallax in latitude. If the latitude of the nonagesimal is added to the arc of the Sun's zenith distance, then this difference must be subtracted from the parallax. When it is subtracted, then the difference must be added. By doing this, the result...

The parallax in latitude <note>Nati: the difference in celestial latitude caused by the observer's position on Earth</note> ought to be distinct. Alternatively, the parallax in latitude is calculated by adjusting the arc of the Sun's ecliptic zenith distance <note>Drikkshepa: the sine of the zenith distance of the highest point of the ecliptic</note> by the Moon's latitude; this also results in a value close to the distinct parallax. However, during an eclipse, the Moon's latitude is very small. Even when the correction is applied, the difference in the parallax is minimal. Therefore, it is my opinion that the ancient teachers ignored this procedure because the difference was so slight. Or rather, why oppose the world? What was done by them is also appropriate.

If the difference between the Moon's latitude at the time of parallax in longitude <note>Lambana: the difference in time/longitude caused by the observer's position</note> and the original latitude is applied inversely to this parallax in latitude, it becomes distinct; or, it can be adjusted by the Moon's latitude. || 4 ||
The parallax in latitude should be calculated from the Sun's ecliptic zenith distance, as the difference is small. Because the Moon's latitude is small during an eclipse, the difference in parallax is likewise small. || 5 ||
For this reason, this procedure was not performed by predecessors such as Brahmagupta and others. This is my own intuition that I have expressed; why oppose the world? || 6 ||

# Vernacular Commentary

The correction of the "latitude of the nonagesimal" <note>Vitribhashara: the latitude of the point 90 degrees behind the rising point</note> mentioned for the sake of calculating the Moon's ecliptic zenith distance is the opinion of Brahmagupta, not mine. The reasoning here is as follows: In a place where the latitude is 24°, if we imagine the Sun and Moon rising at the beginning of Libra, the ascending node will also be at 6 signs <note>180 degrees</note> and the ecliptic will coincide with the prime vertical. At that time, the Moon, though shifted by parallax from the Sun, will not leave the ecliptic due to its own latitude; therefore, the parallax in latitude produced there by the correction of the nonagesimal's latitude is useless. || 1–3 ||

The distinct parallax in latitude is found by applying the difference between the Moon's latitude moved by the hours of parallax in longitude and the previously established latitude inversely to the parallax in latitude. That is to say—

<header>Chapter on Solar Eclipses</header>

If the <term>latitude of the nonagesimal</term> <note>Vitribha-shara: The celestial latitude of the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note> is positive, it should be made negative; if negative, it should be made positive. Alternatively, the <term>parallax in latitude</term> <note>Nati: The apparent shift in a planet's latitude due to the observer's position on Earth</note> becomes nearly distinct when the <term>Sun's ecliptic zenith distance</term> <note>Drikkshepa: The sine of the zenith distance of the highest point of the ecliptic</note> is adjusted by the Moon's latitude. Because the Moon's latitude is very small during an eclipse, the resulting parallax is nearly identical even after the correction. For this reason, ancient authoritative texts such as the *Surya Siddhanta* have omitted this adjustment. || 4-6 ||

### Rationale

Here the teacher has demonstrated the error in the opinion of <term>Brahmagupta</term> <note>A 7th-century mathematician and astronomer whose work was foundational but occasionally critiqued by later scholars like Bhaskara</note> using an example. The latitude (*shara*) is the north-south distance between the celestial equator and the Moon's inclined orbit. The "distinct latitude" in the vertical circle is the north-south distance between the Sun and the Moon when affected by parallax. The difference between this and the previous latitude is the parallax in latitude (*nati*). 

At twenty-four degrees of terrestrial latitude, on the day of maximum declination, there is no zenith distance; the nonagesimal is at the zenith and the Sun is at the eastern horizon point. In this situation, because the ecliptic and the vertical circle coincide, the Moon—even when displaced by parallax—does not leave the celestial equator. Since the distinct latitude is zero, the parallax in latitude should also be zero. However, according to Brahmagupta’s method, a parallax is produced by the correction of the latitude of the nonagesimal; this is incorrect.

Later, in the section beginning with "The difference in latitude during the time of parallax..." <note>original: "lambanakalasharantaramasyam..."</note>, a reconciliation is shown for Brahmagupta's parallax method, showing it to be a close approximation. This is clear. || 1-6 ||

## Now, the Chapter on the Shadow of the Planets is explained. To begin, the author states the mean celestial latitudes of the planets.

> The celestial latitudes, in minutes, for Mars and the other planets are:
> One hundred and ten (110), one hundred and fifty-two (152), and seventy-six (76).
> One hundred and thirty-six (136), and one hundred and thirty (130). For Venus and Mercury,
> the <term>nodes</term> <note>Pata: The points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> become "corrected" when added to their <term>rapid anomalies</term>. <note>Shighra-kendra: The angular distance of a planet from its apogee in its secondary epicycle, used to account for its motion relative to the Sun.</note> || 1 ||

The mean celestial latitude <note>Vikshepa-lipta: The angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</note> of Mars <note>original: *Kshitija*, "Earth-born"</note> is 110 minutes.
For Mercury <note>original: *Budha*</note>, it is 152; for Jupiter <note>original: *Guru*</note>, it is 76.
For Venus <note>original: *Shukra*</note>, it is equal to 136. For Saturn <note>original: *Shani*</note>, it should be known as 130.
Furthermore, the nodes of Mercury and Venus, which are derived through calculation, must be added to their respective rapid anomalies. In this way, they become "corrected" <note>Sphuta: True or adjusted for the observer's reality</note>.

### Rationale

In the explanation of Mean Motion, the rationale for planetary latitude was already demonstrated on the <term>observational circle</term> <note>Vedha-valaya: An instrument or conceptual circle used for sighting astronomical positions</note> through the method of observation. However, when the rapid anomaly is equal to the arc of the maximum sine of correction for a planet, the <term>rapid hypotenuse</term> <note>Shighra-karna: The calculated distance from the center of the Earth to the planet</note> becomes equal to the radius <note>Trijya: The radius of the standard sine-table circle</note>. On that day, whatever maximum latitude is observed on the observational circle is considered the planet's maximum mean latitude. These observed values for Mars and the others have been recorded here.

Now, the "corrected" state of the nodes for Mercury and Venus is discussed. In the <term>Chapter on Revolutions</term> <note>Bhagana-adhyaya: The section of the text detailing the number of orbits each body completes in a Great Age</note>, the node revolutions recorded for Mercury and Venus become "real" only when increased by their own rapid anomaly revolutions. The values previously recorded were smaller for the sake of simplifying the calculations. Therefore, the positions derived from the recorded cycles, when added to the rapid anomaly, result in the "true" nodes based on the real number of revolutions.

As it is said in the *Gola* <note>The *Goladhyaya*, the second half of Bhaskara's treatise focusing on spherical astronomy and cosmography</note>: "The node revolutions recorded here for Mercury and Venus [must be combined] with the rapid anomaly revolutions," and so on.

## Commentary

->The mean <term>latitudinal constants</term> <note>Shar-kala: Literally 'arrow-minutes,' referring to the maximum celestial latitude of a planet used as a constant in calculations</note> for Mars and the other planets, established by observation, are as follows:<-
->Mars: 110' | Mercury: 152' | Jupiter: 76' | Venus: 136' | Saturn: 130'<-

The true <term>node</term> <note>Pata: The point where the planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> of Mercury and Venus is determined by adding their <term>rapid anomaly</term> <note>Shighra-kendra: The angular distance between the planet and its point of greatest distance in its secondary epicycle</note> to the calculated position of their node.

## Rationale

The mean latitudinal constants recorded here are based on the <term>rapid distance</term> <note>Shighra-karna: The hypotenuse or distance from the Earth to the planet in the second epicycle model</note> being equal to the radius of the circle. A detailed explanation of the revolutions of the nodes for Mercury and Venus has been provided in the <term>Chapter on the Spheres</term> <note>original: "Goladhyaya"</note>. || 1 ||

Now, the author explains the method for calculating the actual planetary latitude:

->**From the planet's slow-corrected position, combined with its own node,**<-
->**The sine of the arm, multiplied by the stated latitude constant,**<-
->**And divided by its own rapid distance, yields the latitude;**<-
->**Its direction follows the sphere of the node-added slow-corrected planet. || 2 ||**<-

One should calculate the sine of the arm <note>Bhujajya: The sine of the angular distance from the nearest equinoctial point</note> from the planet’s <term>slow-corrected</term> <note>Manda-sphuta: The position of the planet after accounting for the first equation of center</note> position added to its node. That value should be multiplied by the planet’s prescribed latitude constant and then divided by its <term>rapid distance</term>. The result is the true celestial latitude. If the planet, combined with its node, is within the first six signs <note>0 to 180 degrees</note>, the latitude is North; otherwise, it is South.

### Rationale for this Method:

The slow-corrected planet moves within its own <term>secondary eccentric circle</term> <note>Shighra-pratimandala: A model used to represent the planet's motion relative to the Sun</note>. The <term>node</term> <note>Pata</note> is also located there. The node is defined as the point of intersection between the eccentric circle and the inclined orbit <note>Vimandala</note>. It is from this point that the latitude begins to increase.

Here, using a very straight bamboo stick, one should construct the <term>ecliptic circle</term> <note>Kakshamandala</note> and its corresponding eccentric circle according to the rules of projection. On that secondary eccentric circle, mark the position of the node in reverse order from the start of Aries, and then place the <term>inclined orbit</term> <note>Vimandala</note> there. Create another intersection of the inclined orbit and the eccentric circle at a distance of six signs from the node mark. Three signs east of the node—

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of planetary latitude for the five star-planets. Having provided the base constants on the previous page, the author now demonstrates how to physically model these orbits and mathematically derive the "true latitude" using the relationship between the inclined orbit and the Earth-centered distance.</meta>

<page-num>450</page-num>
<header>On Planetary Calculations—</header>

Using the measure of the recorded <term>latitude</term> <note>original: "vikshepa"</note>, one should fix the <term>inclined orbit</term> <note>Vimandala: The planet's actual path, which is tilted relative to the ecliptic</note> to the north of the <term>eccentric circle</term> <note>Pratimandala: A mathematical circle used to model the planet’s speed</note> by means of some support. Then, by placing the <term>slow-corrected</term> <note>Mandasphuta: The planet's position after accounting for its elliptical orbital speed but before correcting for Earth's perspective</note> position of the planet direct from the start of Aries on both the eccentric circle and the inclined orbit, one should demonstrate the rationale of the latitude. 

In that model, the separation between those two planet-marks is the latitude at that specific point. Now, for its calculation: at the position of the <term>node</term> <note>Pata: The point where the orbits intersect</note>, there is an absence of latitude. At a distance of three signs (90 degrees) from there, the latitude is at its maximum. For distances in between, it is found by proportion. Therefore, the distance between the node and the planet-mark must first be known. That distance is found by adding them together; this is because the planet is measured direct (forward) from Aries, while the node is measured retrograde (backward). Their sum is considered the <term>argument for the latitude</term> <note>original: "sharartham kendram"</note>. 

The <term>sine of the arm</term> <note>Dorjya: The vertical distance from the planet to the horizontal axis</note> for this argument must be calculated. If, for a sine equal to the <term>radius</term> <note>Trijya</note>, the separation between the eccentric and inclined circles is equal to the recorded maximum latitude, then what will the separation be for the sine at the planet’s current position? The result of this calculation is the latitude at the tip of the <term>rapid hypotenuse</term> <note>Shighra-karna: The actual distance from the Earth to the planet</note>. 

Then follows the second proportion: If this is the latitude at the distance of the rapid hypotenuse, what would it be at the distance of the standard radius? Here, since the multiplier and divisor are both equal to the radius, they cancel each other out. Thus, the sine of the argument multiplied by the recorded latitude and divided by the rapid hypotenuse yields the result. This result is the <term>latitude</term> <note>original: "vikshepa"</note> in the region of the orbit in the form of a sine; its arc is the <term>true latitude</term> <note>original: "sphuta-vikshepa"</note>. 

By binding one end of a string to the Earth-mark and the other end to the planet's position on the inclined orbit, that string represents the hypotenuse. The distance between this string and the ecliptic circle is the true <term>latitude</term> <note>original: "shara"</note>. All of this should be demonstrated to the student.

->Commentary in the Common Tongue<-

To the <term>slow-corrected planet</term>, add its <term>node</term> <note>Pata</note> and calculate the <term>sine of the arm</term> <note>Bhujajya</note>. Multiply that by the planet's recorded <term>latitude constant</term> <note>Shara</note> and divide by its <term>rapid hypotenuse</term> <note>Shighrakarna</note>; the result will be the <term>true latitude</term> <note>Sphutashara</note>. If the slow-corrected planet plus its node is less than 6 signs (180°), the latitude is North; if it is more, the latitude is South.

## Rationale

The <term>slow-corrected</term> <note>Mandasphuta: the planet's position corrected for its orbital eccentricity</note> planet travels within its own <term>fast-eccentric circle</term> <note>Shighra-prativritta: a mathematical circle used to model the planet's second anomaly</note>, and its <term>node</term> <note>Pata: the point where the planet's tilted orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> is located there as well. The term "node" refers to the intersection of the eccentric circle and the <term>inclined orbit</term> <note>Vimandala: the actual tilted path of the planet</note>. At this intersection, the <term>latitude</term> <note>Shar: literally 'arrow', representing the vertical distance from the ecliptic</note> is zero, and at a distance of three signs (90 degrees) from the node, it reaches its maximum. Because the node moves in a retrograde direction, adding the positions of the planet and the node results in their difference, which is the <term>sine of the arm of the argument of latitude</term> <note>original: "vkshepa-kendra-dorjya"</note>.

For the desired latitude, the proportion is as follows—

Mars and others is proven. We have written about this in detail in the <term>Section on the Celestial Sphere</term> <note>Goladhyaya</note> within the proof for the verse beginning "Divided by the fast-hypotenuse..." ॥ 2 ॥

Now, he states another clarification regarding the characteristics of latitude that make it suitable for correction with <term>declination</term> <note>Kranti: the angular distance of a planet north or south of the celestial equator</note>.

> Subtract the square of the <term>sine of ecliptic deflection</term> <note>ayana-valana-jya</note> from the square of the <term>radius</term>; the square root of the remainder is the "staff" <note>yasti</note>. The planet's latitude multiplied by this "staff" and divided by the radius results in the true latitude.
> Alternatively, the <term>cosine</term> <note>dyujyaka</note> of the planet's position (increased by three signs) cubed, divided by the cube of the radius, certainly becomes the true latitude suitable for declination correction. ॥ 3 ॥

The <term>deflection</term> <note>valana</note> should be calculated using the <term>cosine</term> <note>kotishinjini</note> derived from the planet's position including the <term>precession of the equinoxes</term> <note>ayanansha</note>, and so on. Here, the word "deflection" refers specifically to the "sine of deflection," not the arc itself. Furthermore, from this point forward, calculations should be performed using the <term>great sines</term> <note>brihaj-jya: the standard sines based on a large radius</note>.

<page-num>४५२</page-num>
<header>In the Computation of Planets—</header>

Since, when using <term>large sines</term> <note>original: "brihaj-jya"; these are the standard trigonometric sines for large circles</note>, the <term>sine of latitude</term> <note>original: "shara-jya"</note> is nearly equal to the arc-minutes of the latitude itself.

The calculation for this is as follows: subtract the square of the <term>deflection</term> <note>original: "valana"; the angular difference between the ecliptic and the celestial equator</note> from the square of the <term>radius</term> <note>original: "trijya"; the standard radius of 3438 arc-minutes</note>; the square root of the result is known as the <term>stick</term> <note>original: "yashti"; a technical term for a specific cosine value used as a multiplier</note>. When the <term>planetary latitude</term> <note>original: "graha-vkshepa"</note> is multiplied by this "stick" and divided by the radius, the result is the <term>true latitude</term> <note>original: "sphuta-vkshepa"</note> suitable for the <term>declination-adjustment</term> <note>original: "kranti-samskara"</note>.

Now, an <term>alternative method</term> <note>original: "anukalpa"</note> is stated: Or, the latitude may be multiplied by the <term>day-radius</term> <note>original: "dyujya"; the radius of the planet's diurnal circle</note> of the planet when increased by three signs (90 degrees). Multiply by whatever that day-radius is for the planet plus three signs and divide by the radius; this becomes the true value. Here, because the divisor is the same and the multiplier is only slightly smaller, the result has a very small difference; for this reason, it is stated as an alternative.

### The Rationale

Here is the explanation: Latitude effectively begins from the end-point of the declination. The planet is located at the tip of that latitude. Therefore, the declination becomes "true" when corrected by the latitude. In this context, it is appropriate that the declination is made "true" using a latitude derived through mathematical calculation. This is because <term>declination</term> <note>original: "kranti"</note> is measured transversely from the <term>celestial equator</term> <note>original: "vishuvann-mandala"</note> toward the <term>celestial pole</term> <note>original: "dhruva"</note>.

However, <term>latitude</term> <note>original: "vkshepa"</note> is transverse from the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>original: "kranti-mandala"</note> toward the <term>ecliptic pole</term> <note>original: "kadamba"</note>. As it is stated in the section on the <term>Sphere</term> <note>original: "Gola"</note>:

> Since all declination lines meet at the celestial pole;
> From the east of the celestial equator, they go south and north to the pole.
> All latitude lines meet at a point 24 degrees <note>original: "jina-lava"; 'jina' is a numerical code for 24</note> away from the celestial pole.
> This meeting point is known as the **Ecliptic Pole**, and it helps in understanding deflection.
> There, relative to the east of the ecliptic, the directions are always south and north;
> This is also known as the circle of the ecliptic pole's rotation.

Therefore, latitude is directed toward the ecliptic pole. How can the addition or subtraction of this latitude be appropriate when combined with declination, which is directed toward the celestial pole, since they are oriented toward different points? The reason for their different directions is the <term>solstitial deflection</term> <note>original: "ayana-valana"</note>.

Now, this is demonstrated upon the globe. Having constructed the globe as described—

One should place another <term>radius-circle</term> <note>original: "trijya-vritta"; a circle with a radius of 3438 units</note> at a distance of ninety degrees all around from the point where the planet is marked on the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>original: "kranti-vritte"</note>. Now, where the cord passing through the celestial pole and the planet's mark meets that circle, the distance between that point and the <term>ecliptic pole</term> <note>original: "kadamba"</note> is the <term>solstitial deflection</term> <note>original: "ayana-valanam"</note>; therefore, its sine is the "base." The sine of the distance between the planet’s mark and the ecliptic pole is the radius, which serves as the "hypotenuse." The square root of the difference of their squares is the "perpendicular." This is known as the <term>stick</term> <note>original: "yashti"; a specific cosine value used to project the latitude onto the declination circle</note>.

From the end of the declination, the <term>latitude</term> <note>original: "vikshepa"</note> directed toward the ecliptic pole acts as a hypotenuse. A proportion is used to transform this into the form of a perpendicular: If, when the radius is the hypotenuse, the "stick" is the perpendicular, then what would it be when the <term>latitude</term> <note>original: "shara"</note> is the hypotenuse? The result is the latitude suitable for the <term>declination-adjustment</term> <note>original: "kranti-samskara"</note>. The declination, once adjusted by this, is called the **true declination**. The north-south distance between the planet (situated at the tip of its latitude) and the <term>celestial equator</term> <note>original: "vishuvan-mandala"</note> is called the **true declination**. 

Now, there is also a rationale for an <term>alternative method</term> <note>original: "anukalpa"</note>. Here, the sine of the declination of the planet plus three signs (90 degrees) is imagined in the place of the "base." The <term>day-radius</term> <note>original: "dyujya"; the radius of the diurnal circle</note> of that point is imagined in the place of the "stick," serving as the perpendicular. There too, the radius is the hypotenuse, and thus the logic is entirely consistent.

### The Radiance.

The "arrow of the celestial wanderer" is the planet's latitude. It is multiplied by the day-radius of the planet when increased by three signs.

### Vernacular Commentary.

By subtracting the square of the sine of the solstitial deflection from the square of the radius, the square root becomes the **stick**. By multiplying the planet's latitude by the **stick** and dividing by the radius, the result is the **corrected latitude** suitable for declination adjustment. Alternatively, by multiplying the planet's latitude by the <term>minimum day-radius</term> <note>original: "paramalpa-dyujya"</note> and dividing by the radius, the corrected latitude is obtained.

The geometric situation in the diagram below is as follows: from the planet's position to the <term>ecliptic pole</term> <note>original: "kadamba"</note> along the ecliptic-pole line, the <term>radius</term> <note>original: "trijya"</note> is the hypotenuse, and in the local radius-circle, the sine of the <term>solstitial deflection</term> <note>original: "ayana-valanajya"</note> is the "base" <note>the horizontal side of a right triangle</note>. # Section on Planetary Shadows

The calculation for the **true latitude** is as follows:
Let *p* = <term>true latitude</term> <note>original: "spashta-shara"</note>, *y* = <term>stick</term> <note>original: "yashti"; the cosine of the solstitial deflection</note>, *a* = <term>solstitial deflection sine</term> <note>original: "ayana-valanjya"</note>, and *m* = <term>mean latitude</term> <note>original: "madhyama-shara"</note>.

->Radius : Stick :: Mean Latitude : (Mean Latitude × Stick) / Radius = True Latitude<-

The <term>declination sine</term> <note>original: "krantijya"</note> of a planet increased by three signs <note>90 degrees</note> is, with a small margin of error, equal to the solstitial deflection sine. Taking that as the "base" and its <term>diurnal cosine</term> <note>original: "dyujya"</note> as the "stick":

->Radius : Diurnal Cosine of (Planet + 3 Signs) :: Mean Latitude : (Diurnal Cosine × Mean Latitude) / Radius = True Latitude<-

In this manner, both methods are derived.

2. According to the Teacher's <note>likely referring to Bhaskara II or the primary authority of this specific school of astronomy</note> view, the first method is precise and the second is approximate. However, in reality, both methods are somewhat approximate. For true precision, the geometric proof is as follows:

In the diagram mentioned above, the "stick" is the perpendicular, the solstitial deflection sine is the base, and the radius is the hypotenuse; this forms one <term>right-angled triangle</term> <note>original: "jatya"</note>. A second triangle is formed where the sine of the true latitude is the perpendicular, the sine of the <term>time-difference of the solstitial visibility correction</term> <note>original: "ayana-drikkarma-kalajya"</note> is the base, and the sine of the latitude is the hypotenuse. These two triangles are <term>similar</term> <note>original: "sajatiya"</note>. The proportion is:

->Diurnal Radius : Polar Diurnal Radius :: Latitude Sine : (Latitude × Polar Diurnal Radius) / Diurnal Radius = True Latitude Sine<-

The cosine of this is the <term>cosine of the true latitude</term> <note>original: "spashako"</note>. By combining these with the declination sine and diurnal cosine of both, we get: (Latitude × Polar Diurnal Radius) / Radius; and (True Latitude Cosine × Declination) / Radius. The sum or difference of these results is the **True Declination Sine** approved by the Teacher. This proportion for the sine of the true latitude is the precise one. *

---

* <margin>Brahmagupta <note>an influential 7th-century Indian mathematician/astronomer</note> assumed the latitude measured on the ecliptic-pole circle to be the same as that on the polar-pole circle because planetary latitudes are generally small. He used this simplified value to calculate the true declination. The Teacher has corrected this specific discrepancy. However, even this does not perfectly align with the spherical geometry of the arc of the diurnal circle at the planet's position. This is why this geometric proof has been written.</margin>

# In Planetary Calculations—

3. In the "Chapter on Helical Rising and Setting" (*Udayastadhikara*) of his work *Tattvaviveka*, **Kamalakara** cites the example: 
> "Having abandoned the junction of the celestial spheres and solstices..." <note>original: *tyaktva golayanadim va*, Verse 36</note> 
Through this and other examples, he demonstrates a deviation or inconsistency in the **true declination** <term>spashta-kranti</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet north or south of the celestial equator</note> calculated by the Teacher <note>referring to Bhaskara II</note>. He argues that, if we exclude the equinoxes and solstices, when the **Ecliptic Pole star** <term>Kadamba tara</term> <note>Likely referring to the pole of the ecliptic rather than a specific star, though "tara" means star</note> is at 90° **latitude** <term>shara</term> in a specific direction on the celestial sphere, its **declination sine** <term>krantijya</term> should be equal to the **minimum diurnal cosine** <term>paramalpa-dyujya</term>. However, this is not proved by the Teacher's standard calculation method.

In the *Tattvaviveka*, two distinct types of declination are defined and calculated: the **polar-circle declination** <note>original: *dhruva-vrattiya kranti*</note>, which is designated as "primary," and the **ecliptic-pole-circle declination** <note>original: *kadamba-vrattiya*</note>, designated as "secondary." By applying a correction based on the **celestial latitude** <term>shara</term> <note>literally "arrow"; the angular distance of a planet from the ecliptic</note> to this secondary value, one arrives at the **true secondary declination**, and subsequently, the **true declination sine**. Because this method is so remarkable and ingenious, it is recorded here.

As shown in the diagram below:

->Secondary Declination = *Gra-Shra*, Latitude = *Pra-Vim*<-
->*Gra-Shra* ± *Pra-Vim* = True Secondary Declination<-

<note>original: Grahacchāyādhikāraḥ</note>

**Avi** <note>An abbreviation for a specific geometric segment, likely the 'refined hypotenuse'</note> = Hypotenuse; **Viṁśrā** <note>Abbreviation for *vimaṇḍala-spaṣṭa-krānti*</note> = **True Declination** <term>spashta-kranti</term> = First side; **Agrā** <note>The amplitude at the horizon</note> = Second side.

In this manner, **Aviśrā** <note>A composite variable</note> = The first **spherical right-angled triangle** <term>chapa-jatya</term>.

**Agra** = Other Declination = Hypotenuse; **Agrā** = Primary Declination = First side; **Agrāṁ** <note>The refined amplitude</note> = Second side. Thus, **Agrāṁ-grāṁ** is the second spherical right-angled triangle.

From the ratio of the second field <note>geometric figure</note>:
**Other Agra** : **Radius** <term>tri</term> <note>The total sine of 90 degrees, often 3438' in this system</note> :: **Refined Agra** : **Sine of the Planet plus three signs** <term>satribha-graha-yujya</term> <note>original: *satri-bhagraha-yujya*; literally the 'day-radius' of the planet shifted by 90 degrees</note>.

From the ratio of the first field:
**Radius** : **Avi-hypotenuse** :: **Sine of the Planet plus three signs** : **Viṁśrā** = **True Declination**.

   Avi-hypotenuse X Radius X Refined Agra   Avi-hypotenuse X Refined Agra
   -------------------------------------- = -----------------------------
       Radius X Other Agra                       Other Agra

That is—
$\frac{\text{Sine of the True Secondary Declination} \times \text{Sine of the Primary Declination}}{\text{Sine of the Secondary Declination}}$ = Sine of the True Declination.

In this same spherical triangle—
**Radius** : **Avi-hypotenuse** :: **Sine of the Planet plus three signs** : **Viṁśrā**

Therefore: **Sine of True Declination** = $\frac{\text{Sine of the True Secondary Declination} \times \text{Sine of the Planet plus three signs}}{\text{Radius}}$

In this way, everything is proven. ॥ 3 ॥

Now, the **Polar Visibility Correction** <term>Ayana Drkkarma</term> <note>The calculation to adjust a planet's position from the ecliptic to the celestial equator for visibility purposes</note> is explained:

> The **polar deflection** <term>Ayana Valana</term> multiplied by the **unrefined latitude** <term>asphuteshu</term>,
> divided by the **day-radius** <term>dyuguna</term>, and then multiplied by 
> **eighteen hundred** <note>original: *purna-purna-dhrtibhir*; using the *Bhuta-sankhya* system: purna (0), purna (0), dhrti (18) = 1800</note>,
> gives the minutes of arc for the planetary visibility correction based on the equatorial rising. ॥ 4 ॥

> Or, the product of the **unrefined latitude and the deflection**,
> divided by the **stick** <term>yashti</term> <note>A technical divisor used in spherical trigonometry for coordinate conversion</note>, results in the minutes of arc for the **polar correction**.
> These are added to or subtracted from the planet's longitude respectively,
> depending on whether the **polar correction** and **latitude** are in the **same or different directions**. ॥ 5 ॥

# On the Calculation of the Planets

<note>original: Grahagaṇite</note>

Multiply the planet's **polar deflection** <term>ayana-valana; the angle between the circle of declination and the circle of celestial latitude</term> by its **unrefined latitude** <term>asphuṭa-śara</term> and divide by the **radius of the planet’s diurnal circle** <term>dyujyā</term>. Multiply this result by **1800** and divide by the **equatorial rising times** <term>nirakṣodayāsu; the time taken for a zodiac sign to rise at the equator</term> of the zodiac sign in which the planet is currently situated. The resulting figures are the **minutes of the polar correction** <term>āyana-kalā</term>.

Alternatively, one may multiply the minutes of the polar deflection by the unrefined latitude and divide by **60**. The resulting minutes of polar correction will be nearly the same; this is considered a simplified alternative method.

**The Direction of Correction:**
If the **hemisphere** <term>ayana</term> in which the planet is moving and the direction of the **planet's latitude** <note>North or South</note> are the same, then these minutes of polar correction must be **subtracted** from the planet’s position. If their directions are different, they must be **added**. Thus, the planet's position becomes corrected for **polar visibility** <term>āyana-drkkarma</term>.

## The Geometric Rationale

The proof for this is explained in great detail in the section on the **Sphere** <note>original: Gola; likely referring to the Golādhyāya of the Siddhānta Śiromaṇi</note>. However, a brief explanation will be provided here as well.

The specific point on the **ecliptic** <term>krāntivṛtta</term> representing the planet does not necessarily touch the **horizon** <term>kṣitija</term> at the same time as the actual planet. This is because the planet is situated at the "tip of its latitude" <note>it is elevated above or below the ecliptic plane</note>. The tip of this latitude is always directed toward the **ecliptic pole** <term>kadamba</term>.

When the **North Ecliptic Pole** is above the horizon, the planet is lifted above the horizon by the latitude directed toward that pole. The distance between the horizon and the ecliptic pole is what we call the **North Polar Deflection** <term>uttara-āyana-valana</term>. Conversely, when the ecliptic pole is below the horizon, the planet is "pushed down" by its latitude; the distance between the horizon and the pole is then the **South Polar Deflection**.

Therefore, the lifting and lowering of the planet occur according to the **deflection** <term>valana</term>. A "lifted" planet has already risen <note>it becomes visible earlier than its ecliptic coordinate</note>. A "lowered" planet will rise later. The calculation of exactly how much time this involves is determined by the **Rule of Three** <term>trairāśika</term>:

1.  If, for a hypotenuse equal to the **total sine radius** <term>trijyā; usually 3438'</term>, the difference between the ecliptic pole and the horizon is expressed as the **deflection minutes**, then what is the value for a hypotenuse equal to the **unrefined latitude**?
2.  The result consists of minutes in the form of a perpendicular drop below the planet.
3.  At the planet’s position, these minutes act as **sines** <term>jīvā</term> on the **diurnal circle** <term>dyujyā-vṛtta</term>. To convert these into the standard circle of the radius, a final proportion is used: If there is this much sine in the diurnal circle, how much would there be in the circle of the radius? The resulting minutes—

# Chapter on the Shadows of the Planets

...these are indeed the **time-units** <term>asu; a unit of time equal to four seconds or one minute of arc of the equator's rotation</term>. Because the arc of the result is very small, it is not calculated separately. To transform these into the **ecliptic** <term>krāntivritta</term>, the final proportion is applied: If by the **equatorial rising times** <term>nirakṣodyāsu; the time taken for a zodiac sign to rise at the equator</term> one obtains 1800 arc-minutes <note>the total minutes in one zodiac sign</note>, then what is obtained by these time-units? The result is the arc-minutes converted to the ecliptic.

When the **deflection** <term>valana</term> is northern and the **latitude** <term>vikṣepa</term> is also northern, the planet—raised by that latitude—is brought to the horizon; at that moment, the point where the ecliptic meets the horizon is behind the planet's position on the ecliptic. That specific point is the planet as corrected by the **visibility operation** <term>dṛkkarma</term>.

To put it simply: having properly placed the **secondary circle** <term>vimaṇḍala; the orbit of the planet</term> relative to the ecliptic on a globe, and having marked the planet’s position there, a mark should be made. Now, where a circular cord drawn from the **celestial pole** <term>dhruva</term> through the planet meets the ecliptic, that is the position of the planet corrected by the visibility operation.

In this way, a triangle is formed by the latitude and the cord drawn from the pole. That cord meets the ecliptic at a distance equal to the **minutes of polar correction** <term>āyana-kalā</term> either ahead of or behind the planet’s ecliptic position. In this context:
*   The **polar correction arc-minutes** are the **base** <term>bhuja</term>.
*   The **unrefined latitude** <term>asphuṭa-vikṣepa</term> is the **upright** <term>koṭi</term>.
*   The segment of the cord between the tip of the latitude and the ecliptic is the **hypotenuse** <term>karṇa</term>.

This triangle is derived from the **deflection triangle** <term>valana-tryasra</term>. Therefore, the polar correction arc-minutes are brought out by the Rule of Three: If for the upright called the **yasti** <term>yaṣṭi; a specific trigonometric sine value used as a divisor</term> one obtains the base of deflection arc-minutes, then what is obtained for the upright of unrefined latitude? The result is the polar correction arc-minutes. Thus, the entire logic is proven.

### Commentary

Multiply the planet's **polar deflection** <term>āyana-valana</term> by its **mean latitude** <term>madhyama-śara</term> and divide by its **diurnal radius** <term>dyujyā</term>. Multiply that result by 1800 and divide by the equatorial rising times of the zodiac sign the planet occupies. The result is the polar correction arc-minutes. 

Alternatively: multiply the polar deflection arc-minutes by the mean latitude and divide by the *yasti*; the result, with only a slight difference, is the polar correction arc-minutes. The planet's hemisphere and...

<header>On the Calculation of the Planets—</header>

When the **celestial latitude** <term>śara; the angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</term> is in the same direction [as the deflection], the **polar arc-minutes** <term>āyanakalā</term> are subtracted from the planet's position. When they are in different directions, the minutes are added. This results in the planet being corrected by the **polar visibility operation** <term>āyana-dṛkkarma</term>.

# Proof

1—The diagram previously described should be kept in mind here.

The "lowering" <note>original: nāmana</note> and "raising" <note>original: unnāmana</note> of a planet due to its latitude is described in great detail in the *Golādhyāya* <note>The "Chapter on the Sphere," a standard section in Indian astronomical texts like the Siddhānta Śiromaṇi</note>.

The Proportions:—

-> Sine of Deflection × Sine of Latitude <-
-> ------------------------------------------------------------------- ; Local result <-
-> Radius <-

This occurs within the **diurnal circle** <term>dyujyāvṛtta; the daily path of a celestial body</term>.

-> Sine of Deflection × Sine of Latitude <-
-> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ = Correction in minutes <-
-> Day-Radius <-

For the value of the polar arc-minutes, the proportion is:—
<note>Where "Rising" = local rising time of the sign in time-units (asu); "30" = the degrees in a sign, here expressed as 1800 minutes.</note>

-> 1800 × Sine of Deflection × Sine of Latitude <-
-> ∴ Polar arc-minutes = ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- <-
-> Day-Radius × Local Rising Time <-

The point where a circular cord drawn from the **celestial pole** <term>dhruva</term> through the planet meets the **ecliptic** <term>krāntivṛtta</term> is the position of the planet corrected by the polar visibility operation. At that location, a triangle is formed: the **polar arc-minutes** <term>āyanakalā</term> represent the base <note>bhujā</note>, the **uncorrected latitude** <term>asphuṭa-śara</term> represents the side <note>koṭi</note>, and the hypotenuse <note>karṇa</note> lies between the tip of the latitude and the ecliptic.

From this, the proportion is made:

-> Deflection Minutes × Sine of Latitude <-
-> --------------------------------------------------------------------------- = Polar arc-minutes. <-
-> Radius <-

In this manner, the entire calculation is proven!

# 2— In reality, the **polar visibility correction** <term>āyana-dṛkkarma; the adjustment for a planet's position relative to the celestial pole</term> becomes precise through the **planetary diurnal radius** <term>vimbīya-dyujyā; the radius of the circle representing the planet's daily path</term>. It is as follows—

->In the diagram provided below:—<-

->In the planetary **ecliptic-pole line** <term>kadamba-sūtra</term>, Planet-Latitude = **latitude** <term>śara</term> = **vertical leg** <term>koṭi</term>.<-
->In the **planetary diurnal-pole line** <term>vimbīya-dhruvasūtra</term>, Planet-Point A = **hypotenuse** <term>karṇa</term>.<-
->In the **ecliptic** <term>krāntimaṇḍala</term>, Planet-Point A = **base** <term>bhuja</term>.<-

Thus, the arc Planet-A-Latitude forms a **spherical right-angled triangle** <term>cāpa-jātya</term>. Here, the mark 'A' <note>The Sanskrit character 'अ' is used as a point marker in the diagram</note> represents the planet as corrected for polar visibility. 
Angle Planet-A-Latitude = 90°; Angle Point A-Planet-Latitude = arc of the **polar planetary rod** <term>āyana-graha-yaṣṭi-cāpa</term>.

Therefore:—

->**Radius** <term>trijyā</term> : **Rod** <term>yaṣṭi</term> :: **Sine of Hypotenuse** : **Sine of Latitude**.<-

->Planet-Y = **Rod** = **vertical leg**; K-Y = **sine of polar deflection** <term>āyana-valanajyā</term> = **base**.<-
->Planet-K = **Radius** = **hypotenuse**.<-

Thus, Planet-Y-K is the first spherical right-angled triangle.

->Diagram,<-

<note>The diagram illustrates the celestial sphere with the ecliptic and the planet's path. It shows how the planet's latitude creates a small triangle against the coordinate grid of the sky, allowing astronomers to calculate exactly where the planet "appears" to be compared to its calculated position on the ecliptic.</note>

**Sine of celestial latitude** <term>śarajyā</term> = **Vertical leg** <term>koṭi</term> = Sine of the planet’s distance from the ecliptic.
**Sine of the hypotenuse** <term>karṇajyā</term> = **Hypotenuse** <term>karṇa</term> = Sine of the planet’s distance from the pole.
The square root of the difference of their squares = **Base** <term>bhuja</term>. This constitutes the **second spherical right-angled triangle** <term>dvitīya-cāpa-jātya</term>.

The proportion is as follows:
**Planetary polar rod** <term>ayana-graha-yaṣṭi</term> : **Sine of polar deflection** <term>āyana-valanajyā</term> :: **Sine of latitude** <term>śarajyā</term> : **Sine of the base of the second triangle**.

In this context, the base of the second triangle is expressed as a sine representing the distance between the planet and the intersection of the ecliptic-pole line <term>kadamba-sūtra</term> within the circle of the planet’s diurnal path. To normalize this to the standard **radius** <term>trijyā</term>, we use this proportion:

**Cosine of the planet's latitude** <term>śara-koṭijyā</term> : **Calculated base** : : **Radius** <term>trijyā</term> : **Sine of the planetary polar correction** <term>gra-a-jyā; shortened form of graha-ayana-dṛkkarma-jyā</term>.

The resulting arc in the ecliptic is established as the base of the spherical right-angled triangle in the form of minutes of the **polar visibility correction** <term>āyana-dṛkkarma-kalā</term>. In this manner, the entire proof is made clear. || 4-5 ||

---

### Now, the visibility correction due to terrestrial latitude is explained.

> When the **ascensional differences** <term>carārdha; half the difference between a 12-hour day and the actual day-length</term> derived from the **true declination** and **mean declination** <term>sphuṭa-asphuṭa-krānti</term> are in the same direction, their difference is taken; when in opposite directions, their sum is taken. The resulting breath-length time units <term>asu; a unit of time equal to four seconds</term> are known as the **terrestrial latitude correction** <term>palodbhava; literally "born of the latitude"</term>. This occurs when the celestial latitude is large; however, if the latitude is small, it may be otherwise. || 6 ||

> Alternatively, the **true celestial latitude** <term>spaṣṭeṣu</term> is multiplied by the **equinoctial noon shadow** <term>akṣabhā</term> and divided by twelve <note>original: "ravi-hṛta" refers to division by 12, as the sun is associated with the number 12</note>. Or, multiply the latitude by the **sine of terrestrial latitude** <term>akṣajyā</term> and divide by the **cosine of latitude** <term>lambajyā</term>. The result is multiplied by the **radius** <term>tribhaguṇa</term> and divided by the **diurnal radius** <term>dyumaurvī</term>. The result is the correction in breath-lengths. || 7 ||

> For a planet in the northern or southern hemisphere, apply this to the **polar-corrected longitude** to find the **rising point** <term>udayākhya-lagna</term> using the direct or inverse method. If the latitude is northern, follow the direct order; if southern, the reverse. To find the **setting point** <term>asta-vilagna</term>, perform the calculation similarly but starting from the planet's position plus six signs <note>original: "bhārdhādhikāt", meaning adding half a circle or 180 degrees</note>. || 8 ||

One must calculate the ascensional differences for both the planet's true declination and its mean declination. If the true and mean declinations are in the same direction, then the difference between the two ascensional differences should be calculated.

If the directions are different, then take their sum. In this way, the **respiration-units** <term>asu; a unit of time equal to four seconds, representing one breath</term> that are produced should be known as **latitude-born units** <term>palodbhavāsu</term>. This method applies when the **celestial latitude** <term>śara</term> of a planet or a star is large.

When the latitude is small, the latitude-born units should be calculated through an alternative method:
The planet’s **true celestial latitude** <term>spaṣṭa-śara</term> is to be multiplied by the **terrestrial deflection** <term>akṣa-valana</term> and divided by the **cosine of terrestrial latitude** <term>lambajyā</term>. 

<margin>Alternatively, multiply by the equinoctial shadow and divide by twelve.</margin>

The result of this is then multiplied by the **radius** <term>trijyā</term> and divided by the **radius of the diurnal circle** <term>dyujyā</term>. The final result constitutes the latitude-born units. This is the alternative rule.

### Rules for Rising and Setting

Now, treating the planet (already corrected for polar visibility) as if it were the Sun, calculate the **rising point** <term>lagna</term> using those latitude-born units.
- If the planet's latitude is **southern** <term>yāmya</term>, calculate the **direct rising** <term>krama-vilagna</term>.
- If the latitude is **northern** <term>saumya</term>, calculate the **reverse rising** <term>viloma-lagna</term>.

When this is done, it yields the true rising point of the planet.

Next, to find the **setting point** <term>asta-lagna</term>, treat that same planet plus six signs <note>original: "sabhārdham"; adding 180 degrees to find the point diametrically opposite</note> as the Sun. Using the same units:
- For **northern** latitude, perform the direct rising calculation.
- For **southern** latitude, perform the reverse calculation.
This result is the planet's setting point.

### The Geometric Proof

Here is the proof <term>upapatti</term>:
In the celestial sphere, as far as the **celestial equator** <term>viṣuvan-maṇḍala</term> is depressed by the degrees of its own latitude, to that same extent the **six-o'clock circle** <term>unmaṇḍala</term> <note>The circle passing through the celestial poles and the east/west points of the horizon</note> rises above the horizon in the northern hemisphere and sinks below it in the southern hemisphere. Because a planet situated there moves toward elevation or depression by its own **ascensional difference units** <term>carārdhāsu</term>, the logic governing the ascensional difference is the same as that for these latitude-born units.

It follows that the number of units in the difference between the ascensional differences of the true and mean declinations is the same as the number of units produced by the latitude, because the difference between those two declinations is the celestial latitude itself. This applies when the directions are the same. 

When a large celestial latitude carries the declination into the opposite direction, then one part of the latitude is northern and the other is southern. Since the total latitude is the sum of these two parts, the latitude-born units will be the sum of the two ascensional differences produced by them. This is the case for a large latitude.

Suppose a planet is in the northern hemisphere and its latitude is also northern. The elevation of the planet due to its latitude—as influenced by the terrestrial latitude—is calculated by the **rule of three** <term>trairāśika</term>:
